en: The Sūtra of the Universal Extensiveness, Spoken by the Bodhisattva Descending from Tuṣita Heaven into His Mother’s Womb, Scroll One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Celestial Mansions (*Devakula-varga*). Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying between a pair of *śāla* trees to the north of the city of Kapilavastu, in the Śākya realm of Śuddhodana, intending to relinquish his physical life and enter *nirvāṇa*.

On the eighth day of the second month at midnight, he personally folded his saṃghāṭī, uttarāsaṅga, and antaravāsaka—each in three layers—and spread them within the golden coffin; he lay upon them with his body pressed against it, his feet overlapping one another.
He entrusted his alms bowl and mendicant’s staff to Ānanda by hand;

the eight great kings all brought five hundred pieces of white cotton cloth and sandalwood and *kālānusārī* incense, which they placed entirely within the golden coffin. They wrapped the golden coffin with five hundred pieces of cotton cloth, and then five hundred chariots carried fragrant sesame oil to pour over the white cotton.

At that time, the Great Brahma King stood on the right side with the assembly of Brahmās; Śakra Devānām Indra stood on the left side with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; and Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, along with the bodhisattvas of the ten directions endowed with supernormal powers, stood before him.
At that time, the World-Honored One desired to enter the Vajra-samādhi and shatter his body into śarīra relics. "Excellent!
This inconceivable Dharma turns this true Dharma within the Sahā world."
At that time, having formed this thought, the worlds of the ten directions all shook in six ways.
Then, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm from within the golden coffin and asked Ānanda:
"Has the bhikṣu Kāśyapa arrived yet?"
He replied, "It has not yet arrived.
The World-Honored One asked again:
"Has the Bhikṣu Gomaya arrived yet?
He replied, "He has attained parinirvāṇa in that heavenly realm; his three robes and alms bowl have arrived."
The Buddha addressed the fourfold assembly:
"I shall now enter final parinirvāṇa.
He then withdrew his cotton robe and entered the inner coffin, remaining silent and still.
After he had extended his hand in this manner two or three times for a brief moment,

the Buddha asked Ānanda and the fourfold assembly (bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās), as well as the eight great kings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and human and non-human beings: "What do you think?"
"Ānanda! Have you received all the Vaipulya Mahāyāna Mahācaryā Sūtras that I have taught from beginning to end? He replied:
"Only the Buddha knows this!
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"I preached the Dharma to my mother, Māyā, in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
do you know of this? He replied, "I do not know."

"How is it, Ānanda? When I preached the Dharma to the dragons in the dragon palace, I caused countless billions of dragon sons and others to attain the Way. I left behind a whole-body relic one thousand three hundred feet in height; do you know this as well?"
He replied, “I do not know. [The Buddha asked,] “In what way?”
Ānanda! While I was in my mother’s womb for ten months, I taught the bodhisattvas the inconceivable practices and the rare Dharma of non-retrogression; do you know of this as well?
He replied, "I do not know.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
I shall now distinguish for you, one by one, the rare and difficult-to-attain practices of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"One hundred and eleven million, one thousand, six hundred and twenty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* worlds to the southeast of here, there is a world named Sitala. Therein dwells a Buddha named Gandhārcis Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who has manifested parinirvāṇa there and has come to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace."

Having passed through countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he served thirty-six times as the Great Brahmā King, thirty-six times as Śakra, and thirty-six times as a Cakravartin King; the sentient beings he delivered never fell into the two vehicles or the various evil realms.
Why is this? It is because all are moved by the spiritual wisdom of the Buddhas. How so?
Ānanda! Does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, have a portion consisting of the womb?
Or does he not have a portion consisting of the womb?
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“The body of the Tathāgata is free from the nature of the womb.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If the Tathāgata has no fetal portion, how is it that the Tathāgata dwelt in the womb for ten months, teaching and preaching the Dharma?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“That which has a fetal portion is empty and quiescent; that which lacks a fetal portion is likewise empty and quiescent.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, manifested himself as sitting, reclining, and walking within the body of his mother, Māyā. He prepared a great high seat eighty *yojanas* in length and breadth, with stairways and railings of gold and silver; celestial silks and canopies hung in the void, while the sounds of singing and music were beyond measure.
Furthermore, by means of their supernormal powers, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered like clouds from eighteen thousand lands to the east of this Sahā world;
the same was true for the south, the west, the north, and the four intermediate directions.
Furthermore, sixty-two billion lands from the lower direction, with their bodhisattvas possessing supernatural powers, also came to the great assembly;
seventy-two billion bodhisattvas from the realm of space in the upper direction likewise gathered like clouds and entered the womb-chamber.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"These great bodhisattvas have gathered like clouds, desiring to hear from the World-Honored One the inconceivable dharmas: the various gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, the samādhi of the single mark, the samādhi of hearing emptiness, the samādhi of the nature of the path, the samādhi of reality, the samādhi of the king of space, the samādhi of the cessation of habitual tendencies, the samādhi of the nature of reception, the samādhi of the traces of practice, the samādhi of subduing Māra, and the samādhi of removing defilement—such samādhis numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas."
"Now, in what samādhi does the Tathāgata abide within the womb-palace to preach the inconceivable Dharma to the great bodhisattvas?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"Observe now: those at the first stage, the second stage, up to the tenth stage, and those in their final birth before Buddhahood—bodhisattvas from all directions shall each remain in their respective positions without confusing one another."
Why is this? Because I now wish to expound the inconceivable Dharma for these great beings.
This present assembly is pure and free from admixture; even those who dwell as branches and leaves are without defilement or evil.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a pure voice, spoke these verses:
"Throughout countless kalpas since the past, I have manifested innumerable Buddha-bodies;
Now again entering the womb, I desire to deliver all sentient beings."
With a body pure and free from evil conduct, Speech that is truthful and without falsehood,
And a mind always characterized by loving-kindness and compassion— This is the pure path of the Bodhisattva.
He takes pity on those classes of sentient beings Who dwell perpetually within the four rushing rivers.
Regarding the views of permanence and annihilation, one should dedicate them toward the path of Bodhi.
Having obtained this body through diligent toil, do not give rise to thoughts of impurity;
consider the body as a burial mound, where jackals lie in wait.
The fool is deeply stained by attachment, Indulging in craving and unable to let go;
This body is ungrateful, Day and night it seeks to devour.
With the nine sufferings as its bolt, It is like a painted jar filled with excrement.
Pressed by the thirst of desire, why do you give rise to suffering?
Like the ocean swallowing all streams, the fool takes it for treasure.
This body is not of the nature of a diamond; do not commit manifold evil deeds.
The body one has received must inevitably perish; why not swiftly practice the Path?
Even if a person were to live for a hundred million eons, they too would have to renounce desire;
how much more so when one's lifespan does not even reach a hundred years—why do you not know contentment?
The fool constantly proclaims to himself: "By virtue of past merit, I have obtained this body;
I ought to indulge myself in pleasure. Before my joy has ended, it shall come to its conclusion;
these desires lack solidity, and no one lacking wisdom can maintain them."
If a person wishes to abandon desire, they should contemplate the ten wisdoms and the state of non-conceptualization;
desire is not a true dharma, arising and ceasing like bubbles on water.
It is created by a magician, manifesting as various forms.
The fool deems it real, yet though he seeks the real, nothing is found.
Emptiness is empty by its very nature; from beginning to end, there is no arising or ceasing.
Through the non-conceptualization of the state of non-perception, one can exhaust the outflows of sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, you should now know!
In the assemblies of the ten directions that are free from outflows,
I have entered the lapis lazuli samādhi and extensively expounded the Vaipulya Dharma.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are no different from what I have said:
out of compassion for these multitudes of beings who dwell eternally in houses of blazing fire,
they pass from one womb to another, going there and returning here again and again.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, Having accumulated practices for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
Though they dwell within the Sahā world, Amidst the kalpas of the five sufferings and five afflictions—
Just as my own worlds in the ten directions Are compared to this land.
Wandering through the five realms of existence, one undergoes suffering most severe here;

yet, understanding emptiness as having no fixed characteristics and likewise no fundamental limit, one realizes the ultimate meaning of the single characteristic: that by nature it is inherently void and tranquil.
Constantly contemplating that there is neither arising nor ceasing, whether with remainder or without remainder;
by my former great vows, I have undergone the wombs of the five destinies—
among those born of transformation, moisture, eggs, and wombs— and have likewise preached the Dharma that is difficult to encounter.
To those attached to the five aggregates, he teaches that nothing exists;
The twelvefold chain of dependent origination is the root of deluded wandering in birth and death.
For those fallen into the four inversions, he teaches the four truths.
The Truth of Suffering has no ultimate reality; the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are likewise so!
Desire, self, precepts, views, and grasping—these, along with the four types of craving—are analyzed as being of the nature of reality: they are empty, non-existent, quiescent, and essential.
Though he has crossed to the far shore of birth and death, he does not abide in nirvana;
now dwelling within a mother’s womb, he preaches the Dharma to awaken all living beings.
Within this Sahā world-system, there are as many worlds as there are sands in countless Ganges Rivers.
Preaching the Dharma while dwelling in the womb, he delivers and saves incalculable beings (*asaṃkhyeya*).
As the realms of empty space are boundless, so too are the Buddha-lands;
sentient beings receive their consciousness-mind (*vijñāna*), yet their true natures differ.
Those transformed by clear wisdom are delivered according to their respective types;
some are delivered upon seeing the Buddha’s body, while others attain liberation by hearing his voice.
Others again contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path to its end.
Contemplating the four foundations of mindfulness, One cuts off [afflictions] through the four bases of power.
The five faculties and the five powers, With the seven factors of enlightenment as its flowers;
The noble eightfold path Is used to adorn the body.
Discriminating that self and other are empty, one possesses the wisdom of signlessness and cessation;
having no desire for anything sought, one dwells forever in the wisdom of emptiness and non-existence.
First entering the meditative concentration with perception, one practices the thirty contemplations on impurity.
Inverting and following, one knows there is vitarka; entering meditative absorption, one understands there is no vicāra.
Entering the first dhyāna through nine successive stages, one discerns the absence of both vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, delighting in the path of cessation, the first dhyāna does not consist of the five dharmas.
When joy and pleasure have ceased in the mind, one enters the four dharmas with peace and security.
The great beings of supernormal wisdom do not take this as their practice;
because of the various afflictions, they should instead adapt themselves to sentient beings.
Having practiced meditative concentration through kalpas, his form withered like dry wood;
yet, perfumed by the fragrance of the third dhyāna, the five branches do not fall away.
The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable; it exists within existence, yet it is not existent.
In unsurpassed, most perfect enlightenment, there is neither birth-and-death nor non-existence.
Since I attained Buddhahood, I have wandered and observed within the third dhyāna;
had I entered the fourth dhyāna, I would have attained liberation through silence.
I contemplate the realm of empty space; sentient beings have no support.
Only through the power and wisdom of the Buddhas can one exhaustively reach its original source.
Those practitioners who have severed the outflows are not yet able to discern it all completely.
The categories of the Path are profoundly subtle, beyond the reach of the two vehicles.
With my divine eye, my wisdom eye, and my Buddha-eye,
I observe the forms received by the four consciousnesses, and likewise transform within them.
There is likewise no earth, water, or fire, nor any form or color to be perceived;
yet by the Buddha’s great supernormal power, all are brought to the further shore.
In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and beyond measure,
they likewise dwell within the realm of empty space by virtue of the foundation of the wisdom of the Way.
Even if one were to use the physical eye to observe the sentient beings within the realm of empty space;
In the inhalations and exhalations of the breath, countless sentient beings enter;
at that time, these multitudes each attain the traces of the Path.
One should know that the Buddha’s Dharma-body is truly inconceivable.
The Buddha is the general of the three realms, Compassionately rescuing all beings;
Within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, He causes them to receive the realization of the wisdom of the Path.
He is likewise free from lust, anger, and the host of delusions;
upon seeing his form, one immediately enters the Path—what need is there for those in training or those beyond training?
In immeasurable Buddha-fields, the attainments of enlightenment differ from one another;
some are achieved through conceptual thought, while others are achieved through non-conceptual thought.
They no longer practice this—this suchness and the Four Noble Truths.
The Bodhisattva’s pure contemplation enters the unimpeded path of dhyāna;
the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas enter meditative absorption each in their own distinct way.
If birth after birth is not seen as birth, how could there ever be a fundamental source of birth?
Foolish and deluded people, stained by attachment, claim that birth is the self;
they speak of "I" and "mine," yet do not perceive that there is a self.
The practice of the four dhyānas of a bodhisattva is something even pratyekabuddhas do not know.
When the Bodhisattva enters the first dhyāna, there are thirty untainted practices and one hundred and seven samādhi concentrations, complete with the regulation of inhalation and exhalation.
In the second dhyāna, there are seventy-two; he personally contemplates the mark of non-self.
Though undergoing suffering for successive kalpas, he does not depart from the practice of dhyāna;
having severed all outflows through the four abodes, he attains this second dhyāna.
Because of the sixth abode, he remains hesitant; his entry into samādhi is like the ripples upon water.
Even with eighty-four thousand practices, one still cannot restrain oneself.
Originally, while at the sixth stage, I regressed for twelve kalpas;
constantly giving rise to thoughts of pleasure, I wandered through the abyss of birth and death.
The Great Sage Dīpaṃkara Buddha prophesied that his mind was firm and steadfast, and that he would not retreat from his resolve; thus he attained the third dhyāna.
Having severed seventy thousand defilements, they were forever extinguished without root.
With the fearless stride of a lion, you proclaim the great Dharma scriptures;
you travel extensively through the buddha-fields, constantly paying homage, serving, and making offerings.
To all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past incalculable eons—
Each, within their own original lands, vows to perform the work of a Buddha;
though their minds never regress, they always fear falling into inferior states.
Even with billions of demonic hordes, not a single hair can be moved.
Transcending the eight stages of practice, one enters into Bodhi.
Regarding that which is delightful and cherished, one forever eliminates it through the absence of conceptual thought;
with the exception of the venerable teacher and one's parents, one feels no attachment to anything else.
Thus completing one stage of dhyāna practice, it is named the Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā).
Cultivating peerless contemplation, it is the foundation of the penetrating wisdom of the ninth stage;
no longer entering the state of cessation, he shifts his seat and immediately attains Buddhahood.
For the sake of sentient beings, he proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree;
extending far to asankhyeyas [of worlds], they all gathered together at the site of enlightenment.
From the immeasurable realms of the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise assembled.
Each one extends his right hand: "Excellent, O Great Lion!
Possessing the ten powers and fearlessness, you have entered the four dhyānas with steadfastness;
out of compassion for all living beings, we pray that you will quickly awaken from meditation."
Those not yet crossed, I shall cause to cross; those not yet liberated, I shall cause to be liberated.
Dwelling in the darkness of the four bases of consciousness, they thirst for the flavor of dhyāna-joy;
failing to comprehend the teachings of the Buddhas, they immediately begin to praise themselves.
Again, he reflects within himself: "Why do I labor with this body?
Having brought it to an end in nirvana, why should I strive to deliver sentient beings?
Then the Buddhas each appear before him and say: "Excellent!"
Śākyamuni! Establish your mind of great vows; do not give rise to thoughts of retreat.
Turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and beat the great drum of the Dharma.
Those who hear it are swiftly liberated, Without passing through the hardships of kalpas.
Swift wisdom, unimpeded wisdom, Discerning wisdom, penetrating wisdom,
Wisdom of the path, wisdom of clear insight, Wisdom of cessation, wisdom of non-arising.
The wisdom of non-arising, exhaustion, and cessation; the wisdom of elimination, the nine successive stages, and the fearless lion’s wisdom;
the wisdom of the thunderous roar, the wisdom of sitting unmoving, and the wisdom of great compassion without obstruction.
The wisdom of the adornment of the physical marks; The wisdom of compassionately protecting others by uprooting suffering;
The wisdom of the liberation from bondage through the untying of knots; The wisdom of receiving distinctions and attaining realization;
The wisdom of subduing Māra and destroying his armies; The wisdom of achieving freedom from the conceit of "I."
The wisdom of courageous and diligent effort; the wisdom of giving without expecting recompense;
the wisdom of practicing patience and enduring insults; the wisdom of the ten powers as firm as a diamond;
the wisdom of remaining unmoved throughout the kalpas; and the wisdom of gathering and harmonizing the multitude.
The wisdom of the supreme guide; the wisdom of the robes of shame and remorse;
the wisdom of the bodhisattva’s vow; the wisdom of the miraculous manifestations of the bases of power;
the wisdom of unimpeded spheres of activity; and the wisdom that severs the mind and extinguishes the fetters.
The wisdom of pure illumination, The wisdom of knowing one's own past lives,
The profound wisdom of knowing the minds of others, The truly pure wisdom regarding one's parents,
The wisdom of manifesting bodies throughout all lands, And the wisdom of remaining undefiled while dwelling in the womb.
The wisdom of consciousness that is never distracted; The wisdom of single-minded faith and acceptance;
The wisdom of entering meditative concentration to observe; The wisdom of discerning the characteristics of the body;
The wisdom of the thirty kinds of impurity; The wisdom that extinguishes calamities and eliminates afflictions.
The sequential wisdom of the bodhisattva, The transcendent wisdom of teaching and transforming,
The wisdom that extinguishes the twelve links of dependent origination, The wisdom realized at the time of the pratyekabuddha,
The wisdom of receiving transformation through hearing the voice, And the wisdom that emerges from the twelve bases.
The wisdom of unimpeded observation, the wisdom of profound discernment that receives the Way,
the wisdom that regards a single night as an eon, the wisdom that regards an eon as a single day,
the wisdom of mindfulness of the Buddha such that the Buddha appears, and the wisdom of the purity of buddha-lands.
The wisdom that has no second vehicle, the wisdom that walks alone without fear,
the wisdom that delights the minds of the multitude, the wisdom that has already accomplished what was to be done,
the wisdom that constructs neither before nor after, and the wisdom that is newless because of cessation.
"The wisdom that enters meditative absorption and eliminates conceptualization, the wisdom that contemplates the body internally and externally,
the Tathāgata’s wisdom of receiving insight, and the wisdom of the noble ones’ silence. At that time,

when the World-Honored One spoke these verses, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of immeasurable sentient beings all set their minds upon the path and established themselves on the ground of perfect faith.

Furthermore, there were twelve nayutas of bodhisattvas on the stage of contemplative practice who did not abide in the three dwellings; they perfected their buddha-lands within the right division, and seventy-seven billion sentient beings attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
The Buddha again addressed Mañjuśrī:
"At present, there is not a single person on these seats who is defiled by impurities or evil, nor anyone who regresses. Why is this so?

All of them possessed sharp faculties; they did not dwell in birth-and-death, being without bondage, without attachment, without cessation, and without arising. Having purified their cultivation of the path, they achieved realization and were eager to hear the inconceivable True Dharma of the Buddhas, so as to subdue all Māras and eliminate arrogance.
Externally, although he teaches and transforms incalculable sentient beings across all Buddha-fields, internally his mind sports within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
These samādhis are: the Lion’s Boundless Prowess Samādhi, the Transcendent Progression to the Stage Samādhi, and the Vast Advancement and Transcendent Step Samādhi.
...the Samādhi of the Joy of the Childlike Truth of Dharma, the Samādhi of the Arising and Ceasing of the Four Paths, the Samādhi of Non-conceptual Equal Practice,
the Samādhi of Proceeding to the Irreversible Bodhimanda, the Samādhi of Contemplating the Minds of All Beings,
the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Stage of One Life Remaining [before Buddhahood], the Samādhi of Formlessness, the Samādhi of Emerging from the Earth, and the Samādhi of Liberation...
The Samādhi of Binding Combat, the Samādhi of Receiving the Supreme at the Crown, the Samādhi of Beings Delighting in Seeing, the Samādhi of Entering the Inconceivable,
the Samādhi of the Inconceivable Buddha-realm, the Samādhi of the Inconceivable Purification of Defilements in the Dharma-realm,
the Samādhi of the Inconceivable Holy Assembly, and the Samādhi of the Inconceivable Arising and Ceasing of Sentient Beings.
The Samādhi of the Arising and Descending of Dragon-Power Inconceivability; the Samādhi of the Inconceivable King Among the Multitude;
the Samādhi of the Inconceivable Valiant Subjugation of Enemies; the Samādhi of Inconceivable Immeasurable Life-Span;
the Samādhi of the Inconceivable Ability to Voluntarily Undergo Suffering Within the Five Paths; and the Manifestation of All Buddhas.
In the inconceivable samādhi and the inconceivable samādhi of the fourfold offerings,
his body was adorned with ten billion one hundred million such samādhis.

Furthermore, there is the one named Swift, who in a single day left home to practice the Way, went beneath a tree to attain Buddhahood, taught and transformed sentient beings, purified Buddha-lands, and attained inconceivable samādhi.

Furthermore, there is the inconceivable samādhi of remaining to await conditions. By relying on this samādhi, the Tathāgata dwells for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas so that sentient beings with whom he has a karmic connection may attain liberation in the realm of nirvana without remainder; rather than entering nirvana himself, he continues to create causes and conditions to practice the bodhisattva path.

Furthermore, there is the inconceivable samādhi of the Buddha’s power, by which one travels from one buddha-field to another in the time it takes a person to snap their fingers while joining their palms, bestowing predictions of enlightenment upon immeasurable and limitless sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
he also causes them all to attain Buddhahood in a single day.
"Such is the supernatural power of the Bodhisattva while dwelling in the womb.

**Chapter Two: On Walking** At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

The Tathāgata has preached the inconceivable Dharma. Now, within this assembly, there are those who have followed the tracks and those who have not; there are those who abide in the stage of faith and those who do not; and there are Bodhisattvas from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Vṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, up to the Ekotika Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; or there are Bodhisattvas from the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
How, then, can he enter their wombs to teach and transform them?
The World-Honored One said:
"Do not ask such a question. Why is this?"
The Tathāgata never speaks of this meaning.
I now ask you; you should answer me:
Maitreya, does emptiness possess a physical form or is it formless?
He replied, "No,
World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said:
“Maitreya, how is it so?
If emptiness is formless and without substance, how can sentient beings undergo birth, aging, illness, and death?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the ultimate sense, there is no birth, aging, illness, or death; for this reason, they are empty and devoid of form or substance.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"If they are devoid of form and substance, who among these sentient beings receives the prediction of enlightenment?"
Who is it that receives the prediction of enlightenment?
How does a bodhisattva approach the foot of a tree, sometimes walking in meditation (caṅkrama) and sometimes entering into meditative concentration (samādhi)?
How does a bodhisattva contemplate the physical marks of his own body and contemplate the physical marks of others' bodies?
How is it that a bodhisattva manifests the walking of seven steps and proclaims his own attainment of Buddhahood and subjugation of the māras?
How is it that a bodhisattva prepares the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and summons all sentient beings from the ten directions?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:

"This too is empty and quiescent, without form and without substance; even the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are merely provisional designations, and even down to the single ultimate meaning, all are empty and non-existent."
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya:
“How does a bodhisattva who practices emptiness travel to the buddha-fields of the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Bodhisattva who practices emptiness does not perceive lands, nor does he perceive Buddhas.
Since the Buddha himself is no Buddha, how could there be a Buddha?
The elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and consciousness, as well as self, person, and life-span, are all entirely empty and quiescent; for this reason, there is no state of gestation.”
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"While you were in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven teaching the Dharma of the practice of emptiness to the devas and humans, was there any trace of footprints left behind in that assembly?"
"Is there no trace to be followed?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Those devas and humans constantly conceive notions of permanence, notions of pleasure, notions of purity, and reckon the self as 'I. Because of this, there is no trace to be followed, nor is there a lack of a trace to be followed."

The Buddha again addressed Maitreya: “Do those devas and humans have the aggregate of formative action with form and the aggregate of formative action without form; the aggregate of retribution and the aggregate without retribution; the aggregate of breaking through existence and the aggregate of not breaking through existence; the aggregate of receptivity and the aggregate without receptivity; the aggregate of sound and resonance and the aggregate without sound and resonance; the intermediate aggregate and the aggregate without the intermediate; the aggregate of this and that and the aggregate without this and that; the ultimate aggregate and the aggregate without the ultimate; and the aggregate of silence and the aggregate without silence?”
"How is this so, Maitreya?
While you were in the celestial palace preaching the True Dharma to the devas and humans, did you say that these aggregates (skandhas) have such names and designations?"
Maitreya said to the Buddha,
“There is none.
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you say,
Maitreya? Have the Buddhas of the ten directions bestowed upon you the prediction that you shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment?"
"Is there a true and correct path, or is there no true and correct path?
Maitreya replied, "There is none!"
The World-Honored One said:
"The 'One who possesses the Way' is likewise a provisional designation.
To speak of 'Maitreya' is also a provisional designation; suchness, intrinsic nature, and the original limit are also provisional designations."

The Tathāgata’s form-body has a body that is itself empty in nature, and its characteristics are themselves empty; from beginning to end it is empty, and from this to that it is empty. How can you know for yourself that you have received the prediction of becoming Maitreya?

“Words are empty by their very nature; existence is empty by its own nature; non-existence is empty by its own nature. Non-existence is eternally abiding; there is nothing that can cause it not to abide. Abiding is empty by its own nature; self-characteristics are empty by their own characteristics. The aggregates are empty by their own nature; the womb is empty by its own nature; and so on, up to the site of enlightenment, where practice is empty by the nature of the aggregate of practice.”
"For this reason, World-Honored One,
there is neither a track to be trodden nor a track not to be trodden!
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya:
"Are there those who follow the tracks and those who do not follow the tracks?
Are there those with the realization of the fruit and those without the realization of the fruit?
Is this the nature of the conditioned or the nature of the unconditioned?"
Is it the unconditioned nature within the conditioned?
Is it the unconditioned nature within the unconditioned?
Is it the untainted nature within the tainted?
Is this the nature of outflowlessness within the state of being without outflows?
Is this the nature of exhaustion within the desire realm?
Or is it the nature of non-exhaustion within the desire realm?
Is there a nature of exhaustion within the realm of form and the formless realm?
Is there a nature of non-exhaustion within the realm of form and the formless realm?
Is the realm of space the nature of the cessation of consciousness?
Is this realm of emptiness not the nature of the cessation of consciousness?

And so on, up to: are conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, intrinsic emptiness, the emptiness of existence by means of existence, the emptiness of non-existence by means of non-existence, great emptiness, the emptiness of grasping, the emptiness of the single characteristic and the signless, the emptiness of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and the emptiness of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*—are these the nature of practice?
"Is it not the practice of the nature?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"One practices both the Dharma and non-Dharma; yet non-Dharma is also not practiced."
“What do you think, Maitreya?
Conditioned phenomena are not unconditioned, and unconditioned phenomena are not conditioned.”
How so? You say: "There is practice regarding dharmas that are subject to practice, and there is also practice regarding dharmas that are not subject to practice."
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Within the dharmas of both having marks and being without marks—the ultimate primary meaning—is one seeking the conditioned not the unconditioned, and seeking the unconditioned not the conditioned?”
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
“I now ask you: regarding the discourse on the true root rather than the groundless discourse, from what do the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) arise?”
"What is its name?
Maitreya addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The nature of emptiness and quiescence—its characters, meanings, and names are all not real; this is a discourse without basis, not a discourse with basis."
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"What is the meaning of 'roots,' and how does one give rise to the discourse on the absence of roots?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the conventional sense, the faculties (*indriya*) are the dharma-nature; the absence of faculties is the realization. It is quiescent and immobile, yet not non-mobile; it is a single characteristic and yet without characteristics. This extends to all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas, resistant and non-resistant dharmas, material and immaterial dharmas, visible and invisible dharmas—neither abiding nor non-abiding: this is the meaning of the absence of faculties."
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!"

The Bodhisattva of Emptiness clearly understands that there is no root; it neither arises nor does it not arise. It has no counterpart in the future, does not abide in the present, and has already ceased in the past. It is without attachment and without cessation, neither abiding nor not abiding.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Vibhaktakāyadarśana who addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now I have heard the Tathāgata speak on the meaning of rootlessness, speak of the existence of bodily marks and the non-existence of bodily marks, and speak of the existence of self-nature emptiness and the non-existence of self-nature emptiness.
As for this teaching on the meaning of rootlessness, does it arise from suchness?"
Does it not come from suchness?
Regarding the meaning of being without roots: is there arising and ceasing, or is there no arising and ceasing?
Is it a dharma with resistance, or a dharma without resistance?
Are they material phenomena or immaterial phenomena?
Are they conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena?
Are they tainted phenomena or untainted phenomena?
"Is there the dharma of having marks, or the dharma of being markless?
Is there contemplation of the body, or is there no contemplation of the body?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Contemplating the Body:
"What is the body? What is contemplation? Who is it that performs this contemplation of the body?"
The Bodhisattva Vibhaṅgakāyadṛṣṭi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Earth, water, fire, and wind are called the aggregates of the body;
the discernment of consciousness is called contemplation.”

The Buddha told him: "One says 'earth,' yet earth is empty of itself; one says 'water,' yet water is empty of itself; one says 'fire,' yet fire is empty of itself; one says 'wind,' yet wind is empty of itself; one says 'consciousness,' yet consciousness is empty of itself; one says 'emptiness,' yet emptiness is empty of itself."
"What is this body?
How is it to be contemplated?
The Bodhisattva Śarīrapratyavekṣaṇā addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the Buddha has taught, the dharma-realm and empty space are both entirely void and quiescent; there is no Buddha, yet one speaks of a Buddha; there is no Dharma, yet one speaks of the Dharma; there is no Sangha, yet one speaks of the Sangha; there is neither this world nor the world beyond; there is neither sin nor merit. Is this not the same as [the views of] the Great Teacher?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Vibhaṅgakāyadarśin:
"When you enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), do you perceive the eye observing forms, or even the mind observing mental phenomena?"
The Bodhisattva Śarīrapratyavekṣaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying: “No,
World-Honored One!”
"Why is this? Because within the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), there is neither arising nor ceasing.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Kāyānupaśyin:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.
When the eye perceives forms, those forms are not my forms, and I am not those forms;..."
Consciousness is not my consciousness, and I am not that consciousness.
This applies likewise to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects: mental objects are not my mental objects, and I am not those mental objects.
In the meaning of rootlessness, there is neither increase nor decrease; the purity of the faculties is also purity, the emptiness of marks is purity, and even ultimate emptiness is likewise purity.
It is one and non-dual; as the five aggregates are pure and their conduct is pure, the Path is also pure.
As the realm of resistance is pure and the realm of non-resistance is pure, form is pure, and the Path is also pure.
When a bodhisattva contemplates that the six sense objects are pure, the Path is also pure.
When the retinue is pure and the nature is pure, the Path is also pure.
When the stages are pure and the abiding is pure, the Path is also pure.
"This is the meaning of the rootlessness of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Śarīradarśana, saying:
"Suffering is pure; neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is pure; the Path is also pure."
"The purity of the gate, the purity of the lineage, and the purity of birth—through these, the Path is also pure.
This is the meaning of 'rootlessness' for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Śarīradarśana:

“The purity of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the purity of the buddha-field, and the purity of sentient beings—such that the path is also pure: this is the meaning of the ‘rootless’ for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The purity of the faculties (*indriya*), the purity of the powers (*bala*), the purity of the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the purity of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)—the path is also pure.”
"How so? Bodhisattva Śarīrapratyavekṣaka!
I now ask you; you should answer me."

When the Tathāgata cultivates the site of enlightenment and sits beneath the king of trees, how does he distinguish among the classes of sentient beings by means of determinate dharmas or indeterminate dharmas?

Dharmas that are determinate are the defilement of afflictions; dharmas that are indeterminate are likewise the defilement of afflictions. By means of what indeterminate state could one bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon sentient beings?
The Bodhisattva Śarīradarśana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Dharmas that are determinate are not afflictions; dharmas that are indeterminate are likewise not afflictions. Why is this?"

The defilements of worldly toil are base and lowly dharmas, whereas dharmas that are determinate or indeterminate are supreme and noble dharmas; one should not equate the indeterminate with the defilements of worldly toil. Why is this?
"The dharmas of worldly affliction are the lineage of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Śarīradarśana: "Stop, stop!"
"Do not speak these words.
You previously stated that the afflictions are the dharmas of birth and death; now you further claim they are the seeds of the Tathāgata?
Bodhisattva Śarīradarśana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is the body of the Tathāgata a transformation-body and not that of a sentient being?
If it were a transformation-body, there would be no afflictions or the destinies of sentient beings.
If the body of the Tathāgata arises from sentient beings, then are the defilements of affliction not the seed of the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Kāyānupaśyin: "So it is, so it is!
It is just as you have said."
"It is through provisional designations and names that there is affliction; within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no affliction.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Śarīradarśana:

“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, constantly uses his divine eye to observe the mental consciousnesses and thoughts of incalculable beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions. He knows those with a preponderance of desire and those with little desire; those with a preponderance of anger and those with little anger; those with a preponderance of delusion and those with little delusion; those whose minds are liberated and those whose minds are not liberated; those who possess overweening pride and those who do not; and those for whom the ultimate goal is easily reached and those for whom it is difficult. The Bodhisattva fully knows and observes them all, and proceeds to deliver them.”
How does a bodhisattva, through the observation of the divine eye, know those who have few desires and those who have many desires?

In this regard, the bodhisattva appears among that assembly in the form of a courtesan and speaks to them of sexual desire, such that its pleasure is difficult to forget and one never tires of gazing upon her.

He causes their desires to give rise to even greater joy and pleasure; subsequently, he gradually teaches them that the body is defiled, impermanent, non-self, suffering, empty, and not a self, and that desire is like a fiery pit that burns and cooks the consciousness, thereby inducing in them a sense of weary revulsion so that they become free from lustful desire.
These sentient beings, while still within the womb, receive the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Bodhisattva Śarīrapratyavekṣaṇa! You should know this:
such sentient beings, free from hatred and delusion, sever desire and attain the Way.

"Or there may be a bodhisattva who, among that assembly, acts as a virtuous friend and tells them that the karmic retribution for killing is a pleasure difficult to forget, saying, 'How joyful it is to kill! It diminishes your lifespan and increases my lifespan. Later, he gradually teaches them that the transgression of killing brings extremely heavy punishment, and explains that the grave sin of the hundred-and-eightfold killing is suffering and affliction. He leads them to enter the restraint of the Path, becoming free from desire and delusion, such that they accomplish the Unsurpassed Way even within the womb."

"Or there may be a bodhisattva who, among that assembly, acts as a friend and speaks of the ten unwholesome paths, teaching what is unwholesome through body, speech, and mind; taking the true to be false, the impermanent to be permanent, the empty to be substantial, the selfless to be having a self, suffering to be happiness, and the worldless to be having a world. Later, he gradually teaches them vast and profound wisdom and immeasurable eloquence, kindling the Dharma, blazing with the Dharma to erect the banner of the Dharma, and gradually leading them into the grove of wisdom, saying:
'O people, you should know!'"
"If there be those who harbor doubts regarding me, I shall burn away their doubting minds with the fire of wisdom.

If a person gives a gift while holding wealth in hand, and there is one who receives it, and they both understand that these three factors are empty and non-existent, they shall immediately attain the Unsurpassed Way within the womb.

"If one sees a person who upholds the precepts, who has perfected the category of morality without transgressing even a hair's breadth, and who understands that all things are empty, quiescent, and non-existent, such a person shall achieve the Unsurpassed Way even while in the womb."

"There may be sentient beings whose minds of patience do not arise; yet if someone comes to kill or dismember them, their minds harbor no thought of resentment, and they cherish nothing—not even their head, eyes, marrow, or brain—and thus they achieve the Unsurpassed Way even while in the womb."
"If there are sentient beings whose minds are like adamant, indestructible and unbreakable, and someone were to address them with gentle words of persuasion:

'The kalpas are immeasurable; wandering through birth and death is difficult to escape. Why not simply liberate yourself here, rather than laboring in vain toil for the sake of those other sentient beings? "
The Bodhisattva’s mind advances with resolve, never regressing or falling back into the cycle of birth and death; thus, he attains the Unsurpassed Way even within the womb.

If a person practices dhyāna such that their consciousness does not waver, then even if the evil Māra Pāpīyān roars like thunder and flashes like lightning from the midst of space, he cannot move so much as a single hair on that person’s body, let alone cause them to retreat from the path of dhyāna; thus, they attain the Unsurpassed Way even within the womb.

"If there are sentient beings who discriminate among various conditioned phenomena, thinking 'this may be practiced' and 'this may not be practiced,' and those who are greedily attached to and delight in the body, I shall immediately preach for them the Dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). I shall analyze each and every essential treasury of the dharmas and eloquently expound the immeasurable realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), whereby they shall attain the Unsurpassed Way even while in the womb."

"Or there may be a bodhisattva who enters the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), pervading the sentient beings of worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of infinite, immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya Ganges Rivers, feeling compassion and affection for them, desiring to bring them to liberation;

just as if one were to take a single grain of sand from within the sands of the Ganges and drop that grain in a land beyond as many Ganges-sands of worlds, such that the grains of sand of the Ganges are exhausted while the mind of loving-kindness is not, so too is the bodhisattva’s resolve firm and unshakable."

Suppose someone were to come and take pieces from the Bodhisattva’s body, cutting them off one by one, such that they immediately fill the trichiliocosm; yet his blood would transform into milk as if a mother were thinking of her child. This is the Bodhisattva practicing the Samādhi of Loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), whereby he attains the Unsurpassed Way even within the womb.

"At times, a Bodhisattva enters the Samādhi of Compassion and pervades the infinite, immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the southern direction—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—with sentient beings of every kind, feeling compassion for them and desiring their liberation.

Taking a single grain of sand from among the sands of the Ganges and placing it in a world-system beyond as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, he continues in this manner until all the sands of the Ganges are exhausted, yet his compassionate heart is not exhausted; he is capable of undergoing suffering on behalf of those sentient beings.

All of this arises from the Bodhisattva’s firm vow. When sentient beings see him, they do so with a pure mind; having distanced themselves from all evils and severed their deluded thoughts, they attain the Unsurpassed Way even while in the womb."

"At times, a Bodhisattva enters the Samādhi of Joy (*muditā-samādhi*) and pervades the sentient beings of infinite, immeasurable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands in the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Cherishing these beings with joy, he desires to bring them to liberation. Taking a single grain of sand from among the sands of the Ganges and placing it one grain beyond every Ganges-sand [of worlds], he continues until all the sands of the Ganges are exhausted, yet his joyful mind remains undiminished. If those beings enter into this joy and find delight within it, it is entirely due to the Bodhisattva’s firm resolve; thus, even while still in the womb, they achieve the Unsurpassed Way."

“Furthermore, there may be bodhisattvas who enter the *śamatha-samādhi* and pervade the sentient beings of the northern direction—limitless, immeasurable, and incalculable as the sands of the Ganges. Fearing that those beings might have deficient or leaking conduct, they nurture and protect them so that they do not sink into ruin. Taking a single grain of sand from among the sands of the Ganges and placing it in a land beyond as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they continue in this manner until all the sands of the Ganges are exhausted, yet their mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) is never exhausted. All of this is due to the firmness of the bodhisattvas’ vows; thus, they attain the Unsurpassed Way even while in the womb.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva cultivated the light of the true Dharma through great kindness and great compassion—a practice not shared by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas—which pervaded the four quarters. He desired that whenever sentient beings heard his voice, he would arrive immediately upon hearing it; this was due to the firmness of the Bodhisattva’s vows, whereby he attained the Unsurpassed Way even while within the womb.

3. Chapter on the Noble Truths. In the *Bodhisattva’s Womb Sūtra*, Chapter Three: The Noble Truths. The Buddha addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, manuṣyas, and amanuṣyas, saying:
“I shall now, for your sake, expound the noble truths of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well! Why is that?

For incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have cultivated the fruits of the Path; passing away from here and being born there, I have circled through the five realms of existence without ever abandoning the noble truths of the Bodhisattvas.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the Noble Truths?

At times, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, a bodhisattva practices the unimpeded dharma, refrains from taking formal realization through the dhyānas, and extinguishes all evil conceptions.

Alternatively, there may be a bodhisattva who, upon entering the stage of the first dhyāna, perceives pure conduct and, feeling ashamed and weary of it, abandons it to advance further, desiring to ascend to the sixth stage while diligently applying himself to his practice.
"Entering the stage of the second dhyāna, his mind suddenly awakened like the moon when clouds have cleared; he observed within himself and made a vow:
'Is this firm? Or is it not firm?'"
Using his own mind, he further observed the minds of sentient beings, fully knowing those who were easy to deliver and those who were difficult to deliver.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with immense joy, thinking:
"I shall certainly attain Buddhahood; of this there is no doubt."
The buddha-field is purified, the defilements of sentient beings are removed, Māra is subdued, and the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma of the noble ones is turned.
How joyful is this karmic reward; all that was wished for has been accomplished.

At that time, the Bodhisattva entered the concentration of non-distraction; with his mind he raised his mind, and with his body he raised his body, thereby immediately accomplishing the noble path of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). He traveled from one Buddha-field to another, paying homage to, serving, and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. He listened to and received the profound Dharma without difficulty or fear, and further entered the third dhyāna, observing that all forms and appearances are entirely empty and non-existent.

“Abiding in the third dhyāna, one observes the various classes of sentient beings and is able to discern them all: how they pass away from there and are born here, or pass away from here and are born there; one personally knows past lives and likewise knows the origins from which others have come—whether they belong to the Kṣatriya caste, the Brāhmaṇa caste, the householder caste, or the merchant caste; who among them are those who should practice and who should not; who are destined to receive the fruit and who are not; their inhalations and exhalations, and those who do not inhale or exhale; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the bases of spiritual power, the factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path;
and one fully knows that such a person has received the prediction [of Buddhahood] and will attain enlightenment among certain sentient beings in a certain country and at a certain place.
This is called the Bodhisattva attaining a pure mind in the stage of the third dhyāna.”

"Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, from the stage of the Third Dhyāna, gazes toward the Eighth Abode, though he gazes, he does not yet attain it. Day and night he exerts himself with diligent vigor, seeking the pure mind, and enters the Fourth Dhyāna. There, he beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions face-to-face, who preach for him the Dharma of non-retrogression regarding the Fourth Dhyāna.

Through unimpeded liberation, he practices the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*): he can divide one body into countless bodies, and merge countless bodies back into one. He enters the Fire-Light Samādhi, which fills the trichiliocosm, causing those sentient beings to see the Fire-Light Samādhi; their hearts are struck with awe and the hair on their bodies stands on end, so that they come of their own accord to take refuge at the Bodhisattva’s dwelling, attaining liberation through the power of that samādhi."

At that time, while within the fourth dhyāna, he discerned the *tathatā* and *dharmatā* of the world; his mind then regressed, and he fell back into practicing the six stages of abiding. The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"I have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression."
"How shall one attain the eight stages? Thus, within the four dhyānas, they practice with diligent application; they purify the conduct of sentient beings and take upon themselves their suffering.

Although they practice this Dharma, they do not praise themselves; they eliminate arrogance and possess no sense of self. They cultivate the six recollections, and though they walk the path while dwelling among the nine abodes of sentient beings, their minds are not stained by or attached to birth and death. Their minds awaken suddenly and clearly, attaining the stage of non-retrogression.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attaining a pure mind regarding the Noble Truths.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva enters the Samādhi of the Sphere of Emptiness and contemplates the mental consciousness of the various classes of sentient beings within this trichiliocosm. Cultivating pure dharmas, he becomes free from bondage and attachment, having no lingering desires; he is able to dwell in his own life-span for one kalpa, two kalpas, up to incalculable kalpas, teaching and transforming sentient beings within those specific kalpas.
The one who is born and the one who passes away are gradually guided toward the attainment of the path of purity; thus, within the womb, they accomplish the unsurpassed way.

At times, the Bodhisattva enters the *vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi* and contemplates the destination of the consciousness-principle (*vijñāna*) throughout this trichiliocosm—whether it proceeds toward the heavenly realm, the human realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the realm of animals, or the realm of hell—and he fully knows those that are easy to deliver and those that are difficult to deliver; thus, within the womb, he accomplishes the unsurpassed way.

"At times, when a Bodhisattva enters the *ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi* and observes the various classes of sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—seeing that some are blue, yellow, red, or white, and that some are many while others are few—he becomes weary of and averse to dwelling there for long, and thus attains the Unsurpassed Way even while still in the womb."

"Or there may be a bodhisattva who enters the samādhi of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and contemplates the destinies of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna*) of sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—those who are born and those who perish, whether they be blue, yellow, red, or white, long or short—causing those beings to know that their lifespans have ended, and thereby attaining the Unsurpassed Way even while still in the womb."

"Then the Bodhisattva enters the Great Emptiness and Great Quiescence Samādhi, observing this trichiliocosm, extending upward to the boundless and inexhaustible lands, and contemplating the destinies of the consciousnesses of all classes of sentient beings; he reflects upon and discerns the dharma of emptiness and non-existence. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attaining the Unsurpassed Way while still within the womb."

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva entered the Samādhi of the Formless Realm and universally observed the various classes of sentient beings within the trichiliocosm; their minds were bound, yet there was no binding, for the consciousness-spirit is formless, and the dharmas of consciousness that are observed are likewise formless. Within these formless dharmas, he attained the Unsurpassed Way even while still in the womb.
The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Descent from Tuṣita Heaven into His Mother’s Womb, Spoken by the Bodhisattva; Fascicle One.
The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Abiding in the Womb; Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Buddha-Tree.

At that time, the World-Honored One, being about to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder, assembled the bodhisattvas of great virtue and supernormal powers, manifesting transformations through his divine feet and preaching the inconceivable Dharma.
"I shall now manifest as trees made of the seven treasures to deliver those submerged in this long-flowing stream of birth and death, enabling them to attain liberation.

He immediately entered the formless *samādhi* of Lapis Lazuli. Sixty-four billion *Ganges-sand* worlds to the east of this Sahā world-system, he manifested trees made of the seven treasures that filled them entirely. Upon the trunks, joints, boughs, branches, leaves, and fruits of each of these precious trees, there were palaces made of the seven treasures; within these palaces were Buddhas, and each Buddha preached the Dharma of the four marks of impermanence.
In the bathing pool of the rear garden, flocks of birds gathered and took delight therein; their joy was beyond compare.
In the waters of that pool grew *utpala* lotuses, *kunda* flowers, and *māndārava* flowers;

upon the land there grew *campaka* flowers and *sumanā* flowers. There were also *gośīrṣa-candana*, powdered incense, and ground incense, as well as celestial silks, banners, and canopies suspended in the air.

At that time, there was a Wind King named Suiyi (Wish-Fulfilling), who released a great fragrant wind to blow upon the leaves of the seven-jeweled trees. As the soft, perfumed branches and leaves brushed against one another, they all produced the eight kinds of natural sounds.
“Excellent! Great radiance has issued forth, and the Tathāgata’s eightfold voice intends to deliver those yet to be delivered.
Who has manifested this auspicious omen? In the past, I have neither heard of nor seen such a thing; that the marks of arising and ceasing are impermanent—is this not perhaps an illusion?”

At that time, from within the palaces of the seven treasures atop the leaves, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas emitted great sounds to proclaim the inconceivable and rare Dharma, desiring to expound upon the adornments of the Buddha-fields within the eighth stage.

"It is like a person who wishes to behold the waters of the great ocean; being a hundred yojanas from the sea and seeing no living trees, he encounters a flood of water and tastes it, knowing that the ocean is still far away.

He then prepares the equipment for entering the sea; not seeing any physical forms, his mindfulness remains fixed as if in space until he finally reaches the shore, adorning his body with a heart free from fear."
“Excellent! Great Sage! That which I have sought, I have now finally obtained.”

Rejoicing in this with a heart free from weariness, they immediately abandoned all their means of livelihood and entered the ocean; there, everything according to their original vows appeared before them.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he is able to sever the stages from the first dwelling to the sixth dwelling, exhausting the fetters and proclivities of sentient beings until they are forever eliminated without remainder.
"Now my attainment of Buddhahood is certain and beyond doubt."
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva adorning the Buddha-tree while in the womb.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva desires to adorn his own physical marks and become fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, is this for the sake of reality?

From the crown of the head down to the feet, the soles of the feet possess a thousand wheels; each wheel has a thousand spokes; each spoke has a thousand marks; and each mark embodies the six pāramitās.
As for the attainment of the mark of the invisible crown of the head, it is accomplished by destroying the mountain of arrogance to achieve the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa*.
"Since incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas past, I have obtained the retribution of never transgressing in sexual desire, thereby attaining the mark of the sheathed organ (*kośagatavastiguhyatā*).

This mark of the sheathed organ destroys those false views; it emits rays of light that pervade *Gaṅgā*-sands of lands in the ten directions. Within each ray of light there is a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*), and each transformation Buddha sits upon a high seat of the seven treasures, emitting a great sound to expound the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), just as all Tathāgatas constantly preach the Dharma: [as follows...]"

Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom; skillful means for understanding all phenomena; the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, immeasurable emptiness, internal emptiness, external emptiness, ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of conditioned activity, the emptiness of marks, the emptiness of retribution, the emptiness of the cessation of the three calamities, the emptiness of the retribution of the three types of supernormal knowledge, the emptiness of the three kinds of wisdom, the emptiness of the three types of penetration, the emptiness of the three equalities, the emptiness of the three periods of time, the emptiness of the threefold Dharma-body, the emptiness of the quiescence of the three realms, the emptiness of the past, future, and present, and the emptiness of self-characteristics—these are called the signs of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who does not incur the retribution of sexual misconduct.

"Throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), I have constantly cultivated purity of speech; I have not heard this from that, nor have I heard that from this, whereby I have attained the mark of the broad and long tongue."
Pervading the asankhyeya worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he emits the light of his tongue-mark;

Each and every ray of light contains a transformation Buddha; each transformation Buddha sits upon a throne of the seven treasures and, with a pure voice, expounds immeasurable verbal practices—the true workings of pure retributive karma—which accomplish the four matters of fearlessness. They clearly understand that all phenomena neither come nor go, their resonance being pure, thereby crossing over the fearful ground of birth and death without any obstruction. They distinguish the individual sounds of sentient beings and expound immeasurable wisdom and eloquence, crossing over the abyss of the five realms of existence as each dharma is perfected. Adorned by the nine liberations and fully endowed with the ten powers, their emptiness is formless and indestructible. All who hear this Dharma believe and understand it; this is called the fruit of the pure tongue-mark of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

"Since countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have attained the mark of the resonance of sound, which pervades the trichiliocosm; it is supple, harmonious, and elegant, and what is spoken is not coarse. My utterances are perfected and do not depend on others for reception; there is no one who is not filled with joy by that voice."

Within these sounds and echoes, there are also countless pure teachings, such as the Dharma constantly preached by all Tathāgatas: the twelve links of dependent origination, deluded conduct, and birth-and-death; observing one's own body, observing the bodies of others, and observing both internal and external bodies; knowing when the breath is long and knowing when it is short; transforming those sentient beings so that they transcend stages to attain realization, yet do not abide in that realization; and emitting the characteristics of sound and light, wherein each and every ray of light contains a transformation Buddha, and each transformation Buddha sits upon a high seat of the seven treasures, universally preaching immeasurable Dharma gates for all sentient beings.

The mind inclines toward liberation through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; it contemplates and realizes that all phenomena are entirely non-existent. Constantly employing the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and the various gates of wisdom regarding the four dhyānas and the four noble truths, one attains the gate of dhāraṇī, the gate of swiftness, the gate of responding to sounds, and the gate of eloquence.

Immeasurable gates of Dharma are ever present before them; their minds constantly sport within hundreds of thousands of immeasurable samādhis. This is called the mark of the sound and resonance of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

“Since countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have constantly cultivated purity of mind; my thoughts have been focused and correct, my conduct has been characterized by shame and remorse, and I have maintained a single-minded resolve free from other divergent thoughts, entirely devoid of defilement. If someone reviles me, I feel no sorrow or distress; even if they offer praise, I do not take pleasure in it, for my mind remains unshakable. My practice is firm and immovable like the earth. Throughout countless kalpas, I have served all Buddhas and preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to all sentient beings; my conduct is without hypocrisy, as I am single-mindedly intent upon the Path.”

Wherever there are those who take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, he would immediately go in person to transform them, expounding immeasurable *dhāraṇī* gateways. As for these discourses, they concern the discourse on giving, the discourse on ethical discipline, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven; that desire is impure and Nirvana is bliss. He guides sentient beings into the samādhi of meditative concentration, discerning the Truth of Suffering to sever the four bonds, eliminating the causes of accumulation (*samudaya*) to extinguish the major fetters, and through the Path (*mārga*), removing all admixture to attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thus they abide in non-retrogression and attain pure contemplation.

Knowing the thoughts and mental inclinations of those sentient beings, he transforms and guides them according to their kind so that they may attain the fruit of the Way. He is like newly made white cotton cloth, which is easily dyed any color. He constantly restrains his own mind and does not criticize the shortcomings of others; he always delights in seclusion and quietude, never dwelling in clamor and bustle. When entering the assembly of bhikṣus, his deportment is fully perfected; when entering meditative concentration, he fixes his intent upon clarity. Whether walking or coming and going, his mind is free from indolence or arrogance. Amidst the great assembly, he can let out the lion’s roar, discerning that the nature of emptiness is entirely devoid of anything existent. This is called the gate of the pure mind of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

“Since incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas past, I have cultivated the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī, which is indestructible: hearing one, I obtain a hundred; hearing a hundred, I obtain a thousand; hearing a thousand, I obtain ten thousand. All the phrases, meanings, and syllables spoken by the Buddhas are entirely retained through this dhāraṇī without being forgotten or lost. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.”

“Since incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have constantly cultivated the practice of contemplating impermanence; all dharmas return to impermanence, for that which is born must perish. In every place, I have promoted the joy of the Dharma and purified Buddha-lands. My speech is truthful, and I possess the knowledge of past lives regarding the places I have traversed. I transform beings by preaching the Dharma, and my consciousness is firm and stable. My supernormal powers are fearless and inconceivable. Having accumulated various ascetic practices over incalculable kalpas, the vows I have made do not deviate from my original conduct. I sport within all dharmas with sovereignty and without obstruction. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the Dharma-gate of *dhāraṇī*.”

"Since incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas past, I have cultivated the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-abhijñā*). I thoroughly know all classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions: those who are suited for practice in emptiness and those not suited for practice in emptiness; those with a concentrated mind and those without a concentrated mind; those with a distracted mind and those without a distracted mind; those with adamantine resolve and those without adamantine resolve; those with meditative contemplation and those without meditative contemplation. Whether in the heavenly realm, the human realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the realm of animals, or the realm of hell, I see and know them all clearly with my divine eye."

He knows those among the realms of sentient beings who attain *nirvāṇa* with remainder and *nirvāṇa* without remainder; he also fully knows those who attain *nirvāṇa* within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). He knows those sentient beings who, being candidates for the fruit of stream-entry, attain the fruit of stream-entry;

those who, being candidates for the fruit of once-returning, attain the fruit of once-returning; those who, being candidates for the fruit of non-returning, attain the fruit of non-returning; those who, being candidates for arhatship, attain the fruit of arhatship; and those who, being candidates for pratyekabuddhahood, attain the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood.

He also observes sentient beings who leave the household life and practice austerities without abandoning their original vows, shaving off their hair and beards and donning the dharma robes, entering the *siṃhavikrāntagāmī-samādhi*, and contemplating the trees while sitting beneath the King of Trees for one day, two days, or even up to seven days.
Whether for one year, two years, up to seven years;
or for one kalpa, two kalpas, up to seven kalpas—
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the supernormal power of the divine eye.

"Since incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas past, I have cultivated the supernormal power of the ear, hearing everywhere throughout the ten directions the karmic retributions of sentient beings: those with black karma have black retribution; those with white karma have white retribution; those with neither black nor white karma have neither black nor white retribution; those with outflows have retribution with outflows; and those without outflows have retribution without outflows.

I hear the pure sounds of those beings—neither male voices nor female voices, but soft voices that are neither male nor female; neither long nor short voices; not the voices of non-humans, but Brahma-voices and pure voices; *kalaviṅka*-like gentle voices; neither coarse nor subtle voices."

Furthermore, with the divine ear, they hear those sentient beings who have removed defilements and severed bonds, who do not abide in the marks of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor abide in the marks of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor abide in the marks of the past, future, or present; who abide yet do not abide, and do not abide yet do not not abide; who do not abide in a self, and neither abide nor do not abide; whether they become Buddhas or do not become Buddhas, attain the Way or do not attain the Way, are born in the heavens or are not born in the heavens, are born as humans or are not born as humans, are born as hungry ghosts or are not born as hungry ghosts, are born in the hells or are not born in the hells, or are born as animals or are not born as animals—discerning these five destinies, they hear and know them all with their divine ear.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*).

"Since incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas past, I have cultivated the supernormal power of the nose, universally smelling the infinite sentient beings of the ten directions and fully discerning all fragrances: good fragrances and foul fragrances, coarse fragrances and subtle fragrances, fragrances of fire and fragrances of water, worldly fragrances and supramundane fragrances, even the fragrance of a Bodhisattva sitting beneath the King of Trees;
the fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, the fragrance of liberation, and the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
the fragrance of great, boundless compassion in teaching sentient beings, the fragrance of pity for sentient beings, and the fragrance of joy and a serene countenance."
The fragrance of universal relinquishment; the fragrance of fearlessness through supernormal power; the fragrance that is the root of the powers of awakening;
the fragrance that shatters pride and arrogance; the fragrance that naturally perfumes everywhere; the fragrance that adorns the Buddha-way;
the fragrance that leads to the three gates of liberation; the fragrance of mutually distinguished marks; the fragrance that is the fruit of clear conduct; and the fragrance that discerns atoms.

Fragrance: the fragrance of light shining afar; the fragrance of gathering and harmonizing the assembly; the fragrance of the purity of the five aggregates; the fragrance of non-arising upon entering the sense bases;
the fragrance of ceasing and extinguishing all defilements; the fragrance of contemplating the extinction of all defilements; the fragrance of hearing the precepts and practicing giving;
the fragrance of shame and remorse free from pride; the fragrance of the Dharma-victory of the sages; and the unimpeded fragrance of preaching the Dharma.
"Perfume, the perfume of the distribution of relics, the perfume of the sealed treasury of the Buddhas, and the inexhaustible perfume of the seven jewels.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The flowers produced on Mount Magadha, And the fragrance of sandalwood,"
All the fragrances that exist within the three realms are not as superior as the fragrance of precepts.
The fragrance of precepts extinguishes all defilements; though one may pass through the Avīci hell, the Bodhisattva does not regress. The fragrance of Nirvāṇa is the foremost.
Just as a skilled archer shoots an arrow into the void;
before the momentum of the arrow is exhausted in the sky, it soon falls back to the earth;
yet the fragrance of virtue spreads far beyond all bounds, never to turn back again.
