Now I shall speak of the fragrance of the Buddha’s body: its precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, one could never exhaust the Buddha’s fragrance;
even if for ten million kalpas the Buddha were to praise the Buddha’s own merits, they would remain inexhaustible.
Even the Great Sage cannot exhaustively describe the fragrance of the Buddha’s body, precepts, and virtue.
The majestic deportment of all Buddhas is uniquely transmitted to those in their final birth before Buddhahood;
the five-colored fragrance from their mouths rises as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Returning once more to the Buddha’s presence, they circumambulated his body seven times.
The devas scattered flowers and incense, extolling this unprecedented marvel;
the fragrance of meditative concentration spread far and wide, delivering countless *asaṃkhyeya* beings.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, twelve nayutas of sentient beings within that assembly attained awakening in their consciousness and all resolved their minds, vowing to be born in the Buddha-field of Fragrant Accumulation.
“This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the supernormal power of the nose. ‘For incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have cultivated the supernormal power of speech;

my verbal teachings come and go without ever being obstructed. Whenever I speak, light emanates: light from every lip, light from every tooth, and light from every tongue. When the Tathāgata preaches the profound Dharma amidst the great assembly, regarding all such dharmas—such as the single syllable ‘A’: “A” signifies non-existence, yet within that non-existence there are thousands of millions of meanings. From within those thousands of millions of meanings of non-existence, one takes a single meaning to deliver immeasurable sentient beings.’”

The second name is "Luo" (Rā). "Luo" means to remove defilement. There are thousands of millions of meanings within "removing defilement," and from among these thousands of millions of meanings, we take the single meaning of removing defilement to remove the defilements of immeasurable sentient beings.

Third is *pacaya*; *pacaya* means "ripening of fruit. There are ten million meanings within "ripening of fruit," and from among these ten million meanings, one takes the meaning of "ripening of fruit" so that immeasurable sentient beings may all reach the ripening of their fruits.

The fourth name is "Nā. "Nā" signifies impermanence. Within the manifold meanings of impermanence—of which there are ten million—one takes up the single meaning of impermanence to enable immeasurable sentient beings to fully understand that meaning of impermanence.

The fifth name is *ca*. *Ca* means "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) and "non-existence. It is called the name of exhaustion and non-existence because one speaks of existence as being non-existent, and one speaks of non-existence as being neither existent nor non-existent. Within the inexhaustible meanings, there are thousands of millions of meanings; from among these thousands of millions of meanings, one takes a single inexhaustible meaning so that immeasurable sentient beings may attain understanding of exhaustion. This is the meaning of *ca* as exhaustion.

The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, witness the majestic deportment of receiving food; from Jambudvīpa up to the Eighteenth Heaven, they all behold the Tathāgata eating.

From Bodhisattvas in the first through the fourth stages, they see the Tathāgata’s body and his lapis lazuli throat; from non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas up to those in the ninth stage, they see the swift-moving devaputra receiving the Tathāgata’s food and even performing Buddha-works in other directions—this is the karmic fruition of the Tathāgata’s divine speech.

When the Tathāgata manifests the tasting of flavors, he experiences each flavor in succession without being moved by them; he does not gulp, nor does he smack his lips. When the World-Honored One raises his rice toward his mouth, he brings to mind all sentient beings of the five destinies throughout the ten directions, wishing that they might equally partake of this flavor. Immediately, according to his thought, they are all fully satiated. It is like a bhikṣu who has attained the nine successive meditative absorptions (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), whose mind becomes supple, beautiful, and full. This is called the purity of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s supernormal power of the mouth.

"In the past, throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I cultivated the supernormal powers of the body and discerned within the body the notions of purity and impurity, and impurity and purity. I repeatedly contemplated that the thirty-six constituents are filthy, exposed, and unreal—hair, body hair, nails, teeth, bones, blood, mucus, and tears—and by means of the nature of my own body, I observed that the bodies of sentient beings are likewise so."
He transforms his own body so that it becomes bloated, foul-smelling, and putrid, with pus and blood flowing forth;

or he manifests a body of bleached white bones, or a grayish-blue color, or a scorched black, or the same color as the earth. When immeasurable sentient beings behold this body, they all give rise to the perceptions of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Furthermore, he explains to sentient beings the dharma of the retribution of bodily karma: "This body is not a body; what, then, is a body?
He analyzes it part by part from head to foot and finds that nothing exists at all. Since there is no body, there is no consciousness.

When sentient beings hear this, they reflect upon their own bodies as foul, evil, and impure, just as those in the Pure Abode (Ābhāsvara) heavens look down upon Jambudvīpa as stinking and filthy, with its foul vapors rising and permeating seventy million *li*. For this reason, Bodhisattvas are not born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

The Bodhisattva Kāyābhijña enters the Vajra-samādhi and shatters his body into particles as fine as dust; each particle becomes a transformation Buddha, delivering immeasurable asaṃkhyeya classes of sentient beings.

He manifests physical forms and characteristics: fire issues from the upper part of his body while water issues from the lower part; water issues from the lower part of his body while fire issues from the upper part; he leaps up in the east and sinks in the west, or leaps up in the west and sinks in the east;
he manifests the eighteen supernatural transformations of a Tathāgata.
When sentient beings behold the transformations of the Tathāgata, they immediately awaken; their manifold fetters are forever extinguished as they enter the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Myriads of transformed Buddhas manifest their bodies to teach and transform, delivering immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings. This is the Tathāgata’s secret teaching through the body without the preaching of words.

"For countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have cultivated the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and perfected the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva. Gathering my mind in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), I travel to immeasurable Buddha-fields; then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, I return to my original place. This bodhisattva of mental consciousness likewise enters into transformation-birth (*upapāduka*), womb-birth (*jarāyuja*), moisture-birth (*saṃsvedaja*), and egg-birth (*aṇḍaja*), manifesting inconceivable miraculous transformations to teach and transform beings, and therein attains the unconditioned path (*asaṃskṛta-mārga*)."
The consciousness of a Bodhisattva is the most supreme and most excellent among all supernormal powers; it cannot be conceived by Pratyekabuddhas or Arhats. Why is this?
"It is not within their realm.

**Chapter Five: The Equality of the Three Times** *The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra* At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Priyadarśana (Joyful Vision). His eloquence was unimpeded, he had ascended the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and he was able to maintain all that the Tathāgata practices. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent!..."
World-Honored One!

Now that I have heard this Dharma, it is most unprecedented. Among the countless Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, there were those who entered nirvāṇa and those who did not enter nirvāṇa.
If you enter nirvana, how can sentient beings of the desire realm attain deliverance?
If the Tathāgata does not enter nirvana, in which Buddha-realm do those various Tathāgatas abide?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana: "Excellent, excellent!
You are truly able to let out a lion’s roar before the Tathāgata."
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall now explain each point to you in detail.
Sujāta replied: “So be it, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha said:

"The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have names and provisional designations that cannot be fully recorded. They are like the births and deaths of sentient beings, which are neither extinguished nor destroyed; they are boundless, limitless, and without beginning or end. The essential assembly of the Buddhas is a mind like the realm of space, and those who enter nirvana are none other than these very sentient beings."
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
It is for the sake of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the sentient beings delivered by the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, were there those who attained parinirvāṇa and those who did not?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana: "How is it,
Priyadarśana?"

"Throughout incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you have served various Buddhas, paying them homage, making offerings of incense, flowers, banners, and canopies; have you ever seen a Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa?"
He replied, “No. [The Buddha asked,] “How so?”
"Prasannadarśin!
I am known as Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; now dwelling within my mother's womb, am I in nirvāṇa or not in nirvāṇa?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
“How is it, Priyadarśana? When bodhisattvas receive the prediction that they shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, is this a real path or an unreal path?”
He replied: "This path is not the true path, nor is it the true path. Why is this?"
To perceive the existence of a Buddha, the existence of the teaching of the Dharma, and the transformation of sentient beings—because of these things, this path is not the true path.
To take sentient beings as conditions is a path; to take the exhaustion of conditions regarding sentient beings is the true path.
Sentient beings for whom the conditions of the past have ceased do not find the true path in the present.
Sentient beings for whom the conditions of the present have ceased do not find the true path in the past.
Sentient beings for whom past and present conditions have ceased do not find the true path in the future.
Sentient beings for whom future conditions have ceased do not find the true path in the past or the present.

Why is this? This path is not the true path; rather, the true path is that which exhausts the conditions of past objects, exhausts the conditions of present objects, and exhausts the conditions of future objects for all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows and perceives this, yet does not abide in it nor enter into it.
Why is this? It is because, like the nine stages of practice, they are not yet exhausted.

The so-called nine grades of practice are: superior-superior, superior-middle, superior-inferior, middle-superior, middle-middle, middle-inferior, inferior-superior, inferior-middle, and inferior-inferior.
If the superior-superior conditions are exhausted while the superior-middle conditions are not exhausted, it is not the true path.
If the superior-middle conditions are exhausted while the superior-inferior conditions are not exhausted, it is not the true path.
If the upper and lower conditions are exhausted while the middle and upper conditions are not exhausted, it is not the true path.
If the middle and upper conditions are exhausted while the middle and middle conditions are not exhausted, it is not the true path.
If the middling-of-the-middling conditions are exhausted while the middling-of-the-low conditions are not, it is not the true path.
If the middling-of-the-low conditions are exhausted while the low-of-the-high conditions are not, it is not the true path.
If the lower-high condition is exhausted while the lower-middle condition is not exhausted, it is not the true path.
If the lower-middle condition is exhausted while the lower-lower condition is not exhausted, it is not the true path.
When the lowest of the low reaches its ultimate exhaustion, this is the true path.

Regarding the nature of reality, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva neither grasps nor abandons; he neither dwells nor does not dwell. The past, future, and present are equal; the path is equal to nirvāṇa; they are one and the same, without duality.

The equality of the nature of dharmas, the equality of spontaneous characteristics, the equality of sentient beings, the equality of defilements, the equality of the five aggregates, the equality of conditions, and the equality of deluded conduct—the path of practice is pure, being neither one nor two.
The exhaustion of the conditions for desire-conduct is not the exhaustion of the conditions for form-conduct;
the exhaustion of the conditions for form-conduct is not the exhaustion of the conditions for formless-conduct;

the exhaustion of the conditions for formless-conduct, the exhaustion of the conditions for form-conduct, and the exhaustion of the conditions for conduct in the desire realm—this is called the bodhisattvas being neither one nor two.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, saying:
"Do you wish to know whether the past Buddhas have entered extinction or not, and their respective lands?

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernatural power, entered the Samādhi of the Fearless Empty Realm, causing the entire assembly to see the body of Śākyamuni in its state of silent stillness, its physical marks fully perfected.

Just as blind people, when discussing matters together in a secluded place, each claim their own view to be correct and engage in mutual contention, so too it is with these classes of sentient beings: their consciousness, perception, and feeling are each distinct and different.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"It is just as if someone were to prepare a meal of a hundred flavors consisting of non-glutinous rice, beans, wheat, and large and small sesame seeds; one who obtains the non-glutinous rice would not know that there are other varieties such as beans and wheat."
“Kāśyapa! It is just so:
consciousness, perception, and feeling are each distinct, yet when one contemplates the nature of all phenomena, they are neither different nor separate.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Kāśyapa:
"By seeing the forehead, one knows there is a head; by observing smoke, one knows there is fire;
by beholding clouds, one knows there will be rain; by examining conduct, one knows the nature of the person.
Empty space and rain have no feet; a reflection of water cannot be grasped."
When speech and deliberation are exhausted, that is the Dharma Master; when the fetters are exhausted, that is Nirvana.
When perception is exhausted, one dwells in non-perception; when feeling ceases, there is no more feeling;
when consciousness ceases, there is no more consciousness—this is the unsurpassed path of pure conduct.
For countless kalpas, I have been constantly deluded by consciousness;
in this life and in future lives, I have not encountered a place of peace and happiness.
Now, while currently within the womb, I am discerning the characteristics of all dharmas.
"One does not perceive the names of perception or feeling; how much less could there be the phenomena of consciousness?

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this verse, five hundred bhikṣus attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); one thousand sentient beings delighted their minds in the practice of emptiness, and they attained mastery over their minds within the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).

Chapter Seven: On Abiding and Non-Abiding. In the *Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra*, Chapter Seven: On Abiding and Non-Abiding. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Anabhirata-dharmacaryā (Practice of Non-Abiding). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

"This great assembly has attained excellent benefit, having been able to hear the immeasurable meanings of the Dharma from the Tathāgata; that which was formerly vowed, we now finally hear. Thereupon, before the Buddha, he praised him in verse: "The realm of space is boundless, And it proclaims immeasurable meanings; The Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise boundless, And he expounds the Dharma without limit. The Tathāgata’s power is likewise boundless, And his skillful means are likewise infinite; He can manifest all manner of forms, Yet his body remains unchanging. Existence and non-existence are neither born nor extinguished; in serene stillness, there is no sensation or perception.
The Buddhas of the past and all others like them cultivated giving, precepts, and patience;
entering meditative concentration with undisturbed minds, their light of wisdom illuminated the world.
His virtue is immeasurable, neither existent nor non-existent;
his voice is supremely pure and subtle, peerless and without rival.
With a single sound he responds to billions; through this, he attains Buddhahood.
The sound of the Dharma drum is heard afar, yet each resonance is distinct;
just as the wheel-turning monarch rains down the seven treasures at his mere thought,
so too does the Buddha’s voice vibrate to the furthest reaches, raining down the jewels of the seven factors of awakening.
Cultivating and purifying the Buddha’s site of enlightenment, adorning the fruit of the Bodhi tree;
neither abiding nor non-abiding, they protect sentient beings with compassion;
their minds and physical marks fully perfected, they do not shrink from the hardships of kalpas.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, Unseal and open the treasury of the Dharma;
We have now heard it and attained Abiding on the shore of the unconditioned.
Excellent is the power of the Tathāgata, Vast, expansive, and without limit or depth!

Having untied the bonds, he does not dwell in existence; the reality-limit and the true nature of phenomena, the afflictions of the desire realm and the world—he teaches and transforms all who are deluded.
The meaning of the Buddha’s profound and secret treasury, he spreads and manifests for the sake of sentient beings.
“The boundaries are without limit, And all shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Non-Abiding had spoken these verses in praise of the Buddha, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the past, future, and present are pure; they neither abide nor do they not abide. This extends even to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the holy life (*brahmacarya*), which neither abide nor do they not abide.”
The objects of the past, future, and middle are ultimately pure and impure, empty, neither abiding nor not abiding.
I do not create, nor do I not create; it is neither the holy life nor not the holy life.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain abiding and non-abiding.

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Non-Abiding, saying: “The characteristic of form neither abides nor does not abide; the characteristic of sensation neither abides nor does not abide; the characteristic of perception neither abides nor does not abide; the characteristic of mental formations neither abides nor does not abide; the characteristic of consciousness neither abides nor does not abide.”

The purity of internal phenomena is neither abiding nor non-abiding; the purity of external phenomena is neither abiding nor non-abiding; the purity of both internal and external phenomena is neither abiding nor non-abiding.
From the first aspiration until reaching the site of enlightenment, one eliminates all conceptualizations and purifies all-knowledge, yet this is neither abiding nor non-abiding.

One removes the defilements of sentient beings and purifies them, yet this is neither abiding nor non-abiding; one adorns the Buddha-lands and purifies them, yet this is neither abiding nor non-abiding; one enters the diamond-like samādhi to solidify one’s resolve, yet this is neither abiding nor non-abiding; and one purifies the śarīra relics of the fragmented body, yet this is neither abiding nor non-abiding.
He sports in hundreds of thousands of samādhis; pure, he neither dwells nor does not dwell.
He does not abide in the stage of ordinary beings, yet does not enter the emptiness of the sages and worthies; pure, he neither dwells nor does not dwell.
He does not claim for himself that he has attained the fruit of the Way; pure, he neither dwells nor does not dwell.

The thirty-two marks of a Great Man emit a great radiance that shines afar across immeasurable worlds in the ten directions; all sentient beings, following the light, come to him and hear the Tathāgata’s profound and subtle Dharma. According to their respective thoughts—whether superior, middling, or inferior speech—he causes them all to be fully satisfied and to discern all dharmas: abiding yet not abiding, and neither abiding nor not abiding.

Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the twelve links of dependent origination; the four unhindered wisdoms; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the four dhyānas and the four immeasurable wisdoms—all are pure, neither abiding nor non-abiding.
By the power of the bases of supernormal power, he enters the five destinies; pure, yet neither abiding nor not abiding.

He enters the gates of liberation—the aggregate of precepts, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; pure, yet neither abiding nor not abiding.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I shall now explain the eight pools of the pure nectar-flavor of the Dharma. What are these eight?

Just as I sit today in the Hall of Sovereign Discourse, looking east toward the pure bathing pool with its surrounding railings made of the seven treasures, at that time I likewise do not preach to sentient beings on suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; yet by drinking the water of this pool, they all attain the fruit of the Way—this is called the power of the Bodhisattva’s spiritual transformations.

It is likewise in the south, west, and north; when I originally attained Buddhahood, I did so from the four cardinal directions, not from the four intermediate points. To have attained Buddhahood from the four intermediate points would be a manifestation that the attainment of Buddhahood is not real.
Why is this? Because throughout incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they have accomplished the Dharma of the eight flavors. What are these eight?

First, the flavor of joy; second, the flavor of exhaustion; third, the flavor of concentration; fourth, the flavor of arrival; fifth, the flavor of tranquility; sixth, the flavor of characteristics; seventh, the flavor of immovability; eighth, the flavor of non-finality—these are the eight flavors of the bathing pool.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva drinks this ambrosial nectar, they shall not enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will achieve the unsurpassed path.
From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the tree of awakening, they will wash away the defilements of the mind until they are forever exhausted without remainder.
What are the pool of the seven factors of enlightenment and the water of the eight liberations?

When the initial mind of liberation has not yet reached the intermediate stage but has already arrived there, and having reached the intermediate stage, one dwells in the two stages—only then is one named a Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva distinguishes the flavors from the waters of the eight ponds, perceiving that "this is flavor" and "this is not flavor," or "this is the path" and "this is not the path," yet their ears do not distinguish sounds, their noses do not distinguish fragrances, and their tongues do not distinguish tastes.
To discern each part as being non-existent, because all dharmas are deaf [to conceptualization], this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s pure cultivation of the pure practice.

Chapter Eight: The Eight Kinds of Bodies The *Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra*, Chapter Eight: The Eight Kinds of Bodies. The Buddha addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered in the assembly:

“Those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and all sentient beings are worthy of making offerings to them.”

There may be sentient beings who, by seeing the stage of the ordinary person (*bhūmi*), the stage of attenuation (*tanubhūmi*), the stage of purity (*śuddhabhūmi*), the stage of the Tathāgata, the stage of the *pratyekabuddha*, the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartikabhūmi*), the stage of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍabhūmi*), and the stage of preaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanābhūmi*)—by means of these eight stages—attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What is the stage of vision?
It is when a bodhisattva resolves their mind and sets out toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, from the initial resolution until sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment, subdues their own mind with the intent to conquer all Māras, and immediately enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon that seat.
As for his samādhis:

the samādhi of removing jealousy, the samādhi of mental supremacy, the samādhi of the secret treasury, the samādhi of eliminating delusion, the samādhi of subduing through majestic power, the samādhi of wordless instruction like that of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the samādhi of manifesting transformations.

At that time, when the evil Māra Pāpīyān came to disturb the Buddha, it was not by his own power that he was able to arrive; rather, it was entirely brought about by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
Why is this so? It is because worldly dharmas are considered inferior, while the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is superior.
For what reason?

When the evil Māra Pāpīyān gave rise to a mind of anger and malice, his voice shook the earth; yet the Buddha, through the samādhi of patience, remained unmoved and unshaken, causing the countless hosts of evil Māras to fall prostrate and overturned, like crickets, ants, and flies unable to stir.
The evil Māra Pāpīyān is likewise; even if Māras were to come, they could not move a single hair of mine.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately entered a samādhi through his majestic spiritual power, causing all the evil Māras throughout an entire Buddha-field to tremble and making their wicked voices resound everywhere.
"The śramaṇa Kotama holds a mind that is weak and lacks the resolve of a man, yet he wishes to seek the Buddha-way in this place of great terror.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān was created by me. As for that Māra’s mind, is it an evil mind or a virtuous mind?"
At that time, there was a devaputra named Kuvika who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha has subdued Māra; this was not by Māra’s power, but by the Buddha’s own spiritual power."
Why is this? Because those classes of sentient beings do not understand mundane dharmas or the dharmas of the Path, he has caused Māra to descend in order to transform these sentient beings.

Any sentient being who beholds these various Māras will find their mind no longer taking pleasure [in worldly things] even when compared to the Thousand-Eyed One (Indra), and tens of millions of such beings will establish their minds in the stage of non-retrogression.

"Furthermore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas descend from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the lands of the ten directions; they do not rely on moisture-birth, egg-birth, transformation-birth, or womb-birth to teach and transform sentient beings."
These bodhisattvas have accomplished the roots of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta-mūla*), and the sentient beings they transform also accomplish the roots of the indeterminate. What are these?
They are the realm of the Buddha Akṣobhya.

There are some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having been born from the Sahā world into the Buddha-land of Northern Radiance, have perfected the roots of both the determinate and the indeterminate; they teach and transform sentient beings so that all achieve these determinate and indeterminate roots—these are the sentient beings of the World of Desire for Joy in the Buddha-land of Sublime Light.

There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from their first resolution until they attain Buddhahood, maintain a mind that is single-mindedly free from manifold thoughts, without hatred or anger, and aspire to be born in the land of the Buddha Amitāyus.
All sentient beings who are born there—the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all possess the same golden color.

To the west of this Jambudvīpa, twelve billion nayutas away, there is a realm called Śithilā (The Indolent). The land is blissful, where musical performances are held; it is adorned with garments, ornaments, incense, and flowers, and features couches made of the seven treasures with revolving joints. When one looks toward the east, the jeweled couch turns accordingly; looking north, west, or south, it likewise turns.

Sentient beings who have previously or subsequently resolved their minds to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha all become defiled by and attached to the Land of Indolence; thus, they are unable to advance and be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Among a multitude of hundreds of millions, there may be but one person at any given time capable of being reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha. Why is this?
It is because all are indolent and their resolve is not firm.
These sentient beings, having refrained from killing themselves and also taught others not to kill, will receive this meritorious retribution by being born in the Land of Immeasurable Life.

Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are fully endowed with the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the wisdom of liberation—who are born in the Buddha-field of Sudarśana (Joyful) to the south, one hundred million Buddha-lands away from this Jambudvīpa; among those sentient beings, there is no thought of delusion, craving, or lust.

Why is this? Because they have all severed the thirty-six kinds of sensual desire from the realm of desire and brought them to cessation; their spiritual lineage is perfected and their conduct is pure, like the radiance of the sun, free from any dust or obscuration.

The sentient beings in that land practice thirteen ascetic practices. What are these thirteen? They practice walking meditation and seated dhyāna at the three periods of day and night without missing their proper times;

they may stay beneath trees, in cemeteries, in open spaces, or in secluded rocky places where no people dwell; they may rely on springs for water; they may eat only once a day, or abstain from food altogether; they wear their Dharma robes neatly and never lose their dignified deportment; they may sometimes preach the Dharma and sometimes not; they circulate and walk in meditation with contentment and fullness; and regarding the Dharma they preach, they teach that few desires constitute the true path while many desires are not the path, and they instruct in calming the mind and concentrating the will through the realization of the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. These are called the practices of the bodhisattvas in the world of *Utpala*.

The sentient beings in that land study exclusively the One Vehicle; there are no vehicles of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas. They are endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, they praise the True Dharma, and they understand emptiness and non-self.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All conditioned phenomena have ceased; consciousness is but an external dharma.
That which is born must all return to extinction; Nirvana is the supreme bliss."
I take refuge in the Buddha of Leaping Joy, the foremost among the Kings of Dharma;
seated beneath the Jambu tree, he was the first to shatter the net of desire,
preaching the Dharma to deliver all people and making offerings to all fields of merit.
Sitting beneath a tree in contemplation, The Brahma King came to entreat him:
"May the World-Honored One arise from dhyāna; Have compassion for those who are ignorant and deluded.
At that time, the Great Brahma Heavenly King Held a lapis lazuli lute in his hand.
Praising and proclaiming the Buddha’s virtues with soft, harmonious, and elegant tones,
there may be those who give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
for the mind of enlightenment is the very foundation of a bodhisattva, and it appears only once in the course of many millions of kalpas.
May you swiftly arise from dhyāna and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in an age,
so does a Buddha appear to illuminate the world and dispel the darkness of all afflictions.
In the world-system of *Nandana*, they hear the precepts and practice pure giving;
it is not like this land of endurance, where beings are stubborn and difficult to transform.
They contemplate the path of meditative concentration, extinguishing the body without seeking personal realization.
The three turnings and five hindrances, the twelve links of dependent origination,
the thirty-two factors of the path, and the sixteen minds of compassion.
Through immeasurable kalpas of antiquity, his vow has been as firm as adamant.
He emits great rays of light, Which universally illumine all Buddha-fields.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Buddha addressed the assembly:

“To the northeast of this Sahā world, beyond as many lands as there are grains of sand in five hundred Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Phalapākā. There dwells a Buddha named Puṣpaketu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He currently resides there preaching the Dharma—excellent in its beginning, excellent in its middle, and excellent in its end; its meaning and flavor are profound, being identical to the Brahma-conduct.”
The sentient beings in that land are not born from a womb, nor by transformation, nor by moisture, nor from eggs; they are born from lotuses.

They possess the divine power and concentration of mind associated with the hundred and seven hardships, and all together they cultivate the Samādhirāja-samādhi. As for all the samādhis therein, they include the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, the Bodhimārga-samādhi, the Vinaya-vinīta-samādhi, the Sarvasattvaduḥkhamūla-prahāṇa-samādhi, the Svaprabhā-prakāśana-samādhi, and the Sattvarasabodhana-samādhi—such as these are the hundred and seven samādhis.

One contemplates the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally; one contemplates internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena; one contemplates internal concentration, external concentration, and both internal and external concentration. Through contemplation, discernment, and clear observation, one realizes that there is no form, no perception, and no thought. Thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the gate of liberation and observes that all phenomena are empty, quiescent, and formless.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Space is without limit, Yet its resonance proclaims the wondrous Dharma;
The ripened fruit is the land and its people, And the flower’s essence is the Most Victorious Honored One.”
Not born from the four types of wombs, they arise spontaneously from lotuses;
free from the notions of self and other, their lifespans are immeasurable.
Their lands are composed of the seven treasures, just like those of Jambudvīpa.
The Wheel-Turning King possesses the seven treasures: the elephant, the horse, the precious queen, the treasurer, the fourfold army, the mani-jewel, and the golden wheel;
wherever he goes, there is no obstruction.
Universally illuminating a single buddha-field, where there is no light from sun or moon,
nor from stars or fire;
he discerns the four noble truths.
"The path of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness causes those classes of sentient beings to abandon the notion of arising and annihilation.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Buddha—
He addressed those gathered:

"To the northwest of this Jambudvīpa, at a distance of seventy thousand Ganges-sands of world-systems, there is a land named Vaidūryaratna. There resides a Buddha named Prajñāsiddhi Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who is currently preaching the Dharma—virtuous in its beginning, virtuous in its middle, and virtuous in its end."

The sentient beings in that land are of a gentle and supple nature; they contemplate the path of impermanence and thereby distance themselves from the three afflictions. They are free from lust, anger, and delusion, and there are no three evil realms—namely, the hells, the hungry ghosts, or the animals.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to the great assembly:
"The various sense-bases and the path of afflictions, As well as the four inversions—
All are forever eliminated and exhausted, Like space, devoid of form or image."
Their lifespan is immeasurable, and none suffer untimely death;
practicing the four dharmas of fearlessness, they achieve the fruit unshakable.

The Buddha-way is unconditioned, pure, and flawless; like a lotus in the water, it is untainted by dust or grime. When the sun shines upon heaven and earth, it eclipses the glow of fireflies; among all mountains that stand firm, Mount Sumeru is supreme; among all stars that emit faint light, the bright moon is foremost; so too, when the Tathāgata appears in the world, his Dharma-lamp is the first.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Severing defilements and eliminating perceptions, The mind is freed from its bonds and attachments;
With the mental faculty stilled in concentration, Pure conduct is brought to full completion.”
Within a single thought and a single moment, Sever the traces of fetters and afflictions;
Eliminate suffering for eternal kalpas, Bringing it to an end so that it arises no more.
The supreme path of emptiness and stillness Is as if existing, yet as if non-existing.
Self, others, and all consciousnesses Are like dreams, reflections, and illusions.
The bodhisattva accumulates ascetic practices For kalpas beyond measure;
Yet if one seeks to explain their fundamental root, It is neither one nor two forms.
If there is a person of wisdom who expounds immeasurable meanings with their mouth—

Chapter Nine: The Relics of the Entire Body At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those gathered in the assembly: "Reflect upon the merits I cultivated in ancient times;
the instances of casting off one body and receiving another were neither one nor two. Now, for your sake, I shall explain the Dharma of the Single Form."
What is called the "single-form dharma"?
This great earth element is eighty-four trillion *li* thick;
likewise, there is a sharp wind element that is eighty-four trillion *li* thick.
Below the wind is water, eighty-four trillion *li* thick;
below the water is fire, eighty-four trillion *li* thick;
below the fire is sand, eighty-four trillion *li* thick.
Beneath the sand lies a diamond realm (*vajra-kṣetra*) eighty-four trillion *li* in thickness; the entire bodily relics (*śarīra*) of all Buddhas are contained within that diamond realm.
The Vajra-land is further eighty-four trillion *li* thick, and beneath it are the *śarīra* relics of the bodies of all Buddhas, all of which are contained within that land.

There is a Buddha-land there named Gandharva (in the Dan-ben edition, "Fragrance"), where the Buddha is named Anihata-tathāgata, complete with the ten titles, who currently resides and preaches the Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.

Having purified the holy life, his buddha-field will be fully accomplished; his buddha-relics will be exceedingly minute, yet they will be able to manifest the body of a Buddha along with disciples and retinues who circulate to bestow transformation, just as I now dwell in the womb and preach the Dharma.

Those sentient beings do not see me, and I do not see those sentient beings; having shattered existence to reach non-existence, they abide eternally in the nature of profound stillness at the place beyond doubt—this is what is meant by the influence of a single relic.
The Buddha again addressed those gathered in the assembly:

"Beneath the scattered-body relics, extending eighty-four trillion *li* in thickness, there is a land named Pure (*Vimala*). There, a Buddha named Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabha*), complete with the ten titles, currently dwells and expounds the Dharma—excellent in the beginning, middle, and end—purely cultivating the holy life."
The light of that Buddha is of various and distinct colors; each individual ray of light manifests a Buddha, and every one of these Buddhas fully expounds the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
What are the six perfections?

Through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, employing skillful means to subdue the mind and consciousness, one does not give rise to delusion; being free from lust and desire, one clearly understands and contemplates all phenomena as the moon emerging from the clouds.

Furthermore, he observes his own body as being no different from that of others; having attained the meditative concentration on emptiness, he achieves complete perfection, sitting upright at the site of enlightenment and extolling the True Dharma with a heart free of timidity.

Eighty-four million *li* below this world, in the Buddha-field of Radiant Light, there is a land named Treasury of Boundless Giving. There dwells a Buddha named Tathāgata Encouraging Aid of the Crimson Land, complete with the ten titles, who currently resides there preaching the Dharma—excellent in its beginning, middle, and end—and constantly practicing the holy life. Whatever gifts he bestows, anyone who receives them immediately attains the fruits of the Path; this is called the Tathāgata’s first unprecedented gift.

Below the world of Infinite Worlds is the world of Dharma Drum, eighty-four trillion *li* in thickness. The Buddha there is named Sudarśana, who is fully endowed with the ten titles; he currently dwells there, preaching the Dharma.

The sentient beings of that land all share the same clan and the same name, with no diverse appellations; upon hearing the Dharma, they understand it without the need for repeated reflection. Furthermore, that land contains entire bodily relics (śarīra), for the billions of Buddhas of the past have all left behind their relics there.
Regarding the śarīra of that land, I too have a share of it, neither one nor two. That Buddha’s śarīra does not abide in a single place, yet it is not that it does not abide;

it circulates throughout *saṃkhyeya* lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Fully endowed with radiant marks, it transforms beings according to their capacities without ever wearying. Thirty-one billion fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been severed and extinguished; twenty-two thousand entanglements of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) have been untied; and through the eighteen supreme, uncommon qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), it manifests teachings to inspire beings to receive the realization of fearlessness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Throughout incalculable eons, I have wandered through the path of birth and death;
Discarding this body, I received another, never escaping birth from a womb."
Calculating what I have experienced, I record but one and do not speak of the rest:
I took the form of a pure white dog for so long that the bones accumulated would equal a hundred million Mount Sumerus;
even when I planted needles into the earth, there was no spot that did not pierce my body.
How much more so for other dogs, their number being immeasurable.
Therefore, I restrain my mind and do not allow it to be negligent on the Path;
like a person standing upon Mount Sumeru holding the medicine of immortality.
A person below receives it in a vessel, pouring the medicine without spilling a drop;
yet amidst the many hardships, they are buffeted by the winds of Sālana.
The bodies of ordinary beings are like dust, with the sole exception of those who have entered and abide [in the stages].
Of these two who carry the vessel, which one is most excellent?
The person of lower station holds their mind upright, yet they are constantly afraid of being tossed east or west;
because they receive the medicine without losing its meaning, this is called the Way of Divine Power.
Possessing a heart of great compassion above, he does not investigate a single teaching;
though consciousnesses are each distinct, the realization of the Way is likewise so.
In this world-realm of suffering that I endure, I have attained Buddhahood through the efforts of those of lowly station.
Having accumulated practice for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*), one is then able to attain the Buddha-way.
From one land to another land, passing through thousands of billions like this;
it is as if a needle were cast into the ocean, yet one can retrieve it simply by extending the hand.
Those who seek water by wringing out space will not obtain it even after the accumulation of kalpas;
so too do the ignorant and deluded people of the world fail to distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome conduct.
They regard Mount Sumeru, composed of the four precious substances, as a mere heap of ashes.
The king of golden-winged birds mistakes a mosquito for his equal;
In the summer heat, the insect in a cow’s footprint does not perceive the vastness of the ocean;
The shimmering mirage is but sunlight on the plain, yet the fool perceives it as a blazing fire.
"That dharma was not created by me; it is accomplished through the conduct of the deluded and confused.
With the consciousness entering and exiting without interval, the refined essence and the arts of the Way are perfected.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this mantra:

“Eṇī maṇī, cāpe cāpale, cuṇḍe, khire khiri. At that time, the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said: “I shall protect virtuous persons who practice the Dharma, as well as good men and good women; I shall protect their bodies with the three lights and three shadows.”
"What are the three lights and three shadows? They are as follows:
today, when I lead the host of rākṣasas, there is the shadow of the body, the shadow of the shadow of the body, and the shadow of the shadow.
"What is the shadow of the body?"
"What is the shadow of the body?
And what is the shadow of the shadow?

"The body is a collection of the four great elements, formed of earth, water, fire, and wind;
though it comes and goes and moves about, even when it dwells, one does not perceive its dwelling."
The body and the one who possesses the body, Throughout life, the body sheds its form;
The meaning of the three phrases regarding shadow and shadow, Is like the Buddha leaving behind his divine light.
A white cotton cloth wraps the Māra, Just as fragrance remains where it has been.
This essential Dharma of all Buddhas is pure and free from blemish.
Through the transformation of body within body, they deliver those who cannot yet be delivered;
or by perceiving the phenomena of bodily forms, they enter meditative concentration with mindfulness of body within body.
"Shadow upon shadow, free from doubt, shall all achieve the unsurpassed Way.
At that time, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, wishing to provide protection for all Dharma-preachers, spoke this incantation:

"Ihe | Mahe | Jambu | Yamalambu | Tututulekhi. I shall protect the Dharma-preachers; within a range of hundreds of thousands of millions of yojanas, I shall ensure there are none who cause disturbance."
The Heavenly King Virūḍhaka immediately rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said:
"I, too, shall protect the true Dharma-preacher.
He then spoke this incantation:
“Kāli, kālī, niti, kumbhīti! May there be no one within hundreds of thousands of millions of *yojanas* who causes disturbance.
Then the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet in salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I shall protect the true Dharma-preacher.
He then spoke this mantra:
"Śamī śamī pāpamahā-malohi. "May there be no one within a billion yojanas who causes disturbance or affliction."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The fragrance, color, and form of the flowers are most exquisite, Moving all the Buddha-lands to respond;
The Buddha, free from all conceptual thought, Has attained the Buddha-way, the single-minded path."
The power of patience has no boundaries; it shatters both existence and non-existence, as well as the two vehicles.
Through the marks of the bodily relics and even down to the finest atoms, it rescues beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, ensuring they do not fall into the three evil realms.
"The Buddha has emerged from the kalpa of diligent suffering, Sheltering all while practicing great compassion;
Sentient beings are without limit, And he causes them to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
At that time, thirty-two billion sentient beings within the assembly immediately resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, impartial path.

Chapter Ten: On the Permanent and the Impermanent. In the *Bodhisattva-tāyā-sūtra*, Chapter Ten, "On the Permanent and the Impermanent," at that time, there was among those seated a bodhisattva named Vision of Impermanence. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“World-Honored One! It is wonderful that you have so clearly explained this meaning. The True Dharma of all Buddhas is inconceivable;

it is beyond the reach of arhats and pratyekabuddhas. Its original, true nature is inexhaustible. When the Tathāgata manifests his form, he appears through the gates of emergence and entry, with transformations occurring without limit: sometimes as fragmented bodily relics (śarīra), sometimes as whole-body relics; sometimes he vanishes and does not appear, and sometimes he is disseminated throughout the world; sometimes he manifests the realm of a single Buddha, and sometimes he manifests the realms of many Buddhas. His supernormal powers, transformations, and the mastery of the power of the Path are most marvelous and extraordinary.”

Like the realm of empty space, it is both eternal and non-eternal; non-eternal and yet not non-eternal; abiding and yet not abiding; non-abiding and yet not non-abiding; its transformations are manifold. I pray that you, O Tathāgata, will explain for me the meaning of the eternal and the non-eternal.
"Am I, as I am today abiding in the ninth stage, permanent or impermanent?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Constant-Impermanence, saying:
"I now question you; you should answer me according to the true nature of things.
How is it so, son of good family?"
"Is form permanent? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
Is form impermanent? He replied:
"No. "Is form permanent or impermanent? He replied:
"No. "Is form neither permanent nor impermanent? He replied:
"No. "How so, son of good family?"
"Is there anything remaining of form? He replied, "No."
"Is form without remainder? He replied, "No."
“Is there a remainder or no remainder regarding form? He replied, “No.”
“Is form neither with remainder nor without remainder? He replied, “No.”
The Buddha asked the son of good family:
"Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent? He replied:
"No. "Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness impermanent? He replied:
"No. "Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent? He replied:
"No. "Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness neither permanent nor impermanent? He replied:
"No. "Are there any remnants of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness? He replied:
"No. "Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also without remainder? He replied:
"No. "Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness with remainder or without remainder? He replied:
"No. "Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness neither with remainder nor without remainder? He replied:
"No," [he replied].
The Buddha then asked the Bodhisattva Constantly Unconditioned: "Is nirvāṇa pure?"
He replied, “No. [The Buddha asked,] “Is Nirvana impure?”
He replied, “No.
[The Buddha asked: “Is nirvāṇa pure or impure?”
He replied, “No. The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Constantly Impermanent:
"What is the true nature of nirvāṇa established upon?
He replied, "It is established in non-establishment."
He asked again:
“Is it that there are neither sentient beings nor no sentient beings? He replied:

"No. Because the conditions have not been severed—from the nature of the five aggregates up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the conditions remain unsevered; there is neither detachment nor non-detachment, neither arising nor non-arising. Therefore, it is said that 'that which is established has nothing to be established.'"

Why is this? Because their nature is naturally empty—this emptiness, that emptiness, internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of nirvāṇa. When a Tathāgata appears in the world of the five turbidities, he does not perceive arising or ceasing, attachment or severance; he does not perceive concentration or distraction; he does not perceive observance of precepts or violation of precepts; he does not perceive patience or anger; he does not perceive diligence or indolence; he does not perceive afflictions or meditative composure; he does not perceive delusion or wisdom; he does not perceive consciousness or mental ideation; he does not perceive this as the Path or this as the worldly pāramitās; he does not perceive the purity of Buddha-fields; he does not perceive the purification of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); and he does not perceive any sentient beings who have severed defilements. This is called the Bodhisattva’s establishment of the non-established.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Brahma-faring with a pure mind destroys the realm of Māra;
The power of patience is the unsurpassed path, tranquil concentration beyond conception.”
For countless kalpas, I have always dwelt in non-abiding;
I have entered single-mindedly into the wisdom of emptiness, adorned with a body of manifold conceptions.
To the sons of noble family who will come in the future, and to all those who exist now—
One should establish all things as being without establishment, understanding the nature of both permanence and impermanence.
The various obstacles of defilement destroy my practice of wholesome deeds;
once these defilements are completely eliminated, one is like gold free from blemish.
Wisdom is the general of the world, showing the Way and opening the eyes of the sightless;
it causes those who are ignorant and deluded to deeply understand the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā).
Through the path of unconditioned causes and conditions, it opens the way for the advancement of the six supernormal powers (abhijñā).
The inexhaustible great Dharma-treasury is bestowed upon those of inferior capacity.
Craving the three gates of liberation, they are unattached to the three periods of time;
regarding all phenomena of the present, their defilements are exhausted as they enter the Buddha-concentration.
The Tathāgata’s great light of wisdom cuts away the dharmas of doubt;
the marks of delusion are serenely purified, and he explains the path of emptiness and impermanence.
All those who reckon themselves as permanent beings are greedily attached to birth and death.
Not being free from conditioned phenomena, one is bound and attached by afflictions.
Regarding the dharmas of the six perfections and three wisdoms, as well as precious treasures, wife, and children—
if one cuts through attachment without regret, the path of renunciation will be accomplished.
People have thoughts of good and evil, categorized as superior, middling, and inferior;
revolving through the five realms of existence, their arising and ceasing possess no true nature.
The root of suffering is boundless, arising life after life without ceasing;
the Dharma drum resounds throughout the great trichiliocosm, shaking the realms of Māra.
You multitudes of sentient beings, rely upon the six supernormal powers!
When the mind contemplates the body, it follows accordingly; wherever it goes, there is no obstruction.
Cultivating the Way through the passing years and months, one does not miss the proper timing day or night;
by accumulating merit like Mount Sumeru, one achieves the realization of the Buddha-fruit.
Arising and ceasing are like illusions and transformations, And also like reflections in a mirror;
Entering the thirty-six bases, One enters meditative concentration and thereby attains the Way.
The Tathāgata’s true Dharma Is undefiled and free from attachment.
Practicing loving-kindness, one gives rise to the seven perfections; The various jewels naturally form a necklace.
The thirty-two billion fetters Are bound so tightly they are difficult to untie;
One must use the sword of wisdom To cut them away until nothing remains.
Furthermore, with the nectar-like juice of the Dharma— the eight liberations—
I cause those who are parched with craving to be filled until they are free from conceptual thought.
Formerly, when I had not yet practiced dhyāna, I constantly dwelt amidst a mass of ignorance.
Bound by the four inversions, seeking liberation is difficult to achieve.
Wandering through the four unhindered dhyānas, one is sovereign and free from timidity;
With a concentrated mind and firm resolve, one exhausts all births and no longer undergoes rebirth.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, eight billion four hundred million sentient beings resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, establishing themselves in faithful practice and never again regressing.
The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb, Scroll Three;
The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.

Chapter Eleven: Rejoicing At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Śikhin (Crown King), who, leading twenty-five thousand people, came from the eastern world-system of Pratiṣṭhita to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. After a short while, he withdrew slightly from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

“I have heard that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, possesses immeasurable miraculous transformations while dwelling in the womb to teach and transform beings; that his palace of seven jewels is accomplished of all precious substances, and that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, honor and revere him.”

The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, as well as those of the future and present, have never before spoken of this rare and marvelous Dharma; the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are inexhaustible.
Having accumulated practices through diligent toil over incalculable kalpas, there have been births and deaths throughout that interval.
I now wish to hear how many lands have been transformed by the Tathāgata’s divine power, and what the distinctions between them are.

"May all practices be equalized as they enter the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and may the eight liberations and the pure Brahma-conduct of the youthful ones cause us to forever be free from hesitation.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
“O Great Being, Cūḍāmaṇi! That which you have asked is profound and immeasurable; it brings great benefit, delivering the ignorant and deluded, and its merit is inexhaustible.

At that time, by the power of his samādhi and dhyāna, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm downward, passing through twenty-two billion Buddha-fields, and lifted up the seven-jeweled divine stupa of the Tathāgata Śikhin. It was eighteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Surrounding the stupa was an outer enclosure with railings made of the seven jewels; the ponds, waters, and garden fruits were all composed of the seven jewels. In the bathing pools of the rear garden, there were stairways and balustrades of gold and silver. Within those pools, there was naturally the eight-flavored nectar. On the banks of the water were hundreds and thousands of species of extraordinary birds, such as ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks; their voices sang with plaintive melodies as they enjoyed themselves together in a bliss so supreme it was beyond compare.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to the Bodhisattva King-Crowned:
“The past Buddha Śikhin had a divine stupa made of the seven treasures;
The flower trees were of various colors, with golden flowers and silver stems.”
The waters of the bathing pool possess eight qualities; they satisfy those who are hungry and thirsty.
By providing merit, one obtains its fruit and reward; while in the womb, one’s virtues are perfected.
Next, following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one accords with the fundamental and original Honored One.
The stūpas of that Buddha, made of the seven precious jewels, fill lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
interspersed with various treasures, their bliss is likewise unsurpassed.
After that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, he was the most honored, the foremost, and the most supreme.
There are also stūpas made of the seven treasures, filling the entire realm of empty space.
Those with clear vision and true knowledge revere them with a heart of deep respect;
they eliminate arrogance and do not act haughtily, nor do they crave gain or offerings.
With fruits from ponds of the seven treasures, he contemplated the severance of thoughts and non-attachment;
he also manifested birth from a womb and transformation, spreading [the Dharma] through countless eons.
Following that, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was Kanakamuni.
His divine virtue is profoundly pervasive; those he delivers are twice that of the three Buddhas.
He teaches and transforms his disciples, ensuring that the Three Vehicles are never interrupted.
To the east of this land, within a womb, he manifests transformations.
He exhorts and comforts those who come after, intending to lead them into tranquility.
Next is the Buddha, the Honored Kāśyapa, who sits upright for hundreds of millions of kalpas;
with the devas as his retinue, he remains silent and unmoving.
There is also a stupa made of the seven treasures in the Vajra Buddha-field,
which protects all who have fallen and prevents them from falling into evil paths.
I, Śākyamuni, now emerge with unique valor.
Resolutely fixing his will, he does not cling to the path of birth and death.
Though the Buddha-field be corrupt and evil, those he delivers are immeasurable;
now dwelling within a mother’s womb, he finds joy in his own spiritual transformations.
“Sentient beings of the desire realm and others, falling into the cauldrons of boiling water,
are led forth as if moths casting themselves into a flame.

At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernatural power, transformed this trichiliocosm so that it shone with a brilliant golden light, causing the assembled multitude to see the world of Sukhāvatī.

All those bodhisattvas sit upon lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems; their disciples and retinues are all golden in color; and as for the food and drink they consume, their meditative concentrations, liberations, precepts, and dignified deportment are never at variance with the Dharma.

“O Crown King Bodhisattva! Regarding the merit of having previously manifested in those lands and realms where Buddhas travel and transform beings, and having made offerings and served them—is that merit not great?”
The Bodhisattva Śikhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is very much so, very much so!
World-Honored One!”
"Why is this? The merit of making offerings to even a single Buddha-field is immeasurable; how much more so for as many Buddha-fields as those.
The Buddha said:
"If there is a bodhisattva who has passed beyond the stage of non-retrogression and resides in his final birth before enlightenment, manifesting miraculous transformations while still in the womb—
those who revere such a bodhisattva possess the most supreme merit."
Why is this? Because these Bodhisattvas perform the Buddha-work that is inconceivable.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Śikhin:

"I now tell you that the Eightfold Noble Path which removes the eight inversions surpasses the merit of filling the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with stupas made of the seven treasures; such an offering does not equal the vastest merit of providing a Bodhisattva of the Eightfold Noble Path with robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, medicines for the sick, pounded incense, blended incense, sandalwood, powdered incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and all manner of personal requisites."

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) within the womb-born, transformation-born, moisture-born, and egg-born [beings], practices them for one day, two days, up to seven days; one month, two months, up to seven months; one year, two years, up to seven years; one kalpa, two kalpas, up to seven kalpas—if there were sentient beings who served and made offerings to the aforementioned seven precious stupas, or even to a bodhisattva of the Eightfold Noble Path, their merit would not equal that of this person who makes offerings to the bodhisattva of the four foundations of mindfulness; the latter’s merit is the greatest.

If a Bodhisattva in his final birth before enlightenment turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma while within the mother’s womb, encompassing all manner of countless transformations; if this Great Being of divine virtue moves to and fro without obstruction, yet remains as a single undifferentiated entity;

if there are sentient beings who make offerings and serve him with all the necessities of life without any sense of attachment—just as I today, having severed and extinguished all perceptions throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, now enter the womb for my final body to teach and transform, so that through the realization of spiritual powers all may attain liberation, just like fruit that ripens and changes without ceasing.

The Buddha’s body is empty and devoid of precepts, concentration, wisdom, or liberation; yet it naturally perfumes itself with virtue, morality, and dignified deportment, never losing the twelve dhūta practices—this single aspect of austerity is my domain.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Crown immediately rose from before the Tathāgata and praised him with these verses:
"Consciousness is the root of birth and death, And it is also the path to nirvāṇa;
Resting within the womb, It sports through immeasurable realms."
The four types of beings attain Buddhahood in their lands; With sixteen supernormal powers, they descend [to aid].
In the path where there is originally not a single mark, Their vows are each and all the same.
Because sentient beings are bound by attachments, There appear those who are superior or inferior.
Formless and invisible, it is only now that I am able to observe it.
The bodies of the Buddhas of the past have left behind teachings without limit;
this unsurpassed Dharma of the Eightfold Path leads all sentient beings toward liberation.
The physical form of the Dharma-relics of the sutras spreads through the world by means of supernormal powers;
now those whom I lead and follow shall hear of the inconceivable.
The divine jeweled stupas of the six Buddhas are towers of seven treasures containing precious treasuries.
Each and every point is deeply analyzed; its meaning and flavor are immeasurable.
The path originally traversed by the Buddha is like space, without attachment;
now dwelling in the womb of his divine mother, he receives transformation in manifold ways.
Having attained the Tathāgata-nature, Abiding likewise in the true mark (lakṣaṇa);
With all pride and arrogance removed, I now pay homage to the empty and natureless.
Each and every radiance from the śarīra relics Universally illumines all Buddha-fields;
Those transformed by him are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; this is moved by the Buddha’s spiritual power and virtue.
Though the lands from which they come are far removed from here, they have received the Buddha’s path of ambrosia;
now they wish to return to their own countries to proclaim the Dharma of the Tathāgata.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva King of the Crown (Mūrdhābhiṣikta-rāja) had praised the Buddha with these verses, he circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.

Chapter Twelve: The Search for Consciousness in the Five Paths (*Pañcagati-vijñāna-paryeṣaṇa-parivarta*). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to manifest the destinations of consciousness—namely, the consciousness of the Path and the consciousness of the mundane; conditioned consciousness and unconditioned consciousness; tainted consciousness and untainted consciousness; the consciousness of flowers and the consciousness of fruits; retributive consciousness and non-retributive consciousness; the consciousness of devas and nāgas; the consciousness of ghosts, spirits, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; and extending upward to the consciousness of the twenty-eighth heaven and downward to the consciousness of the Avīci Hell—proceeded to do so.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a skeleton of linked bones within his womb, filling the trichiliocosm.
The Buddha said to Asita:
"Are you able to discern the consciousness within these skeletal remains?"
He replied, “I do not distinguish them. Why is this?
"You have not yet attained thorough penetration, nor has the power of practice reached its full extent.
The Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"In this heaven, have you not yet attained supernatural powers?"
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying,
“There are those who achieve it, and there are those who do not.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
“Observe this skeleton linked by chains; cause all sentient beings to know where consciousness goes, and through discernment and resolution, let them be free from doubt and obstruction.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, took up a divine staff made of seven precious jewels and adamantine, and struck the chained skeleton, listening to the sound of the bones. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This person, at the end of life, had many fetters of anger; their consciousness has fallen among the dragons.”
Next, he again struck the bone:
"This person, having fulfilled the ten tracks of conduct in his previous life, has attained rebirth in the heavens.
Next, he again struck the bone.
"This person, in a previous life, broke the precepts and violated the Vinaya, and was born in hell.

Thus he struck the bones [to discern] the outflowing and non-outflowing, the conditioned and the unconditioned, from the twenty-eighth heaven above down to the Avīci Hell below, revealing the destinations of consciousness and the retributions of good and evil—the white and black karmic results.

There was a whole body-relic (śarīra) without any deficiency; at that time, Maitreya struck it with a staff and sought this consciousness, but he could not find the location of the consciousness at all.
Having struck three times in this manner, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The consciousness of this person is utterly unknowable; could it be that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa?
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"You shall succeed to the Buddha’s position in a future age; you will surely attain Buddhahood and realize the Unsurpassed Way.
Why then do you strike the śarīra, failing to recognize its true location?"
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha is inconceivable and immeasurable; he is beyond the scope of calculation for those such as us.
Now we have a doubt; we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it."
The divine consciousnesses of the five paths are all capable of knowing where the good and evil of others lead; we dare not harbor any doubt regarding the Tathāgata’s domain.
Now, these śarīras remain without deficiency or diminution; we pray that you will explain this consciousness so that we may understand it.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"The dissemination of the relics of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present is not something that can be discerned by your sphere of experience."
Why is this? These relics are my very own relics; how could one possibly investigate the divine consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the Tathāgata?
Now I shall distinguish for you the superior, middling, and inferior consciousnesses of the Tathāgata, up to the *sarvajña* (omniscience), each of which is distinct.

A Bodhisattva in the first stage has not yet established the power of their faculties; although they have attained supernormal powers, a Bodhisattva in the second stage, by observing with the divine eye, knows the destination of those beings—whether they will regress or not—and likewise observes those in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Furthermore, they observe those born in countless *Ganges-sand* numbers of Buddha-fields in the eastern direction, making offerings to various Buddhas and upholding the precepts without hindrance; they also know the number of eons for which those beings have received predictions, from a single eon up to hundreds of thousands of billions of eons.

There may be a bodhisattva who, while in the third stage, perceives that the consciousness of the śarīra and its objects of knowledge proceeds toward either nirvāṇa with remainder or nirvāṇa without remainder; yet, they do not perceive the destination of the consciousness that operates within the fourth stage.

"Bodhisattvas dwelling in the fourth stage perceive the consciousness-dharmas of the first, second, and third stages; yet they do not perceive the destination of the consciousness-dharmas of the śarīra (relics) of the fifth stage.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage differentiate the lower grade; regarding the portion of the sixth stage, they may perceive or not perceive the destination of the consciousness-dharmas."

From non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas up to those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), one does not perceive the direction of the mental consciousness as the Tathāgata lifts or places his feet.

Bodhisattvas at the stages of *anupūrvika* perceive eight, seven, or six [steps], yet even they do not perceive the lifting or placing of the feet of one in their final birth; how much less could one wish to strike the linked skeletons with a hammer to analyze them? Such a thing is impossible.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"You should know this! Regarding the ten titles—Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān—it is only a Buddha who knows the thoughts within the consciousness of a Buddha."
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, spoke in verse:
"Wandering through the depths of the five realms, One’s consciousness and spirit labor in vain;
The defilements of the ears, nose, body, and mind Cannot be removed or left behind by oneself."
The fetters of perception and conceptualization are heavy defilements; They are scraped away with the sword of wisdom.
Wisdom can illuminate the darkness of folly, Enabling one to reach the field of fearlessness.
The Buddha’s consciousness perceives all things universally: The śarīra bones linked together like chains.
Even if ground into dust so fine it cannot be seen, the Tathāgata discerns each one, responding to the laws of good and evil.
The Buddha’s consciousness is most subtle; it neither acts nor does not act.
In one teaching, he delivered ten trillion *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings.
When Maitreya attains Buddhahood again, he too shall relinquish his relics;
regarding the mother from whom he was born, the manner of her conception shall be just as it is now.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Maitreya Bodhisattva circumambulated the Buddha seven times, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to his original seat. Chapter Thirteen:

The Equality of the Practice of All Buddhas and the Absence of Difference *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb* At that time, the World-Honored One again manifested a wondrous and extraordinary form, transforming all the bodhisattvas so that they all became the bodies of Buddhas, complete with radiant marks and signs. They all together, with different mouths but one voice, preached the Dharma, analyzing how impermanence leads to birth and how all that is born returns to extinction.
