Their virtues were immeasurable as they venerated one another; and though they preached the sublime Dharma with majestic deportment and ritual propriety, there was no bowing, yielding, bending, stretching, lowering, or raising. Each sat upon an exquisite, high throne made of the seven treasures, beneath canopies of fine gauze.

In the first teaching, he delivered beings beyond measure, consisting solely of men and no women; in the second teaching, he delivered solely women and no men; in the third teaching, he delivered solely those with right view; in the fourth teaching, he delivered solely those with wrong view; in the fifth teaching, men and women were equal in number; and in the sixth teaching, those with wrong and right views were likewise equal.
At that time, all phenomena were fully accomplished, and the fruit of the Way matured without a self.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas to preach the Dharma, to discourse upon the Dharma, and [to demonstrate] supernormal powers as the third; there are eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of emptiness, eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of signlessness, and eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of wishlessness, each of which contains immeasurable meanings.

It is like a wise person who has a thousand heads, each head having a thousand tongues, and each tongue having a thousand meanings; even if such a person wished to exhaustively master the meaning of these three dharma-gates, they would not attain even one part in a hundred thousand.
"This is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas, all of which has been accomplished through the learning of previous lives.
At that time, the Buddhas, with one voice and in unison, spoke these verses:
"What we originally vowed, is now fully realized and accomplished."
The golden body is supple and resonant, Fully endowed with all the marks of excellence.
Those who seek the infinite wisdom Will ultimately have no doubt;
Excellent, O Honored One of the Three Realms, Supreme and beyond compare!
In the past, when I was in the Tuṣita Heaven, I chose the place of my rebirth;
descending to enter the mother’s womb, I gathered together all the Tathāgatas.
To those external beings who lacked the necessary conditions, they said that I had not attained the Way.
The sentient beings born from wombs and through transformation are twice as many as those at the time of attaining Buddhahood.
The sutras previously and subsequently preached fill eighty-four billion elephants;
even with the strength of elephants and men combined, they could not bear such a load.
May my joyful son possess a powerful memory, never failing or losing it;
though he does not attain the Way through the bequeathed Dharma, may he propagate the True Dharma of the Womb.
The Buddha’s practice is without distinction, equal and without variation.
Only a Buddha can know a Buddha, The meaning of the extent of his merits.
If one wishes to conceive of a Buddha And the extraordinary deeds he performs,
Even through countless eons, One could not attain even a hair’s breadth of it.

At that time, after the Buddhas had spoken these verses, those for whom the first teaching consisted solely of men and no women immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression while seated upon their thrones, their faith being indestructible.
At that time, Śākyamuni withdrew his majestic spiritual power so that he was no different than before, and immediately spoke these verses:
"The fruit of the Eightfold Noble Path is realized; Spontaneously awakened without a teacher;
The leader who walks alone through the three realms Has himself attained the path to Nirvāṇa."
The fundamental nature of phenomena is without a single characteristic; it is the meaning of swift eloquence.
I have now attained this fruition, free from craving and without defilement.
The original nature of the five aggregates is such that neither good nor evil is perceived.
By his supernormal power he delivers beings from suffering, the path of serene and tranquil extinction.
You who have gathered here, your aspirations are now fulfilled;
what was not yet attained has now been gained—how wonderful is this meritorious deed!
Bound by the fetters of causes and conditions, they are forever eliminated until no trace remains;
the net of the self and its dharmas naturally falls into ruin.
Deluded and ignorant, they do not see the truth, and thus fall of their own accord into the conditions of the four colors.
Without yet attaining the contemplation of the secret truth, one discriminates the fundamental nature of suffering.
As for me, now that I have attained the Way, my labors are beyond description;
yet later Buddhas will let out the lion’s roar amidst the blazing fires and evil sword-pestilence kalpas.
The smelting and forging of suffering sentient beings taint their original purity with various colors;
though they endure harm with patience, they do not retaliate when it returns to them.
They hold their minds like empty space, for all things are subject to change and do not abide long.
At that time and in that world, those who commit the five heinous crimes suffer such affliction that they are difficult to transform and impossible to deliver; though not saved by the Buddhas,
for their sake the Buddha immediately manifests the root of conditions to lead them toward the realm of the unconditioned.
Shattering that stubborn and rigid mind, Through single-mindedness, one attains liberation.
At first, he taught the instruction of a single dharma: Non-arising, and no ceasing or perishing;
All are led toward the Buddha-way, Ensuring that none are left behind.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the assembly of men, the assembly of women, the assembly of the righteous, and the assembly of the heterodox all attained complete faith and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
The Buddha again addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:

"You who wish to see the inconceivable path of the Tathāgata’s supernatural transformations, wherein the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fully matured and devoid of male or female; wherein the skillful means of expedient teaching involve receiving a woman's body without the prediction of Buddhahood; and wherein Māra, Śakra, and Brahmā possess no marks of reality."
“Do you wish to know whether these four groups of followers shall attain individual Buddhahood?

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Akṣayamati who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have never heard the Tathāgata preach the Dharma such that these four kinds of people could attain Buddhahood; today, at last, he has been able to expound this great meaning.”
He then addressed the Buddha again:
"Is it by casting off the body, receiving a new body, or attaining Buddhahood in this very body?
The Buddha told Akṣayamati:
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
I shall now distinguish each point for you one by one."

Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Brahmā King named Mahāpratibhāna, who distinguished between the ancient and the present and always delighted in dwelling in seclusion within his celestial palace. He thought:

"Now, I should transform these palace women and the various Brahmās; once I have attained Buddhahood, may the devas attend upon me as my retinue. Having shaved off my hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, to attain the Way all at once—would that not be most delightful?"

Having formed this thought, he immediately went from his celestial palace to the Pārijāta tree; sitting upright in contemplation with single-minded focus, binding his mindfulness before him without any other distracting thoughts, he attained Buddhahood, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics.
The bhikṣus who practiced the true Dharma among the retinues of the devas attained arhatship; all of them possessed sharp faculties.
Among those goddesses, some attained the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, or anāgāmin; they will not return to this world, but shall attain parinirvāṇa right there.
"This is what is meant by the Brahma Heaven King not abandoning his body, receiving a new body, and manifesting his current body to attain the Way of the Buddha.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:

"In the past, seventy-six kalpas ago, there was a sixth heaven king who presided over a trichiliocosm; his name was Haie (Harmful Evil). From the sixth heaven downward, he possessed sovereign power without obstruction."
While dwelling in that celestial palace for countless eons, he reflected deeply:

"I regret my past deeds of slandering the Triple Gem and obstructing the fruits of the Path. Even if I must undergo retribution by falling into the three miserable realms and never escaping the evil paths, it would be better for me now to reform my heart and my evil conduct; together with all the celestial retinues of this palace, we shall collectively cultivate the Brahma-conduct to seek the Unsurpassed Way. Would it not be joyful to advance toward Buddhahood?"
He further reflected to himself:

"The pleasures provided by the entertainment of the goddesses within this sovereign realm are immeasurable and limitless; even if I were to attain Buddhahood, it would be exactly equal to this realm and no different."
Gradually, his indolence and arrogance increased further over the course of kalpas.

Māra had a spiritual friend who, having attained the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), spoke of the Buddha’s merits, describing how he left the household life to cultivate the Way and was fully endowed with all the marks of a great man. Upon hearing this, Māra’s mind was opened and awakened; he changed his heart, entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and became free from discursive thoughts, possessing sharp faculties and swift intelligence.

Immediately within that celestial palace, he attained mastery of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*), adorned the Buddha-lands, and no longer underwent further rebirth; he then became the Unsurpassed, Most True, Perfectly Enlightened One (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddha*). Emitting a great radiance that shone universally throughout the realm of Māra, there was none who did not see with their own eyes as they witnessed Māra becoming a Buddha.
Three hundred million devaputras conceived this thought in their minds:
"This is a magical illusion of Māra, not the true Buddha.

They all withdrew and returned to their palaces. However, one billion six hundred million devaputras came to follow him closely, serving and making offerings to him no differently than they would to the Buddha; immediately upon their seats, they all attained the four fruits of the path.
"This is how the Great Heavenly King Haimavata, without abandoning his current body, underwent a transformation of existence and attained the Buddha-way.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:

"In the past, sixty-one kalpas ago, there was a Śakra-devānām-indra in the eastern direction who cultivated the purity of the divine eye and delighted his mind in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). He constantly desired to seek renunciation and advance toward the Buddha-way."

When the signs of decline appeared among those devas, indicating that their lives would soon end, their retinues gradually diminished. They became attached to sleep, their bodies were covered in dust and grime, and their celestial flowers withered on their own. They took no pleasure in their jeweled thrones and found their food distasteful. Thereupon, they went out to the rear gardens to bathe and wash themselves, thinking:

"Now, with this celestial body, my eyes can see through to all directions. In which direction is there a Buddha? I shall go there to pay homage, offer service and offerings, and receive the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts; by means of this very body, I shall attain the Way of Buddhahood."

Having formed this thought, he sat upright in contemplation and, with his divine eye, beheld above a Buddha named Immeasurable Sky-Walker (Amitagati), whose world was named Pure (Vimalā). He was currently preaching the Dharma, which was excellent in its beginning, middle, and end.

Then, by means of his supernormal power, in the time it takes a person to bend and extend their arm, he arrived at the place of that Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
He then praised the Buddha’s virtues with these verses:
“Your radiant marks illuminate the ten directions, Subduing all the hosts of Māra’s enemies;”
He reveals the path of the Way, severing doubt so that there is forever no delusion.
Those of pure Brahma-conduct all receive his most supreme practice;
he preaches the true Dharma according to their capacities, never deviating from the fundamental laws of conduct.
"I am the lord of the devas, desiring to cultivate the pure path;
may the Buddha deign to have compassion for me, so that I may reach the place of peace.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

You have conceived a vast aspiration to rescue sentient beings from suffering: to cause those who have not attained to attain, those who have not acquired to acquire, and those who have not accomplished to achieve accomplishment; to cause the blind to see light, the deaf to hear sound, the hunchbacked to straighten their backs, and those without hands or feet to obtain them. Return now to your own palace and sit beneath the Bodhi tree to distinguish the various aggregates of phenomena—those that are gathered and those that are dispersed.”
Upon hearing these words, Śakra immediately came forward to pay homage to the Buddha; having failed to find him there, he returned to his celestial palace.

All the celestial retinues came to seek refuge in him, and his merit grew ever more magnificent. The signs of decline were forever extinguished without remainder; sitting upright with body and mind composed and unwavering, he attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The ninety-three billion celestial maidens he led attained the fruits of the four paths; this is called the Deva Śakra not abandoning his body, but attaining the Buddha-way through a transformation-body.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
"Fifty-four billion Ganges-sands of kalpas ago, there was a world named Flame."
The Buddha is named Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
He teaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, skillfully cultivating the holy life, and bestows the gift of the Four Noble Truths upon all.
The people of that land all assume female bodies; they understand impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and through discernment they enter into states free from afflictions.

Loathing the suffering of the body, they share a single vow and give rise to great, far-reaching resolve, donning the armor of fearlessness with the desire to deliver sentient beings, purify Buddha-lands, and eliminate [defilements].
Regarding impurity, they established firm resolve and delighted in non-retrogression.

At that time, there were seventy-two trillion women in a vast wilderness, a place frequented by non-human beings, who were all practicing in unison. Having realized the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, in a single day and at a single moment, they attained the threefold penetration and immediately perfected the Buddha-way. They were endowed with all the marks, possessed mastery over life and death, and could enter the small through the large and the large through the small. On that very day, they delivered incalculable and immeasurable sentient beings, leading them to nirvana without remainder; this is called attaining the Buddha-way by not abandoning the present body to receive a new one.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The nature of dharmas is like the great ocean; It does not record whether there is right or wrong.
Ordinary beings and sages alike— They are equal, without high or low.”
It depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements; to realize the proof is as easy as turning over one's hand.
When the Way is perfected, one reigns over the three realms and proclaims the lion’s roar.
To discriminate is fundamentally without dharma; there is no practice of male or female.

"Now, dwelling in this world of five turbidities, one who currently possesses a physical body yet severs the view of annihilationism and abandons the calculation of permanence will remain obstructed for the duration of many kalpas.
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these verses, eighty-four trillion sentient beings established firm resolve; they all vowed to attain Buddhahood without undergoing further rebirths.

Chapter Fourteen: On the Definitive and Indefinite Practice of Samādhi At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Constant Laughter (*Nityaprahasita*). He possessed the six supernormal powers and profound discernment; his power of virtue was sovereign, and his eloquence was fearless. Having exhausted the bounds of birth and death, he was unattached to the four [dhātus]. His words were trusted and accepted, and he understood that all dharmas are empty—like a transformation, like a dream, like a mirage, like a red leaf floating in water that a foolish beast mistakes for meat but fails to obtain when the water dries up, or like an echo in the mountains. He thoroughly realized that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, desiring to sever the doubts of all sentient beings.
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One, I have a slight doubt or lingering confusion; if you would grant me leave, I would venture to speak of it."

The Tathāgata, the Great Sage, possesses unimpeded divine wisdom: he foreknows the past, understanding how beings are bound by causes and conditions and how their various activities accumulate; he clearly perceives the future, discerning the success or failure of destinies, the convergence and dispersal of causes and conditions, and the differing ways in which virtuous and non-virtuous karmic actions arise from the initial resolve of the mind.

Now I have heard that the Tathāgata’s activities for the sake of sentient beings born from wombs or eggs differ: there are those with resistance and those without resistance; those with retribution and those without retribution; and those with black-and-white actions and those without black-and-white actions.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, from their first aspiration, pass through kalpas without attaining accomplishment; yet there are also sentient beings who, upon conceiving the mind of the Way in the morning, immediately attain Buddhahood.
"I wish to hear it with joy; may the World-Honored One please speak.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Constant Laughter:

"The meaning of what you have asked is entirely moved by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata; it is intended to bring all dharmas to fulfillment, so as not to sever the true nature of the Tathāgatas of the past and future."
"Why is this? Because the *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata cannot be grasped or maintained, nor is it something known by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately manifested his broad and long tongue through his supernormal powers; the radiance from the mark of his tongue illuminated infinite *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields in the eastern direction, causing sentient beings of the five realms who beheld the light to follow that light and arrive at the place where the Tathāgata was.

At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which shone upward, reaching the sentient beings in eighty-four billion Ganges-sand world-systems as far as the abode of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Constant Laughter and spoke in verse:
"Thirty-one sounds and resonances, Whose karmic retribution is pure and white;
Forty-eight defilements, And fifty-five celestial practices."
The Bodhisattva’s seven-jeweled hair awakens the minds of sentient beings;
the trees of the four fruits of the path have minds and consciousness fixed and undisturbed.
Those with meager wisdom and no merit receive many retributions for their verbal karma.
Knowing moderation in eating, maintaining dignified deportment in walking,
and regarding all beings with an impartial mind of compassion— this is what is called the path of a bodhisattva.
In this world of the five turbidities within the three realms of existence, beings are inverted and attached to the realm of Māra.
The roots of wholesome karma are destroyed, yet like a shadow they do not depart.
The nature of the faculties may be sharp or dull, and the mind’s progress and retreat are unstable;
yet by making the vow to deliver sentient beings, one’s merit becomes fully perfected.
The body endowed with the ten powers is a conditioned phenomenon of the mundane world;
its contemplation is difficult to measure, for as one ceases, another arises again.
Like fire consuming a mountain forest, the mind’s thoughts ignite the phenomena of existence.
Extensively reaching as far as incalculable [worlds], his body is clad in the armor of *saṃnāha*.
With valor he subdues those who are difficult to transform;
from the pores of his human body, sixty-four thousand [rays] emerge, their wisdom able to discern and distinguish all things.
Due to the karmic retribution of his past deeds, he was born in Jambudvīpa with an extremely hideous form; every pore was covered in hair.
Sparse and coarse, lacking any density, it was unlike the adamantine body of the Tathāgata.
The pores and hairs are thirty-seven in number, Densely packed and without gaps.
They cannot be burned by fire; Neither Māra nor the Māras’ devas, Nor śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, Nor Brahmā or the hosts of Śakra [can harm them].
Even with supernatural powers, spirits, and the like, one might wish to sever a single hair from the Buddha’s body, yet this can never be accomplished.
The realm of space might become the earth, and the sun and moon might fall; [but such a feat remains impossible].
To wish to sever the Buddha’s hair and beard is ultimately impossible.
This is the karma of worldly phenomena, not the characteristic of the unconditioned;
one receives the retributive fruits of performed karma, and their various characteristics each differ.
The Buddha’s body is of vajra-nature; its external appearance is the result of karmic retribution.
This, too, is a worldly retribution, far removed from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The true Dharma of the Buddha’s marks never manifests externally.
"If you wish to know the internal characteristics of a Buddha, it is this: the miraculous power that moves and transforms.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Constant Laughter:

"The retribution of conditions, the retribution of the conditions of conditions, the retribution of the unobstructed ultimate Way, the retribution of the true nature of the Three Jewels, the retribution of practicing toward Nirvana, the retribution of non-attachment to the mundane world, and the retribution of single-minded ultimate realization—these are called the most supreme primary meaning of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."

It is unstained and unattached, incapable of being grasped or maintained; it does not cling to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), nor is it apart from the realm of desire. It transcends the past, future, and present; it is not a retribution of the past, the future, or the present. It is without arising and without cessation. For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained unobstructed penetration, causing sentient beings of equal disposition to understand the fundamental nature of emptiness as their own retribution, and achieving mastery over vocal karma such that his resonance is fully realized.

"Or there may be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, in a single moment, can cause the trichiliocosm to become a water realm, just as a bhikṣu who has attained dhyāna contemplates an immeasurable water realm. In this watery nature, aquatic creatures such as soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, tortoises, and turtles are not disturbed or harmed; through the merit of kalpas of accumulated practice, it is neither destroyed nor decays. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s entry into the water-realm samādhi."

There may be sentient beings who, seeing the Bodhisattva enter meditative concentration, mistake it for water; or they may take tiles, stones, grass, or wood and throw them into the "water" of the Bodhisattva in concentration. Yet the Bodhisattva’s mind is like empty space, and he does not perceive any touch or disturbance. This is called the power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva entering the water-element.

“Furthermore, there may be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, having gathered his mind through meditative concentration, enters the *tejodhātu-samādhi*, causing this trichiliocosm to blaze forth as fire. Deluded and ignorant sentient beings think that the bodhisattva has encountered the conflagration of the kalpa and flee in all four directions, yet they do not leave the presence of the pure and heatless light of the fire. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva entering the *tejodhātu-samādhi*.
The majestic power of this samādhi is difficult to fathom, and it cannot be investigated even by arhats or pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who enter the immovable meditative state of the fivefold dharma-body (pañcāṅga-dharmakāya), whereby they cause all classes of wriggling and crawling creatures within the trichiliocosm, down to the smallest ants, to be received through their majestic power so that they do not encounter afflictions for seven days and remain in peace; subsequently, when their lives end, they are all reborn in the heavens.

Just as I today preach the Dharma in various places and manifest transformations everywhere, those who behold the Tathāgata’s divine power have all their defilements extinguished and are reborn according to their vows, whether in this world or in the Buddha-fields of other directions; this is what is induced by the concentration of the fivefold Dharma-body of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the *asaṃhārya-siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*, he is able to cause the trichiliocosm to quake in six ways. All sentient beings therein submit to him, cultivating pure conduct, donning the garment of shame and remorse, and casting off arrogance. He leads sentient beings to the Eightfold Noble Path, removes the notion of self from the seventy-seven mental states, and eliminates all accumulated defilements and stains in a single moment. This is called the awe-inspiring movement of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s fearless prowess.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the meditative concentration of the dissolution of the body (*kāyavibheda-samādhi*), he discerns the aggregate of consciousness as to whence it comes and whither it goes. He discerns each part as empty, non-existent, and quiescent, with no beginning, end, or middle. This is called the manifestation of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s entry into the meditative concentration of the dissolution of the body."

"Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the Samādhi of the Pinnacle of Patience, he is able to cause this body to become handless and footless insects that fill the trichiliocosm. Sentient beings who see them cannot name them, perceiving them only as masses of flesh; yet those who take them as food find their taste to be like nectar, which completely satisfies the hunger and thirst of all sentient beings. This is called the miraculous manifestation produced by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva entering the Samādhi of the Pinnacle of Patience."

"Furthermore, there may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by the power of samādhi, cause the mountains, rivers, and rocky walls of this trichiliocosm to transform into ambrosia, appearing like rock honey, such that one never tires of eating it; they cause the four heavy afflictions of those sentient beings to be eliminated forever without remainder. Sentient beings then make vows, aspiring to be born in the World of Infinite Life. This is called the manifestation of the spiritual power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the Samādhi of Solitary Progress, he causes all sentient beings throughout this trichiliocosm to see the Bodhisattva’s walking—whether lifting or lowering his feet. Those who encounter the Bodhisattva and witness his strides are able to restrain themselves from falling into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm. This is entirely due to the purity of the Bodhisattva’s body, speech, and mind; having made a vow to deliver others to ultimate liberation, he never regresses. This is called the manifestation of the immeasurable virtuous merit and mental vows of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through the concentration of supernormal powers, enters the *dharmasvabhāva-samādhi* (the samādhi of the nature of dharmas), causing all classes of sentient beings in this trichiliocosm to come and seek refuge at the Bodhisattva’s place, requesting to leave the household life and cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*) with a unified resolve. Having shaved off their hair and beards and donned the dharma-robes, they are then instructed in the teachings on majestic deportment and prohibitive precepts according to the constant law of all Buddhas;

thus, they are able in a single moment to abide in the stage of clear wisdom (*vidyā-bhūmi*). This stage of clear wisdom is the practice of Bodhisattvas in the eighth abode (*aṣṭama-vihāra*), which cannot be cultivated by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); this is called the manifestation of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s spiritual power."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through the Buddha’s great compassion, enters the unimpeded samādhi, acting as parents, brothers, friends, kinsmen, and acquaintances to all classes of beings within this trichiliocosm. He provides them with wealth where they lack it, granting whatever is required—up to kingdoms, property, wives, children, elephants, horses, gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, agate, white pearls, amber, crystal, lapis lazuli, jade, and various treasures; clothing, food and drink, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick. He causes them to be fully satisfied with fragrant flowers and perfumes, and therein he teaches and transforms them so that each attains fulfillment, inspiring sentient beings to abide in the ground of delighting in the Dharma."
What is the stage of delighting in the Dharma?
For those who should be guided toward the path of the *srotāpanna*, he teaches them the essential truth for severing the three views;
for those who should be *sakṛdāgāmins*, he teaches them that through seven births they shall eventually attain the Way.
To those who are candidates for the stage of Anāgāmin, he teaches the wholesome Dharma that is free from the obscuration of the five aggregates;
to those who are candidates for Arhatship, he teaches the realization of Nirvana without doubt;
and to those who are candidates for the Bodhisattva path, he teaches the Dharma of the six perfections and the supreme patience, so that they may resolve their minds and advance toward it.
To those who are directed toward the Buddha-way, he speaks of the ultimate purity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

He cultivates and purifies buddha-fields and transforms sentient beings, traveling from one buddha-land to another, making offerings to and serving the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and attaining the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): his eye can see through all things, his ear can hear through all things, he knows his own past lives and the minds of others, his body can fly, and all defilements are exhausted; furthermore, he no longer harbors doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha. This is called the power manifested by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s entry into the *dharmaprīti-samādhi*.

"Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the Vajra Samādhi, he can cause the trichiliocosm to transform into the seven treasures, providing for the destitute and the needy; to those seeking drink he gives drink, and to those seeking food he gives food, and he immediately preaches to them the fruits of stinginess and greed."

If a person is greedily attached, at death they will enter the evil realms of hungry ghosts or animals; they will be impoverished and barefoot, their clothing failing to cover their bodies, and loathed by others; or they will become slaves or servants, driven by others, or fall among the animals to bear heavy burdens.

At times, the Bodhisattva teaches them the practice of non-lustfulness for the sake of rebirth in heaven, explaining that lust is defiled and evil, leading to death and entry into the evil realms: the mountain of knives and swords, the chariots of fire and glowing coals, the Iron Jaw hell, the Black Rope hell, the Boiling Excrement hell, and the Ice Mountain and Pestle hell, where one undergoes immeasurable suffering.
Or they may enter the Lotus or Utpala hells, where winds blow and flames scorch until their bones and joints fall apart.

Amidst this, the Bodhisattva preaches to them the impermanence of the body: it is not a place for long dwelling; it is like fire struck from flint, or lightning passing in a day—a manifold illusion. Why endure such suffering while your spirit rots away, with no hope of escape?

In this way, the bodhisattva expounds the essential truth for them, causing those who have incurred retribution to completely extricate themselves from suffering and reach the ground where there is no suffering; this is called the movement of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva through the power of the Buddha’s great compassion, samādhi, and concentrated mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Sentient beings who desire liberation From the obstacles of the three realms and five paths,
Should be diligent and never indolent, Abiding securely in the unconditioned path.”
Just as when a person builds a house, it is not accomplished by mere timber;
first one must prepare the ground, and next erect the walls and pillars.
The Buddha-way is like the great void; it is not accomplished by a single practice alone.
Hold fast to your resolve with firm stability; let the mind be free from attachment and longing.
Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have passed away, and those yet to come shall never be exhausted.
Some achieve realization through gradual stages, while others transcend them entirely.
I have now awakened those who were not yet awakened, leading them to the Eightfold Noble Path;
having heard this, they shall not receive it again—by whom was this Dharma created?
In the past, when I contemplated the sacrifice of my own body, I did not find the number of kalpas to be difficult.
Self-awakened without a teacher, he has become a guide for all.
When a Teacher appears in the world, he does not descend by chance;
wishing to deliver those yet undelivered, he reveals the city of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

When the World-Honored One spoke these verses, fifty-six billion sentient beings—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River—extinguished their deluded perceptions and ceased all further longing for worldly household affairs; simultaneously, they made vows to seek the unsurpassed path.
The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.

Chapter Fifteen: Entering the Realms of the Six Classes of Sentient Beings At that time, the World-Honored One entered the meditative concentration of immeasurable universal observation (*anantavyūha-samādhi*).

Observing that the minds of those in the assembly harbored doubts and hesitations, and wishing to resolve their uncertainties by manifesting the truth, he immediately extended his right toe and pressed it down upon this earth-element, causing the sentient beings of the six destinies to each manifest their respective modes of conduct, arrayed and standing before him.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly:
"Do you all see these sentient beings of the six realms? They replied:
“Yes, I have seen them.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Īśvara, who had attained the inexhaustible dharma-gate of the *Gaganagañja* (Space-Treasury) and possessed divine wisdom and eloquence such that his responses were unimpeded—this being the foremost among the sixteen noble sons of this Bhadrakalpa. Wandering through the lands of the ten directions, he performed the Buddha’s work. He then rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Now, O Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, I wish to hear you speak of the karmic fruits and retributions of the beings within the six realms of existence.”
"Your question is subtle and profound; we pray that you will grant us an explanation at this time.
At that moment, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene and joyful countenance in the midst of the great assembly.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, that they do not smile without cause; there must be a reason for their smile.
If there are sentient beings born in the Brahma Heaven, at that time the Buddha smiles;
if there are those destined to become Wheel-Turning Sage Kings, the Buddha again smiles;
and if there are those who become the wardens of hell, King Yama, the Buddha likewise smiles.
When there were those who had taken birth in the bodies of hungry ghosts, the Buddha immediately smiled;
when there were those who had become kings of animals, the Buddha likewise smiled.

At that time, five-colored light issued from the Blessed One’s face, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm, and then returned to be absorbed back into the crown of his head. He then addressed the Bodhisattva Īśvara:
"What you have asked is sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata and protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions; thus you are able to pose this question.
I shall now explain to you, one by one, the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of sentient beings within the six realms of existence."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy. The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Sovereign:

"Now, look up toward the east and observe the Brahmā Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Śuddhāvāsa Brahmā Heaven, and so on up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. These gods and humans previously cultivated the Brahma-conduct; they are all of the Buddha-seed who have cultivated various merits. Yet, because they were stained by attachment to the five pleasures through their craving for karmic rewards, they received celestial bodies as the fruit of the path due to those causes and conditions. I shall now explain to you one by one the calculation and measurement of the blessings of these Brahmā heavens."
Filling this trichiliocosm, there were universal monarchs (cakravartin) accompanied by their retinues of the seven treasures.
As for these seven treasures: first was the elephant treasure, possessing thirty-two tusks and pure white hair; its feet tread upon lotus flowers, and its body is capable of flight.

Second is the Horse Treasure: its body is deep blue-black in color with a mane and tail of vermilion; it is able to fly through the air without obstruction wherever it goes, and it knows the thoughts in people's minds.
Third is the Jewel Treasure: its radiance shines through, filling the entirety of space and illuminating all four continents.

Fourth is the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*). The wheel has a thousand spokes, exquisitely carved and engraved; one never tires of gazing upon it. This is the fourth insentient treasure. Fifth is the Woman-Treasure (*strīratna*). She is the most exquisite among women, her nature and conduct gentle and mild;

she is so exceptionally beautiful that she is rare in the world. She is neither tall nor short, neither too fair nor too dark. Her body emits the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and her mouth the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*). She is reverent and humble, understanding the noble king’s intentions and inclinations.

Sixth, there is the Treasure-Store Keeper Minister; whenever the king requires jewels, he takes the divine vessel in his hand, uses it to scoop from the void, and pours out whatever jewels are needed, taking or ceasing at the king's will.
Seventh is the Jewel of the Military Commander. When the Holy King goes forth on a tour, he requires the fourfold army; the King addresses him, saying:
"I now wish to go abroad on a tour of the realm; quickly assemble the troops before my palace so that not even a shadow shall shift."
He immediately obeyed the king’s command; turning his body to look east, he saw the elephant troops already assembled in formation to the east;
turning his body to gaze south, he saw the cavalry already assembled in formation to the south;
turning his body to look west, he saw the chariot troops already assembled in formation to the west.
Turning his body to look north, he saw that the infantry had already assembled in ranks to the north.

The Wheel-Turning Sage King would mount whatever he desired—whether horse or elephant—and travel to Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru, or Aparagoyānī; wandering through the four quarters with his feet never touching the ground, he enjoyed natural blessings for a hundred years, a thousand years, or even several thousand years.
Even if the body of a Cakravartin Universal Monarch were to fill the four continents, it would not equal the body of Śakra. Why is this?

For Śakra presides over seven precious palaces and a retinue of jade maidens; seated within his seven-jeweled hall, he delights in celestial music, forgetting the east while looking west and forgetting the south while looking north—his bliss is beyond words.

That Śakra’s body is not equal to that of the sixth Heavenly King; his body possesses thirty marks, his spiritual power is sovereign, he manifests transformations according to form, and they are accomplished by mere thought. The troops he leads are beyond counting, and his meritorious deeds and blessings, as well as his practice of giving, are unimpeded.

The merit of the six heavenly kings and others who fill the four continents does not equal the vastness of the merit of a single Great Brahmā Heaven king, who presides over a trichiliocosm; his assembly of Brahmā deities is immeasurable, limitless, and incalculable, and his lifespan is exceedingly long, ending only after more than one Bhadrakalpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Īśvara:
"Now, lift your eyes and look to the south; there, countless wheel-turning sage-kings (cakravartin-rājas) stand in a row to the south."

The extent of the merits of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is as described above: observing the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, reverently serving the worthy and holy, maintaining the vows of the rishis, and practicing the eightfold pure fast; with faculties thus interconnected, acting with compassion for humanity and a heart free from harm, the karmic retribution he receives is of incalculable merit.
"Therefore, you shall succeed to the position of a Wheel-Turning King.

The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Sovereign: "Now look westward; you see the Lion King standing in a row on the western side. He stands firm and motionless through his constant practice of the six matters; his fur is pure white and his chest is square and upright—all resulting from the meritorious retribution of his virtuous conduct in previous lives. Although he has received the body of a beast, he distinguishes between good and evil; his feet tread upon lotus flowers, unsullied by dust or defilement, and he never kills living beings, eats meat, or drinks blood."

At the single roar of a lion, birds fly away, beasts fall, and those that run crouch down; this too is a reward obtained because one did not violate the three transgressions of the five precepts, such that although one fell into the realm of animals, one turned to attain the Way upon changing bodies.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Sovereign King: "Turn your gaze northward and look upon the seven-jeweled palaces of the hungry ghosts;

their attendants on all sides all partake of the natural nectar of the Dharma-flavor. Although they bear the name 'hungry ghost,' it is because they were protected by the accumulated merits of their time among humans. They also possess spiritual powers to reach various Buddha-fields, where they pay homage to the Buddhas and receive the essential teachings. They know when to act and know how to act; they know when to abide and know how to abide. Their movements respond to the times without adhering to fixed laws. They roam this Sahā world where all virtues converge; if they turn toward it, they shall achieve the Way before long."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Īśvara:
"Turn your gaze downward and look; you shall see King Yama governing and transforming beings through five matters, without any crookedness.
What are these five?"
The sinner was immediately interrogated face-to-face:
"While you were among humans, did you know there is a Buddha, there is the Dharma, there is the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, and that there are fathers and mothers?"
The sinner replied, "Indeed there are,
Great King!"
At that time, the Holy King asked in verse:
“Manacles, fetters, and iron chains; The cauldron of boiling water and the heated copper pillar;
Molten bronze, hot tongs, and forks— The retribution for these shall not be long delayed.”
The root of causes and conditions is created by oneself; the retribution of karma is not made by another.
Neither parents nor brothers can take one's suffering upon themselves—who else could?
I vow to leave the household life to study, observing the precepts without transgression.
"Even those who practice the equality of the True Dharma are still boiled three times a day.
At that time, King Yama questioned them with these five matters and immediately commanded the wardens of hell to hand them over for punishment according to the gravity of their offenses.

When those among the sinful hear the sound of the Buddha-dharma, their offenses are extinguished and merit arises; they return once more to human form and cultivate pure conduct. This is called the Bodhisattva’s such-like retribution for sentient beings within the six realms of existence.

After the Bodhisattva Sovereign had prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his original position, there were eight thousand *koṭis* of sentient beings in that assembly who took no pleasure in dwelling in suffering or falling into the paths of the six realms; they all resolved for supreme, quiescent emptiness and departed from birth and death.
Chapter Sixteen: Turning the Wheel of Dharma The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra, Chapter Sixteen: Turning the Wheel of Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One was about to manifest the immeasurable physical relics and karmic responses of all Buddhas, so as to cause all those in the assembly—the *bodhisattvas* with supernormal powers, those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and *upāsakas*—[to witness them].
Surrounded by the fourfold assembly of *bhikṣus*, *bhikṣuṇīs*, *upāsakas*, and *upāsikās*, he manifested the receiving of retribution in this very life and turned the Great Wheel of Dharma—
a wheel that neither śramaṇas, brahmins, Māras, nor devas of Māra could turn. By means of his supernormal power and concentration,
he emitted light from all the joints and pores of his body, shining far across the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
Within each and every ray of light, there are three thousand great thousandfold Buddha-lands; in each and every Buddha-land, there are manifested Buddhas;
and in each and every manifested Buddha, there are the various classes of sentient beings of three thousand great thousandfold worlds.
Each of these Buddhas expounds the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma to those in their respective assemblies—a teaching of infinite wonders, peerless and beyond compare.
The Dharma and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are profoundly deep; that which is taught therein is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
It removes lust, anger, and delusion, and uses the waters of the eight liberations to wash away the defilements of the mind.

At that time, the Buddhas manifested within the waters of the pond a high platform made of the seven treasures, rising seven fathoms above the surface. Upon that jeweled platform, they arranged high thrones of precious gems; at each of the four corners hung golden bells, interspersed with various other jewels, and suspended were silk banners and canopies in five colors—red and yellow—such that the bliss was beyond description.

At that time, the beings seated there heard the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma; sitting upright in contemplation with undistracted minds, they all aspired to hear the secret essentials of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, according to the constant practice of all Buddhas, again emitted light from his *uṣṇīṣa*, which extended upward to countless billions of Buddha-fields.

In a Buddha-field within the realm of empty space, there was a Buddha named Ratna Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Seeing the light from the *uṣṇīṣa* of Śākyamuni, he immediately addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas in that land:

“Below there is a Buddha, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He is currently in his mother’s womb extensively expounding the profound and essential, unsurpassed treasury of the Dharma, drawing forth bodhisattvas from the ten directions who possess supernatural powers. You should go to pay him homage and inquire after his welfare, and also convey my name to Śākyamuni, asking whether his virtuous transformation is daily advancing and whether he is in good health as he moves about.”
"Are the sentient beings of that land easy to transform?
You should maintain your dignified deportment when you go there; for the sentient beings of that land are subject to much affliction and harm, and their arrogance is rampant."

At that time, the bodhisattvas of that land adjusted their Dharma robes; fifty-seven million two hundred million bodhisattvas prostrated at the feet of that Buddha and, vanishing instantly, arrived in this Saha world.

The Buddha Śākyamuni, again employing the supernormal power of meditative concentration, caused those bodhisattvas who had come to not see Śākyamuni. He surrounded the site where he preached the Dharma on all four sides, extending from Jambudvīpa throughout the trichiliocosm, so that they could search for the Buddha Śākyamuni in the Sahā world-system.
Those bodhisattvas each said to one another:
"The realm of empty space above is extremely far from our own buddha-fields. Is it not possible that the Buddha Śākyamuni is about to enter parinirvāṇa and has emitted this light?"
"Have we attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) without loss?
For what reason?
Though we travel throughout the ten directions and all worlds, we do not know where [the Buddha] is located."
Each of them conceived this thought within themselves:
"We would rather return to our own realms.

Having formed this thought, none of them were able to reach their original Buddha-fields. Each was filled with fear, the hair on their bodies stood on end, and they thought that they had lost their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and that weariness had arisen in their minds, preventing them from exhausting the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma.
Why is this? It is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of Śākyamuni.
The Buddha, fully knowing the minds of those bodhisattvas, immediately employed his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to receive the bodhisattvas into the mother’s womb.
At that time, the bodhisattvas paid their respects with increased reverence and, having been sent by the Buddha to inquire after his well-being, each sat to one side.

Then, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, further manifested great radiance through his supernormal power, illuminating the world-system of Jvalana in the eastern direction. That land was named Kūṭa, and its Buddha was named Gambhīrārtha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He was currently teaching the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end. Seeing the great radiance, he addressed the bodhisattvas:
"You should adorn yourselves and proceed to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha in the Sahā world to hear the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma, which will bring great benefit."
"Why is this? For in that land, all the bodhisattvas are in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha); there must surely be extraordinary and inconceivable dharmas there.

The bodhisattvas respectfully received the Buddha’s instruction, prostrated at the feet of that Buddha, and suddenly vanished. They arrived at the realm of Endurance (Sahā-lokadhātu) where they went to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha; bowing their heads to his feet in salutation, they each sat to one side.
The Buddha summoned the Māra Pāpīyas by means of his spiritual power; because he intended to produce a profound transformation, he caused the Māra to arrive.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew that the sentient beings had assembled, and the devas performed music and offered hymns of praise for the immeasurable meritorious deeds of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Cease the music of the devas; I wish to preach the Dharma.
The Buddha then addressed those who had gathered for the assembly:

“The appearance of a Buddha in the world occurs but once in hundreds of millions of billions of kalpas, like the udumbara flower. For a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the fundamental dharma of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) consists of this: the elimination of mental constructions and the removal of recollections is called ‘exhaustion’;
not perceiving the state of non-conceptualization where outflows are exhausted is called ‘non-exhaustion.’”
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva calculates upon the body and remains bound by attachment, failing to reach the other shore, this is called "having an end.
If they can eliminate the perception of a body and abide neither here nor there, this is called "without end."
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already untied their fetters and bonds yet does not abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), this is called "having an end.
When they do not perceive the emptiness of fetters and bonds nor the notion of self, this is called "without end."
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the contemplation of inhalation and exhalation and realizes that all worlds are utterly non-existent, this is called "having an end.

When they discern emptiness and non-existence, seeing neither those who are saved nor those who are not saved, and perceiving no multiplicity in the realms of nations, this is called "being without end."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the sixteen sublime dharmas to deliver incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings, this is called "having an end.
When the self-nature of these sixteen sublime dharmas is empty and quiescent, such that neither deliverance nor non-deliverance is perceived, this is called "without end."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas extensively cultivate buddha-fields, yet do not consider it a hardship to take up suffering for the sake of sentient beings, this is called "having an end.
When they do not perceive sentient beings or buddha-fields as either pure or impure, nor as being one or many, this is called "being without end."
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva reverently upholds the precepts, cultivates the Dharma, and enters the three gates of liberation, this is called "having an end.
When they do not perceive sentient beings as having deficient precepts or complete precepts, this is called "without end."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva clearly understands and discriminates the meanings of phrases, meanings of sentences, and meanings of syllables according to their appropriate applications without fixed direction, this is called 'having an end.
Not perceiving the meanings of phrases while discriminating the meanings of syllables is called 'without end.'"

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva discriminates between the realms of gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hells, and therein delivers beings so that they attain liberation, this is called "having an end.
Although he dwells within the five turbidities, he is unstained; being unstained, he has no attachment. This is called "without end."

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva eliminates greed and arrogance yet remains free from overweening pride, and likewise does not disparage himself while cultivating pure conduct, this is called "having an end.

When the nature of phenomena is empty and quiescent, such that there is no mind of self-aggrandizement, no perception of negligence or sloth regarding the Dharma, and no perception of diligent effort toward receiving the realization of the fruits of the Path, this is called "without end."

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva adorns the Buddha-tree and expounds countless teachings, with a pure voice heard throughout the ten directions, destroying attachment and inducing the practice of giving—this is called "having an end.
When one does not perceive the formation and destruction, the arising and ceasing of worlds, nor harbor attachment therein—this is called "without end."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva shatters the fetters of the triple world with a diamond-like mind; from the first aspiration until the stage of non-retrogression, they do not perceive sentient beings as subject to annihilation or obstruction—this is called "having an end.
They are free from attachment to a self and realize there is neither "I" nor "mine"; how could there be a self when the very notion of self is itself non-existent? This is called "being without end."

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva extinguishes their clan name, they do not cling to worldly dharmas by saying, "This is mine" or "this is not mine," or "This is my father, this is my mother, this is my elder brother, this is my younger brother. They do not think, "My clan is supreme while that clan is inferior," or "I am a son of noble birth while he is not a son of noble birth. To calculate such names and titles is called "having an end.

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, one does not see the existence of a 'becoming' nor does one see a 'Buddha. All provisional names and designations are entirely empty and quiescent; one does not see even emptiness as existing. How can there be emptiness? Who created this emptiness?
"Since emptiness itself is empty, how can one speak of it as 'empty'? This is called the inexhaustible.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva explains the Dharma, explains the meaning, explains the phrases, and explains the syllables—ranging from ignorance (*avidyā*) to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and even unto birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)—and if the causal conditions of the dharmas of ignorance, craving, and grasping are not exhausted; if they remain bound by the delusions and inversions of ignorance, passing from darkness into darkness, and are unable to be pulled out and rescued—this is called the exhaustible."

With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;

with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise. By eliminating attachment, bondage, and clinging, one becomes free from attachment. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.

Old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise conditioned by birth; birth arises conditioned by becoming; becoming arises conditioned by clinging; clinging arises conditioned by craving; craving arises conditioned by feeling; feeling arises conditioned by contact; contact arises conditioned by the six sense bases; the six sense bases arise conditioned by name-and-form; name-and-form arises conditioned by consciousness; consciousness arises conditioned by volitional formations;

and volitional formations arise conditioned by ignorance. With the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, volitional formations cease; and with the cessation of volitional formations, ignorance ceases.
One understands that the various natures of phenomena are neither extinguished nor non-extinguished; one perceives neither extinction nor non-extinction.
What is meant by "extinguishing extinction so as to be without extinction"?
This is called the inexhaustible.

“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva discerns and clearly understands the dharma of arising and the dharma of ceasing. He knows that arising does not come from anywhere, and he knows that ceasing does not go anywhere. Arising is without arising, and ceasing is without ceasing; this is called ‘the inexhaustible.’”
To clearly understand that arising and ceasing have no location whatsoever, being like space and without attachment—how can there be non-attachment while not perceiving non-attachment?
That non-attachment is itself devoid of this "non-attachment" is what is called inexhaustibility.

“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain the dhāraṇīs, samādhis, and the four types of unimpeded wisdom (pratisaṃvid), they practice walking meditation day and night until their entire body feels light. When first practicing the contemplation of the Dharma, they rise from the ground to the height of an āmalaka fruit; gradually it becomes like a vibhītaka fruit; then it becomes like a harītakī fruit; rising from the ground to the height of a finger’s shadow, and gradually rising to the height of seven human shadows—this is the mundane dhyāna of ordinary sages and practitioners. The bodhisattva studies this but does not abide therein; therefore, it is called ‘that which is exhaustible.’”

The mind penetrates without obstruction; it does not abide in the five supernormal powers, yet it is not that it does not abide in those powers. It understands that the dharma-nature of all phenomena is spontaneous, and that both ignorance and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are entirely spontaneous, yet even this spontaneity is non-existent.
What is spontaneity (*svayambhū*)?
Not seeing spontaneity nor the absence of spontaneity—this is called the inexhaustible.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through emptiness, extinguishes conceptualization and does not grasp at form, and views all sentient beings as equal without perceiving any distinction or gradation; when dwelling in a secluded and tranquil place, they contemplate and maintain mindfulness, neither seeing created form nor seeing uncreated form, but proceeding resolutely toward the gate of Nirvāṇa—this is called the exhaustible.

One contemplates the body as impermanent through the application of giving, morality, concentration, and wisdom; one does not fear falling or drowning in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Though dwelling within birth and death, one is like a bird flying through the sky, leaving no trace of form or shadow. One fully knows that nothing exists, which is called the extinguishing of fire into a heap of ashes where no heat remains. Seeking the substance of the "master of fire," one finds no person, no self, no life-span, and no vital principle. One observes and analyzes who it is that creates; even consciousness (*vijñāna*) is without the nature of consciousness. When the eighteen realms and sense-bases (*dhātu-āyatana*) are investigated, they are found to have no root. The hundred-and-eight attachments are entirely non-existent. One penetrates the coming and going without seeing the seen or the unseen; there is nothing to be guarded or maintained, nor is there anyone to maintain it. How, then, could there be maintenance?
"Holding that which is not held—this is called the inexhaustible.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Suvarṇavarṇa (Golden Color), whose six supernormal powers were pure and penetrating, who deeply understood the Buddha’s wisdom, whose merits were immeasurable, and whose skillful transformations were manifold. Desiring to ask the Tathāgata about the meaning of the inexhaustible, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"To what extent is it called the meaning of the inexhaustible?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Golden Color:
“That which is the inexhaustible Dharma is beyond words and beyond explanation.
Why do you ask me to explain the meaning of the inexhaustible?”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to the Bodhisattva Suvarṇavarṇa:
“Space has no form or image, And its arising has no origin;
The stages of the womb are immeasurable, Like a river flowing into the sea.”
The inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma, the parents of the Buddhas of the three periods—
those who wish to seek its ultimate exhaustion only give rise to a deluded mind.
When one understands that the characteristics of phenomena are empty, defilements are extinguished without remainder.
Attaining the Buddha’s vajra-body, complete with all its majestic marks;
discerning that the Buddha-body is empty, with no attachment to internal or external things;
though expounding inexhaustible treasures, in billions of eons he does not speak of even one.
At that time, when the Tathāgata spoke of the inexhaustible treasure, the bodhisattvas seated there— both those in training and those beyond training—

as well as the devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans, all resolved their minds toward the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma and gave rise to the unsurpassed aspiration, establishing themselves in non-retrogression.

Chapter Seventeen: The Five Supernatural Powers At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Miaosheng (Wondrous Victorious). He was fully endowed with the six perfections and skillful means (upāya-kauśalya); wherever he taught and transformed others, his influence was all-pervasive. He entered among the multitudes everywhere, and all who saw him were filled with joy. With right contemplation and a concentrated mind, he served as a field of merit for the world. If good men or good women encounter such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, all their evils are eradicated and they universally give rise to blessings and joy. Contemplating the gate of the Dharma of equality and non-duality, he constantly uses dharmas that are like illusions, like transformations, and like dreams to ferry across the masses of living beings. He cultivates the Buddha-way without distinctions of self or other.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Victory rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
How can a bodhisattva possessing the five supernormal powers come to know and discern their respective practices?"
"What dharmas must one cultivate to attain the power of the divine faculties?
The Buddha told Miaosheng:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall analyze and explain perfect wisdom for you.
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said, "Miaosheng!"

Within this desire realm, these good sons and good daughters do not require the supernormal power of the divine eye to see, from birth, all classes of sentient beings within a single Jambudvīpa—whether coarse or subtle, beautiful or ugly, blue, yellow, red, or white—as well as their cities, walls, houses, mountain crags, and trees.

There may be sons or daughters of good family whose eyes are able to behold two continents, three continents, or four continents, perceiving them naturally without needing the supernormal power of the divine eye.

There may be good men or good women who, without needing the supernormal power of the divine eye or the clarity of the divine ear, hear the voices of men, women, horses, and chariots throughout the world; they are able to discern and recognize every sound they hear without having to cultivate the supernormal power of the divine ear to understand each one individually.

There may be good sons or good daughters who, without practicing or studying, spontaneously recognize their past lives, knowing: "I have come from such-and-such a place to be born here; my father's surname was such-and-such, my mother's surname was such-and-such; and I can fully distinguish the names, surnames, and clans of my brothers, sisters, and kin."

There may be sons or daughters of good family who, without cultivating supernormal powers, know the mental activities and conduct of others—whether they perform good or evil deeds; whether they are headed for an evil realm or a good realm; whether they will be born in the heavens, among humans, as hungry ghosts, in hell, or as animals; and whether these sentient beings possess the conditions for liberation or lack such conditions.

There may be sons or daughters of good family whose bodies are able to fly, traveling back and forth without having cultivated the supernormal power of the body; yet their bodies can fly without obstruction, treading upon space as if it were solid ground, and treading upon the earth as if it were empty space.
The Buddha told Miaosheng:
"These five kinds of people are not truly those with supernormal powers who have regressed;

rather, there may be sons or daughters of good family who cultivate the noble supernormal power of the eye, eliminating form and severing defilements so that their mindfulness does not shift, thereby reaching the ultimate gateway of the Way."
What is called the gateway to the Path?
It is the three concentrations on emptiness.
By means of these, one is able to see a thousandfold world system, a two-thousandfold world system, and a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.

There may be sons or daughters of good family who cultivate the noble supernormal power of the ear; entering meditative absorption in stillness, they hear with purity throughout one world-system, a thousand world-systems, two thousand world-systems, or a trichiliocosm. They distinguish and know each sound—whether the voices of men or women, elephants or horses, or the sounds of carriages, bells, and drums—and discern whether these sounds are pleasant or unpleasant. They know that this sound arises from a being born in heaven, they know that this sound arises from a human, they know that this sound arises from a hungry ghost, they know that this sound arises from an animal, and they know that this sound arises from a being in hell. They know which beings have conditions for rebirth and which beings lack such conditions, discerning and understanding each and every case with complete clarity.

There may be sons or daughters of good family who cultivate the Way with purity, removing the defilements of consciousness so that they are without flaw within or without; attaining the sagely penetration of intent, they personally recognize their past lives.

One can fully know the places from which one has come throughout one life, two lives, three lives, four lives, and even up to incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as well as one’s parents, brothers, and the purity of those lands.

There may be sons or daughters of good family who cultivate the six supernormal powers and understand the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); who possess strong memory without forgetfulness and whose minds are stilled upon the path of awakening; who discern the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) with undisturbed concentration, and are thus able to know the thoughts of others' minds, as well as their origins through one, two, three, four, or even incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—all of these they fully know.
They know all about their parents, brothers, lands, names, surnames, and lineages, which are all pure.

There may be good men or good women who contemplate the Dharma through observation, sustaining the body with the mind and the mind with the body; they know moderation in eating, remain awake from sleep, and maintain a mental intention as empty as space. They do not exert effort toward lust, anger, or delusion; calculating that the body is selfless, their mental dharmas are pure. Through concentration, their consciousness can lift the entire body. Whether for one beat, two beats, or even seven beats of a drum, they gradually practice this concentration. They travel through one world-system, two world-systems, and even up to a trichiliocosm; they enter the earth as if it were empty space, encountering no obstruction from mountains, rivers, stones, or walls.

There may be sons or daughters of good family who, when on the verge of attaining Buddhahood, use the power of their wisdom to remove the defilements of sentient beings; they sit beneath the King of Trees in formal meditation and make this vow:
"I shall not rise from this seat until I have attained Buddhahood."

"Just as in the past, when I sat beneath the Jambu tree and contemplated the tree for thirty-eight days, at the moment I made this vow, heaven and earth were moved and shook six times. Although the evil Māra Pāpīyān led his hosts of troops and rained down sand, gravel, and stones with thunder and lightning roaring, he could not move even a single hair on my body."
"Why is this? Because his compassionate moisture is universal and he pities all sentient beings, he has attained the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) that are pure and transparent as a Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The supernormal powers attained by ordinary beings are like those of flying birds;
some are near and some are far, yet they do not transcend the path of birth and death.
The Buddha’s supernormal powers are the unimpeded Dharma, truly real and free from defilement.”
When one recollects, one reaches the ten directions, traveling back and forth without weariness.
By recollecting sentient beings with compassion, one attains unimpeded supernormal powers;
yet the fivefold wisdom of the sages may regress and fail to be perfected.
"I have mastered the firm dharma; I must enter the gate of nirvāṇa.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was preaching this dharma to the Bodhisattva Wondrous Victory, there were seventeen billion sentient beings who abandoned the five mundane supernormal powers and attained the wisdom of the six supernormal powers.

Chapter 18: The Abodes of Consciousness *The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra*, Chapter Eighteen: The Abodes of Consciousness At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Samantaprabha. He possessed great kindness and great compassion, mastery of the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and delighted in profound virtues. Having practiced for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he had rescued sentient beings by uprooting the source of suffering and attained the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*). Wherever he traveled, the Buddha’s work never ceased. He then rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have already heard that the Tathāgata has distinguished the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) which are unimpeded and pervade the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions. Even if the True Dharma of all Buddhas is equal and without distinction, this present consciousness-dharma abides in non-abiding; as for the consciousness-dharma of the six supernormal powers, is this one dharma of consciousness manifold?"

If consciousness were a single dharma, such that the Tathāgata—possessing a golden body and supernatural powers—travels through various Buddha-fields at the site of enlightenment, does consciousness bring about the body, or does the body bring about consciousness?
If the body brings about consciousness, then there would be no six supernormal powers;
if consciousness brings about the body, this is called the single dharma that is neither body nor consciousness.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this meaning to me.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhāsa:
"Regarding the meaning you have asked, is it a question concerning the ultimate truth (paramārtha),
or is it a question concerning conventional truth (saṃvṛti)?"
If one asks according to conventional meaning, the dharmas of consciousness are manifold and lack any fixed characteristic.
If one asks according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is neither body nor consciousness. Why is this?
The self-nature of dharmas discerned by consciousness is empty and quiescent; it neither comes nor goes, and is free from defilement or attachment.
