As for your question regarding the golden color—this is a conditioned dharma composed of the five aggregates, not a spontaneous dharma, nor is it the ultimate truth (paramārtha). To speak of the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya) in terms of the ultimate truth would be erroneous.
I shall now explain for you the dharma of the characteristics of consciousness.

When a bodhisattva practices the six supernormal powers, bodily consciousness and the body arise together; it is not that consciousness comes first and the body follows, nor that the body comes first and consciousness follows.

Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena is such that consciousness does not depart from the body, nor does the body depart from consciousness; it is like two oxen yoked together by a single harness: if the black ox is in front and the white ox is behind, then the seed will not germinate.
If the white ox is in front and the black ox is behind, the sowing will not succeed.
If it is neither the case that the black ox is in front and the white ox is behind, nor the case that the white ox is in front and the black ox is behind, then the sowing will succeed.
The path of the bases of psychic power and its fruits are likewise thus: body-consciousness and its accompaniments have no before, after, or middle.

The physical body of the Tathāgata has a before, an after, and a middle; this is a conventional phenomenon and not the ultimate truth. Within the dharma of emptiness and stillness, there are no such distinctions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s golden body is honored and revered by those of the three periods of time;
He acts as a great burden-bearer for humanity, the unsurpassed and infinite Honored One.”
The devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven scatter flowers day and night;
the Brahmā heavens and their retinues perform music for their amusement.
Within a hundred yojanas, they completely fill the realm of empty space.
He raised his voice and exclaimed, "Excellent! The consciousness of the Buddha cannot be seen.
Having no interior, exterior, or middle, he manifests the dharma of the six supernormal powers for the sake of deluded fools in the world."
The radiance of its marks is as it is now; yet if one seeks the fundamental source of consciousness, it is quiescent and invisible.
Its manifestation is exhausted, yet there is no exhaustion; this is the mindfulness of the out-breath and the in-breath.
Not attached to existence within the three realms,
golden-colored and empty, without attachment; consciousness and phenomena are likewise thus—
without past, future, or present.
There is no present body nor future body; by discerning each and every characteristic, one reaches the place of eternal peace.
It is also called the dharma of the six hindrances, the dwelling place of the six consciousnesses.
Birth and cessation are inexhaustible, like bubbles upon the water; once extinguished, they arise again.
The nature of consciousness is inherently empty, yet it flows and rushes, filling all directions.
The body-consciousness is accompanied by two things; walking alone without equal, he teaches the unsurpassed path.
His destination follows his physical marks; though he dwells, he does not dwell.
To transform those who suffer:
consciousness acts as an obstruction in the interim; form does not come to enter the eye, nor does the eye go out to meet form.
One discriminates between this and that phenomenon, and through consciousness one knows good and evil; yet consciousness itself has no phenomena to cognize.
The ear distinguishes sounds and the nose distinguishes fragrances; these six activities arise spontaneously from conditions, and thus one performs deeds of good and evil.
The nose, mouth, and mind are likewise; phenomena arise through mutual conditions.
Without attachment, they are empty and non-existent.
Through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one perceives the realm of space as tranquil and still.
Signless and wishless,
through the discrimination of sensation and perception, one seeks the true mark of consciousness,
yet finds no place where it abides.
The four immeasurables and the fearlessnesses; understanding that all phenomena are empty, consciousness ceases and formations likewise cease.
There are no phenomena of past, future, or present; consciousness is like the path of illusory transformations.
Not dwelling in this or that, consciousness ceases and returns to emptiness;
provisional names have no reality.
With thoughts eliminated and no attachments, one erects the high banner of the sublime Dharma.
He expounds the dharmas that characterize consciousness,
yet does not depart from consciousness itself; only the Honored One, supreme in the three realms,
is able to thoroughly investigate the nature of consciousness.
Just as one atop a mountain peak can see clearly across the four directions and discern good and evil deeds,
so too is the power of the divine eye supreme, seeing the realms of the ten directions from afar;
a person of wise intelligence perceives all things as clearly as viewing a bright jewel in the palm of their hand.

At that time, as the World-Honored One spoke these verses, eighty-four billion sentient beings sought to distance themselves from the dharmic characteristics of the six consciousnesses; they took no pleasure in the transmigration through the five realms of birth and death, and gave rise to the mind of great vows to abide in the ground of non-consciousness.

Chapter Nineteen: Skillful Means (*Upāya-kauśalya*) From the *Bodhisattva Womb Sutra*, Chapter Nineteen: Skillful Means. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Udyatahasta (Lifting the Hand), who stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I wish to hear of the countless and incalculable skillful transformations of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
The Buddha said:

"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly practices skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), neither here nor there, nor in between the two. According to those before him, he adapts his transformation through explanations of meaning, explanations of phrases, and contemplation of the underlying intent. He adorns the Buddha-lands, fulfills the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) up to the mutual knowledge of the cessation [of suffering], and guides others through skillful means without any obstruction."

He is neither self-exalting nor arrogant; his appearance is upright and his dharma-robes are perfectly arranged. He accepts the faithful offerings presented before him and does not abandon them until they have been fully measured.

His radiant marks are majestic and his speech is pure. For the sake of a single sentient being, he remains for a hundred million kalpas, leaving his physical form behind to teach and transform others in other regions; such emanations of his body are inconceivable.

In those places where he wanders and transforms beings, there are none who perceive him; yet within the realm of ghosts and spirits, he manifests great supernormal powers, causing even those ghosts to deliver and transform sentient beings, passing the teachings on to one another so that they do not lose the Way of the Buddha.

Furthermore, through skillful means, he manifests the form and image of a Buddha, his radiant marks shining brilliantly. Those who behold him or hear the Dharma he preaches find its words—beginning, middle, and end—to be peaceful, secure, and blissful. It encompasses dhyāna, the factors of enlightenment, clear wisdom, and liberation; it includes sūtras, geya-sūtras, vyākaraṇa-sūtras, and adbhuta-dharma-sūtras; nidāna-sūtras, upadeśa-sūtras, vaipulya-sūtras, jātaka-sūtras, vaipulya-sūtras (extensive), acintya-sūtras, aupamya-sūtras, avadāna-sūtras, nidāna-sūtras, and itivṛttaka-sūtras. According to their inclinations, he teaches the profound Dharma to explain emptiness and non-self, so that although the thoughts of sentient beings differ from one another, he is able to lead them all to enter the gate of liberation.
It is like a multitude of springs and ponds, where five rivers flow with great speed, each having its own name; yet once they have all returned to the sea, they no longer retain their original names.
It is also like Mount Sumeru, standing firm and immovable, upon which birds of various colors go to dwell and take refuge; once there, they all become the same color and lose their original colors.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s teaching and transforming of sentient beings and purifying of Buddha-lands is likewise so.

Although the mental consciousnesses and various thoughts of sentient beings differ, he is able to cause them all to reach the gate of liberation through the extinction of conceptual thought and intentionality; thus they become free from their original notions and attain a single liberation. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s inconceivable skillful means and adaptive transformation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as a farmer, Selecting a fertile and excellent field,
Sows his seeds without missing the season, And irrigates them at the proper time."
Nurturing the sprouts to fulfillment, Free from frost, insects, and locust plagues, One ultimately harvests the fruit, Storing it away without anxiety or fear.
The true Dharma of the Bodhisattva Is the field of the six perfections; Thus, one attains the supreme fruit And dwells in peace, free from all distress.
Eliminating the mind of stinginess and greed, Irrigating it with the water of ambrosia,
Through the path of skillful means and expedient methods, And clearly understanding the laws of coming and going,
I guide the various classes of sentient beings To reach the place of non-extinction.
Birth, old age, sickness, and afflictions burn away the roots of goodness within the mind;
through the protection of skillful means and expedient wisdom, one understands the principles of coming and going.
When a person wishes to leave the household life, they take the prohibitive precepts as their primary concern;
they do not cling to the dharma of ornamental finery, but practice the bodhisattva path through skillful means.
They devote their lives without sparing their own bodies, never violating the precepts even by so much as a hair’s breadth.
The body is like grass, soil, or dung, to be torn and cut by others as they please;
yet patience is like Mount Sumeru, firm and unshakable.
Through the skillful means of guarding the precepts, one neither increases nor decreases in the face of blame or praise.
Emerging from darkness to abide in light is the Bodhisattva’s path of skillful means.
Manifesting his body among humans out of compassion for all beings,
he may appear in subtle forms, entering and exiting without obstruction.
The Buddhas sit at the site of enlightenment, having extinguished the fetters so they arise no more;
those who reach that site of enlightenment have their fetters exhausted forever without remainder.
They are like a great guide leading a multitude of merchants.
Entering the sea to gather rare treasures— coral, amber, pearls,
and moon-bright gems to be had at will— he returned safely to his native land.
His parents, brothers, kinsmen, servants, and laborers [all rejoiced].
With a harmonious and joyful mind, as if in meditative concentration one has removed all conceptualizations,
bodhisattvas who practice skillful means seek out the inexhaustible treasury;
having discerned its rare and wondrous treasures, they adorn their own bodies with necklaces of jewels.
The Great Teacher of Skillful Means has the six perfections as his wife and children;
With the four immeasurable minds as his canopy, dust and defilement do not cling to his heart.
In this world there are many people deluded by folly, Who cling to stinginess and do not practice giving.
Having accumulated wealth amounting to thousands of millions, one claims, "This is mine.
Yet when the end of life approaches, one sees evil spirits with one's own eyes;
the wind of the sword dissolves the body, and there is no longer any inhalation or exhalation.
Driven by greed, their consciousness follows all evils, and the retribution they receive is most bitter and painful;
as they approach the place where they shall suffer punishment, it is too late for regret to avail them.
The Buddha, through his skillful wisdom, delivers them and preaches the Dharma right there.
Those of sharp faculties reflect upon their own transgressions; with a mind of repentance, they do not conceal them.
Hearing the Dharma, they attain liberation—this is the Bodhisattva’s path of skillful means.
It is like a person born blind, who cannot distinguish between the colors black and yellow.
Having encountered the Sage, the skillful artisan, he was treated with the medicine of the Dharma;
though he had previously heard of the five colors— blue, yellow, red, white, and black—
once he had attained the clear eye of discernment, he no longer distinguished between blue, yellow, and red.
"The Bodhisattva’s path of skillful means Discriminates until reaching the ultimate;
It sweeps away the dharmas of the eight difficulties, Neither arising nor ceasing.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, ten billion householders practiced the path of skillful means, ultimately attaining the unconditioned and dwelling in the stage of non-abiding.
The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra, Scroll Five;
The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.

Chapter 20: On Ignorance. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Wisdom-Purity (Jñānaviśuddhi), who discerned emptiness, non-arising, old age, sickness, and death, as well as those with much lust, anger, and delusion, and those with little lust, anger, and delusion.
Distinguishing the three grades of sentient beings, [the Buddha asked: "Among those with equal portions of afflictions, which illness is the most severe?
That which is most severe is false view.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Jñānaviśuddhi rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has nothing he does not know and nothing he does not see. Regarding the past, the future, and the present—the classes of beings that crawl, breathe, or stand upright—he knows the thoughts in their minds, the words spoken by their mouths, and the good or evil deeds performed by their bodies; he knows their profound prohibitions, their majestic deportment, and their precepts and rules, knowing them in their many and few, their heavy and light.”
Now, as for my question: it is neither empty nor non-empty, neither existent nor non-existent, neither the emptiness of existence nor the existence of emptiness;
among the three categories of sentient beings, which is the lightest?
What constitutes the grave?
What constitutes retribution in the present life?
What constitutes retribution in the next life?
What is the retribution in a future life?
What is the cessation of perception and feeling? And what is nirvāṇa?
"What is meant by 'without remainder'?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Jñānaviśuddhi: "Excellent, excellent!"
"Excellent that you inquire into this meaning!
Out of compassion for all beings and to bring great benefit to many, you have been able to ask about the Dharma of equality before the Buddha.

Return to your seat; I shall explain to you the meaning of the words in their beginning, middle, and end sections—how black karma receives black retribution and white karma receives white retribution—analyzing each part in detail so that you may understand."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as when a person plants a fruit tree, If the seed is bitter, the fruit will also be bitter;
So too, for committing evil, one receives dark retribution, Suffering through the passage of kalpas."
Planting sweet, one obtains sweet fruit; one returns to receive the retribution of sweetness.
Fragrant, pure, and exceedingly delicious, one receives the retribution of purity and clarity.
It is like a person in a pool of water, whose interior and exterior are thoroughly purified.
Windless and free from dust or defilement, it is fragrant, exquisite, and cool.
Any sentient being who beholds it finds such delight that they cannot leave;
the pure practice of the Buddha-way is no different from that.
Sentient beings who receive black retribution fall into the perils of the three miserable realms;
like high and low ground following swift waters, they drift through places of calamity and distress.
At that time, the suffering of afflictions is endured alone, with no one to take its place.
Their bones are shattered and marrow exposed; they are burned and boiled beyond measure.
Having reached the hell of no rescue, they contemplate awakening to seek liberation;
yet, shrouded by ignorance, they do not see the radiance of wisdom.
Like a person traveling on a road who has lost their way, taking south for north;
though they do not awaken in mind all day long, they do not believe even when they hear [the truth].
They undergo the heavy suffering of retribution, as piercing pain is added to their bodies.
Long after their offenses have been exhausted, they are still loathed and despised by the world.
Their bodies are foul-smelling and hideous, like a pig lying in a deep latrine;
they writhe as they enter the cauldron of boiling water, dying only to be born again.
What is fundamentally created by ignorance receives its retribution like a shadow or an echo.
Good and evil are both equal; this is the meaning of the "equal-part" (sabhāga) sentient beings.
There is no path that shows partiality, yet in practice there are degrees of excellence and inferiority.
Those who uphold the precepts are reborn among devas and humans; yet their merit from non-giving is minimal.
When eating solid food, they fear being seen by others, for out of shame they do not expose themselves.
Though they have hosts of celestial maidens, their music lacks harmony and elegance.
Occasionally going out for excursions and observations, one fears encountering the gods of wondrous power.
If one is fully endowed with precepts and generosity, the nectar of immortality, clothing, and food will arrive;
surrounded by music before and behind, one is as bright among the stars as the moon.
After a long time, he went out on an excursion; his retinue was magnificently adorned, and celestial music played spontaneously.
This was because, in the human world, he had maintained the precepts and practiced generosity; thus, the retribution of merit followed him like a shadow.
Although the devas enjoy blessings, they too face the hardships of kalpas;
when the time of their death approaches, they realize the law of decay.
As wholesome thoughts turn faint, they must once again undergo rebirth.
Wandering through the five realms of rebirth, One passes through incalculable kalpas.
When experiencing the retribution of good and evil, One does not avoid the powerful, the noble, or the lowly;
Yet among them, one can alone extricate oneself, Like I, Śākyamuni.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, seventy-seven thousand *koṭi-nayuta* of devas and humans within the great assembly all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Wisdom-Purity, saying:

"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is in his final birth before Buddhahood may, through skillful means, be born into a lowly and humble family. Desiring to manifest the removal of the fetters of ignorance, he remains in the womb for ten months; on the day of his birth, he appears without hands or feet. When his parents see him, they believe him to be a ghost and abandon him in the wilderness so that no one shall see him."

Why is this? It was because the Bodhisattva, through his skillful means and transformations, desired to cause his foolish parents and kinsmen to behold the light of the Path. Several months later, the mother again became pregnant; when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son who was upright, beautiful, and rare in the world. He was born by day and died by night, whereupon the parents wailed and wept, beating their breasts toward the heavens:
"O mountain spirits and tree spirits, why do you not have pity on us?"

"Previously, you had one son who lacked hands and feet and was abandoned in the wilderness; now you have given birth to a son of incomparable beauty, like a celestial being, yet he dies at night after being born by day. My heart is torn asunder—what am I to do?"

After several more months, his mother’s pregnancy reached full term; she gave birth to a male child with three heads, eight feet, four eyes, and eight arms. Those who beheld him stood with their hair bristling in awe, and his parents and kinsmen wished to abandon him and depart;
however, the Bodhisattva manifested his power so that they were unable to leave.
His parents asked:
"Is this a deva? Or is it a nāga, a ghost, an asura, a gandharva, a garuḍa, a kiṃnara, a mahoraga, a human, or a non-human?"
At that time, the newborn son addressed his parents in verse, saying:
“I am not a deva, a yakṣa, or a ghost; nor am I a kumbhāṇḍa or a garuḍa.
To dispel my mother’s ignorance and darkness, I have temporarily been born into my parents’ home.”
Formerly there was no child with hands or feet, yet that too was my own body;
born in the morning and dying by evening—such is the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One dwelling in the eighth stage.
Now I have received this physical form, with three heads and eight hands and feet.
Why have you abandoned me and gone toward the gates of hell?
In hell all manner of sufferings are complete; eighteen cauldrons of boiling brine seethe there.
Each of these cauldrons is surrounded by sixteen partitions.
Suffering for immeasurable eons, they find it exceedingly difficult to seek liberation.
Their parents are deluded and ignorant, failing to recognize the true nature of phenomena;
through false views they pray at shrines, believing that they shall thereby escape their hardships.
Like a blazing flame, when further fueled by dry wood and grass, it consumes the roots of virtue; even to seek its extinction then is difficult.
Now I have restored my body and manifest my original, upright form.
The Way is rooted in a firm mind; practicing the threefold wisdom, For incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he vowed to deliver those not yet delivered.
Guarding the precepts without losing his vow, he took birth in the home of his parents.
Throughout successive lives, he has sacrificed his body and life, as numerous as motes of dust.
In every place he has traversed, there are none who have not received his blessings and protection;
though the various classes of beings differ in their conduct and traces.
One should deliver them through joy, and likewise transform them through fear;
according to the inclinations of those sentient beings, one causes them to fulfill their heart's aspirations.
Since the ailments of sentient beings are not of a single kind, one administers the nectar-like medicine accordingly.
Leading them to enter the path of restraint, so they do not enter deviant ways;
the joy of the gods receiving blessings, the joy of ambrosia removing illness,
the joy of not contravening the holy teachings, and the joy of liberation and nirvana.
"When the Bodhisattva spoke these verses at that time, his parents, kinsmen, and all those assembled there all conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation."

Chapter 21: On Ascetic Practices. *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling in the Womb*, Chapter Twenty-one: On Ascetic Practices. At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, mahoragas, kiṃnaras, humans and non-humans, those in training and those beyond training, and the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—the Tathāgata observed and knew the thoughts in the minds of all these beings. By upholding the precepts, one dwells in a hall of the seven treasures, where hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens attend.
There, one enjoys celestial music for one's own amusement, with every thought free from sorrowful conceptions.
The Buddha’s power and omniscience universally moisten all people;
having first advanced in the five supernormal powers, he is naturally moistened by the nectar of the Dharma.
He extols the meaning of the four lines of verse, which have no beginning, end, or middle.
Phenomena naturally blaze as phenomena; the nature of phenomena pervades both within and without.
Just as I have previously created them, bound by the latent tendencies of craving, I have wandered through the five realms of existence, making them my dwelling place and hall.
The Way of Heaven is like the luster of polished stone; its investigation knows no end.
A blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log may happen from time to time, but once a person loses the root of life, it is difficult to regain it even in ten million kalpas.
The waters of the ocean are deep and vast, numbering three hundred and thirty-six [yojanas];
were a single needle cast into the sea, it might still be found.
But once the human life and body are lost, it is even more difficult to regain than that.
Those who revere the Vinaya and uphold the precepts are difficult to encounter in this world;
even in hundreds of millions of *kalpas*, a Buddha appears as rarely as the *udumbara* flower.
Sentient beings with the requisite conditions receive transformation through the Buddha-way.
"Severing and eliminating the fetters and latent tendencies, one attains eternal exhaustion and is free from the perception of grasping.

When the Buddha spoke this verse, twelve nayutas of sentient beings established the faculty of faith firmly so that it was no longer subject to deviation, and they all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment.

Chapter 25: On Light and Shadow. *The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb*, Chapter Twenty-Five: "On Light and Shadow. At that time, while the World-Honored One was within his mother’s womb, he extensively expounded upon the inconceivable Mahāyāna. As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he manifested the divine power of light and shadow, causing all those in the assembly to become of one color, like the golden hue of the Buddha, without any distinction.

The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—some of whom were still practicing toward the goal and some who had attained the fruits—he caused them all to become of one color. He desired that they hear of the Tathāgata’s concentration of light and shadow, the establishment of meritorious virtues, unimpeded liberation, the four analytical knowledges, swift and nimble eloquence in response, and the extinction of perception and cognition through which beings may be rescued.

Carrying the heavy burden of humanity, his every movement—whether walking or standing—never lost its dignified deportment in accordance with the Dharma of all Buddhas; he constantly preached upon suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, guiding sentient beings into the four foundations of mindfulness.
The Dharma achieves the power of the lion’s fearlessness in severing mental afflictions; it is the Noble Eightfold Path, empty, signless, and wishless.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Bhadraprabha. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha:

"Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—You have emitted this radiance that universally illumines the trichiliocosm. Is the transformation effected by this radiance the same as the transformation effected by the Buddha?"
The power and merit of the Buddha are neither one nor two, and the reach of his radiance is inexhaustible; what, then, is the distinction between these two virtuous qualities?
We pray only that the World-Honored One will unravel this knot of doubt, so that those who have not yet gained faith may forever be free from uncertainty.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadra-prabha, saying:
"That which you have asked is entirely through the spiritual power of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?"

The Tathāgata’s divine light saves and delivers sentient beings without any obstruction, shining from Jambudvīpa up to the Bṛhatphala Heaven. Its radiance shines afar as it expounds the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Just as the Buddha’s divine voice delivers sentient beings without distinction between "other" and "self," it rescues countless asaṃkhyeya beings, all of whom are sheltered and cooled under the canopy of the Buddha’s light.
At that time, the radiance produced a spontaneous sound, which spoke in verse:
"Countless Buddhas of the past, None failed to emit this light;
Each and every ray of light Expounds the six perfections."
Precepts, patience, and the gates of liberation—delighting in the Dharma for one’s own enjoyment;
first teaching the three concentrations on emptiness, thereby gradually accomplishing the Path.
Those whose three poisons are equal, who are neither bound nor attached;
for whom there are no fetters among the forty-eight, and no gate of sin from which there is no rescue—
such are not true practitioners of the Path, nor are they those who have traversed the stages of realization.
The three gates of joyful activity are noble, for they bear the traces of divine beings.
Having traversed the path of the Supreme Victor, one reaches the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Establishing practice without regression, one possesses the majesty of fearless supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*).
The salvation brought about by the contact of divine light is not merely a matter of hundreds of billions;
it is as if that single radiance were divided into as many particles as there are motes of dust.
From each particle are manifested all lands, infinite and beyond measure.
The power of the Buddha is inexhaustible; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
A single ray of light expounds the Dharma, delivering and liberating incalculable beings (*asaṃkhyeya*).
The Dharma-body is naturally empty, its internal and external conduct pure.
Though afflictions number eighty-four thousand, my concentrated mind does not give rise to distraction.
In the past, for ninety-two eons— too numerous to exhaust—
I sat upright beneath the King of Trees, practicing the Way without withdrawing midway.
Humans, devas, asuras, and pretas, you are exhorted to inquire about my teaching;
with divine light reaching afar, I deliver and liberate them in incalculable numbers.
The Buddha of the past, Śikhin, left behind radiant light for the sake of future transformation;
having entered within that light, one extinguishes the afflictions of the three poisons.
Next was the Honored One Vipaśyin, whose divine virtue is immeasurable.
He likewise leaves behind his radiance, rescuing those afflicted by suffering.
Kanakamuni, the most eminent honored one who transcends the three realms,
now dwells upon Mount Ṛṣigiri, his brilliance shining forth resplendently.
Kia-lou, God among Gods, Unattached and unstained;
Having entered nirvana in quiescence, He leaves behind light for later transformation.
Kāśyapa was originally no superior, Yet those he delivered were beyond measure.
Furthermore, by means of the virtue of his radiance, he causes those who have not yet crossed over to do so.
I, Śākyamuni, while dwelling in the womb, preached the Dharma;
this light of my body and that [light] of his fill all Buddha-fields.
This is not something that a person of minor virtue could possibly fathom;
only a Buddha can measure a Buddha, for their merits are without distinction.
All future Buddhas likewise shall transform all beings through their radiance.
"I shall now deliver sentient beings, first by means of light and thereafter by means of the Dharma.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, one billion seven hundred million sentient beings sitting upon that very seat, having heard the Buddha speak of this divine merit of light, all conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation.
The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra, Scroll Six;
The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.

Chapter Twenty-Six: Refuting Erroneous Views At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of Right Concentration and manifested transformations by dividing his body to emit great radiance—desiring to cause the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to shatter the realm of Māra and abide in the ground of correctness. He addressed those gathered:
"I recall that ninety-one kalpas ago, to the south of the Snowy Mountains and north of the city of Qingming, my teacher and five thousand followers were practicing austerities in the mountains."

Among that assembly, I was the youngest disciple; I recited the scriptures and was thoroughly practiced in calculation, the arts and crafts, astronomy, and geography—there was nothing I did not master.
It is the constant custom among that assembly that when a disciple has completed his studies, he must repay the teacher’s kindness.

At that time, I alone possessed no wealth or treasures to offer to my teacher; therefore, I prostrated myself in gratitude and intended to descend from the mountain into the human world to beg for alms.
The teacher would not grant permission.
Thus he entreated him with compassion and begged for it a second and a third time, yet the teacher still did not grant permission. Why was this?
Because I was most eminent among the assembly for my clear understanding of the scriptures,
the Master said to me:
"I possess a secret and essential treasury of scriptures that you have not yet recited."
"Why do you abandon me to beg for alms among humans?
At that time, the teacher immediately gave me a single secret essential phrase consisting of five hundred words, instructing me to recite it.
Before several days had passed, I had completed my study and recitation, and I went before the teacher and said:
"I have requested permission to go down the mountain to beg for alms, wishing to repay my teacher’s kindness.
My teacher again refused to grant it and said to me:

"You should study the secret prophecies and scriptures; you do not yet understand the calamities and anomalies of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, nor the portents of misfortune and fortune, such as the shifting of mountains and the trembling of the earth."
"Why do you wish to leave me to beg for alms among humans?
He further produced a single sentence from a sutra consisting of a thousand words and commanded me to recite it.
Before many days had passed, I had mastered it and informed my teacher that I wished to repay his kindness; however, the teacher would not permit it.
"I possess yet another scripture of ten thousand words in a single sentence, containing the myriad treasures within its texts, which you have not yet recited.
On what grounds do you wish to abandon me and seek elsewhere?

He then produced the scripture for him to recite; before many days had passed, he had already mastered it, becoming fully proficient in all technical arts, portents, anomalies, and the movements of the stars.

At that time, his teacher earnestly wished for him to remain and stay, as there were no other scriptures available for him to study; thus, he took leave of his teacher and descended the mountain to go to a village to beg for alms.
There he saw a multitude of five thousand heterodox brahmins gathered in a great settlement to perform a communal sacrifice to the gods.

According to that ritual for sacrificing to the gods, one must slaughter five hundred heifers, five hundred rams, five hundred camels, five hundred horses, five hundred of the finest elephants endowed with six tusks, five hundred women, one golden staff, one golden water-pitcher, one thousand pieces of white cotton cloth, and fifty thousand coins each of gold and silver; once these various precious objects have been used to sacrifice to the gods, they shall be delivered to the preceptor.

At that time, I descended from the mountain, my robes covered in dust and grime; having previously practiced asceticism in the mountains for many years while wearing deerskin garments, I heard that within that village a group of five thousand heterodox brahmins and their teachers had established a great sacrificial assembly, and so I passed by it.
At that time, my preceptor asked me:
"Those with many scriptures and skills shall occupy the seat of seniority; those with few scriptures shall occupy the lower seats.
Although my preceptor possessed knowledge, he was unable to penetrate the secret essentials and prophetic records, and thus he appointed me as the senior monk.
The teacher became angry and said: "Who is this person?
These treasures and various goods should now belong to me."
"This man has robbed me; if we should meet again in a future life, I must certainly take my revenge, no different from how he robbed me now.

At that time, I immediately said: "Your wrong views are inverted, neither true nor real. You discriminate between existence and non-existence while claiming it is Nirvana; you speak of the absence of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and the absence of 'that' or 'this. Yet, within this, you contemplate the self-characteristics of phenomena as pure and possessing the four fearlessnesses. You claim that merit leads to rebirth in heaven and sin leads to hell, that stinginess and greed result in the realm of hungry ghosts and debt-owed animals; thus, the retribution for good and evil follows one like a shadow follows a form."
At that time, the minds and consciousnesses of five thousand people were awakened, and they immediately requested me to be their teacher.
At that time, although elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and camels all deserved to be killed, I did not kill them.
"I should take the golden staff and the water jar; I shall give them immediately to the elder who was angry.

As for the five hundred women, I returned them to the master of the shrine. Of the fifty thousand gold coins, I took five hundred; of the fifty thousand silver coins, I took five hundred; the remainder I entrusted to the master of the shrine.
"Traveling from village to village and from kingdom to kingdom, I gradually arrived outside the eastern gate of the city of Qingming.

There I saw five hundred brahmins, aged and of long-standing virtue, who had practiced the Way for many years; their forms were withered by the sun and scorched by fire, and their appearance was hideous. I immediately gave them five hundred gold coins, one for each."

Taking my leave, I entered the city and saw that the people within had sprinkled scented water upon the ground to remove all dust and impurities; they hung silk banners and canopies, arranged in solemn rows, and were all about to depart the city. I walked forward a short distance and saw a woman holding seven flowers. I looked to the left and right, searching for incense and seeking more flowers, but could find none.
I then asked the woman: "If you have flowers available, I wish to purchase them."
The woman replied to me, saying:
"This is the King of Flowers; the Buddha is about to enter the city and will take it to offer to the Buddha, so it cannot be obtained.
The Bodhisattva, again employing skillful means, further addressed the woman:
"I have five hundred precious coins; for each flower, there is a hundred coins. If you will give them to me, I shall pay you with the coins.
The woman, greedy for the treasure, immediately gave him the five flowers.
After walking several dozen paces, the woman thought to herself:
"This man has a handsome countenance and wears a deer-skin garment; yet he was so greedy for my five flowers that he did not spare his silver coins—there must certainly be a reason for this."
Turning his head, he called out,
"Man! For what purpose do you use these flowers?"
He replied, "To the Buddha.
When the girl heard the name of the Buddha, she immediately took two flowers and entrusted them to me.
I immediately left the city and saw the Buddha approaching from afar. The roads were so crowded with devas and people that there was not a single empty spot where one could prostrate.
Before the Buddha was a pool of water large enough to hold one person; I immediately untied my hair and spread it upon the water, then praised the Buddha with this verse:
"Having shattered the mind of craving and pride, You are able to extinguish desire, anger, and delusion."
The first mark of light is complete; only the Buddha illuminates my heart.
The vow I sought in the past, today I have seen the Buddha fulfilled.
Now I scatter these five stalks of flowers, praying that I may attain non-retrogression.
"These two remaining non-flower offerings, the princess has entrusted to me to present to the Buddha;
may the Unsurpassed Great Teacher, out of compassion, tread upon my hair.
At that time, the Tathāgata Prabhāsa, seeing that the great resolve I had formed was indestructible, praised me with these verses:
“The Māṇava has conceived a great resolve, To extensively save countless beings;
With vast vows not for his own sake, He plants the roots of manifold merit.”
After incalculable kalpas, in an age of the five turbidities and the five cauldrons, you shall attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings; your name shall be Śākyamuni.
Your marks and signs will be thirty-two, and you shall be the most extraordinary and honored among men.
When the Buddha had finished bestowing the prophecy upon Śrīmatī, the earth shook in six ways.
Devas, humans, and all the people of the world, seeing that I had received this prediction,
constantly contemplated the extinction of their various fetters and all vowed to be born in my world.

"At that time, the Tathāgata Prabhāsa stepped upon my hair with his foot and passed over it. By the Buddha's supernatural power, he took up my five flowers and my body, placing them in mid-air; two remaining flowers rested upon the left and right shoulders of the Buddha."

In the past, I destroyed the sacrificial implements for fire-worship used by five thousand Brahmins and caused them to practice right view and the eightfold path of equality. Whether sitting, lying down, or walking, I benefited sentient beings at every step, delivering them across. Since then, I have never fallen into the three miserable realms, the eight difficult conditions, or among those with worldly cleverness and eloquence, nor have I been born in remote lands or after the passing of a Buddha.

At that time, among the sentient beings of the Māra realm seated there, those who adhered to the views of eternalism or nihilism, who spoke of suffering as being pleasant, who regarded the impermanent as permanent, and who perceived a self where there is no self—practicing these four perversions and failing to recognize clear wisdom—were themselves shrouded by the five hindrances and greedily attached to gain and offerings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to deliver such people of wrong views, spoke again in verse:
"Wrong views are not the true path; They are like those iron-beaked insects That break through the bone to enter the marrow and brain, Causing suffering beyond measure."
“Gain and offerings corrupt moral virtue; this is not practiced by the wise.
One who personally practices with a firm mind purifies the dharma of ignorance.

At that time, as the World-Honored One explained these meanings of the phrases, meanings of the flavors, and meanings of the characters regarding this false view, and as he preached the true Dharma, countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Transformation of Mañjuśrī’s Body The Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Transformation of Mañjuśrī’s Body At that time, the World-Honored One, the Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha, entered the supreme samādhi of noble concentration. He observed the number of kalpas for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present, and those who should enter parinirvāṇa after one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to hundreds of thousands of countless billions of kalpas.
There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having achieved the merit of making offerings to all Buddhas, transform sentient beings and purify Buddha-lands.

There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the eighth stage of the state of youthfulness (*kumārabhūta*), refraining from taking a wife or children and eliminating thoughts of sexual desire; abiding in their own stage without father, mother, or brothers, they attain unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Reveal to them your ancient state from seventy-nine kalpas ago, when you were in the Flower Radiance World, preaching the Dharma while in the womb and manifesting your entire body as relics.”
The inhabitants of that land are one thousand yojanas in height, while the Buddha’s body is ten thousand yojanas.

To the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, they are immeasurable, limitless, and incalculable, beyond the capacity of any mathematician or his disciples to compute.

"O Mūlapariśuddha, you were originally there; through the Buddha’s bodily radiance, marks, and the manifestation of supernormal powers, you have enabled this great assembly to behold you once, thereby benefiting sentient beings within the lineage of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Mañjuśrī has been a Buddha from the beginning; While in the womb, he manifested transformations:
His square body measured ten thousand yojanas, And his radiant marks were brilliantly manifest.”
Eyes like blue lotus flowers, lips and mouth radiant as pearls and fire;
forty teeth, square and white; eyes blinking, welcoming with both upper and lower lashes.
To him, the devas, nāgas, and spirits offer incense and flowers, taking refuge and paying homage.
Now, as I dwell within this womb, compared to your realm there,
it does not equal even a sixteenth part, nor so much as a hair’s breadth.
The Tathāgata’s spiritual power and transformation are all-pervasive and unimpeded.
The fragrance of your prohibitions spreads afar, and all Buddhas praise you.
Now those gathered here in this assembly wish to inquire about the Dharma that is difficult to encounter;
Mañjuśrī, manifest your power and dispel the knots of the net of doubt.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, without leaving his original seat, by means of the power of his supernormal concentration, reached the assembly within the mother’s womb of Śākyamuni in the Sahā world—just as a strong man might extend or contract his arm—in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.

The two Buddha-worlds do not obstruct one another; the Buddhas manifest their bodies, complete with all the marks and secondary signs, sitting beneath the King of Trees and expounding the profound, most supreme Dharma. The Bodhisattvas of that land also come to approach Śākyamuni Buddha, making offerings and serving him with incense, flowers, banners, and canopies.

The disciples of the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni likewise go there to pay homage, serve, and make offerings to him; they discourse upon the profound and wondrous Dharma with one another, mutually illuminating it without obstruction. When he speaks of non-arising, this is also so; when I speak of the foundations of mindfulness, that is also so. Regarding the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, there is no difference between us. When he speaks of suffering, emptiness, and non-self, this is also so.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke in verse:
"Observing the purity of both the internal and external, The cessation of conditions and the perception of suchness are likewise;
Throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, Their divine virtues are without distinction."
All this arises from the faculties of sentient beings, which manifest as either superior or inferior;
yet, calculating my own Buddha-body, this land is the smallest of all.
Because there were doubts among those in the assembly, I manifested transformations within the womb.
My body is like a mote of dust, now residing in the lands of other Buddhas.
The thirty-two marks are brilliant, manifesting everywhere without exception;
formerly I was the teacher of capable men, but now I am a disciple.
The Buddha-way is most vast and expansive, pure and without increase or decrease;
yet those who wish to see the Buddha’s body find that two Honored Ones do not stand together.
Those who receive instruction in this realm see the Buddha’s body in my land.
In this land there is the conflagration at the end of an eon, yet my realm suffers no destruction.
The Buddha’s power pervades all things, yet the minds of sentient beings are not one.
Listen, you gathered assembly, as I speak further of that which remains beyond this.
The Buddha-field is named Unobstructed; the Buddha’s name is Honored Ascended Immortal.
The lands increase manifold, pure and free from blemish.
The cities and palaces are all made of the seven treasures; the ground is of crystal and lapis lazuli.
In the eightfold pool of the nectar of liberation, they bathe away all defilements;
established in the state of non-obstruction, they suddenly behold the Great Radiance.
As for those Buddhas who have ascended to transcendence, do not consider them to be extraordinary beings.
Those in this assembly who wish to know: I am here as Mṛdumūrdha.
Setting this aside, there is yet another buddha-field named Niṣṭhāgata;
its Buddha is named Mahājñāna, who surpasses all bodhisattvas in measure.
In that state, there is no training in the two vehicles—neither pratyekabuddhas nor śrāvakas.
For the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, there is no desire, anger, or delusion;
when the roots are destroyed and the leaves do not grow, how much less could there be any fruit?
Endowed with the marks of a Great Man, he first rescues others and later saves himself.
Life is like the flow of five rivers; there are the five messengers and the five fetters.
The five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) gnaw and suck, as one revolves through the five realms of existence.
The seven latent tendencies are firmly entrenched, preventing one from leaving the seven realms of birth;
By practicing the eightfold noble path, one eliminates the eight types of perverse karma;
With the eightfold pure wisdom of contemplation, one washes away defilements with the water of the eight liberations.
The eight abidings and the eight bases of mastery, The conditioned path of the eight dharmas;
The dharma of suffering has nine aspects, The conduct of sentient beings in the six realms.
Ultimate mastery of the nine unhindered knowledges, Adorning the tree of the Buddha-way.
Possessing the ten powers and the fearlessnesses, he donned the armor of great compassion and vows;
grasping the sword of wisdom in his hand, he cut down the forest of fetters and afflictions.
The sentient beings of this realm are greedily attached and give rise to arrogance.
A grave illness from which a skilled physician has departed is treated with even more severe remedies;
just as a wild fire rages, burning through mountains, forests, and marshes,
driven by the great winds of the storm, when will its flames ever be extinguished?
"Now, in our world, we extensively expound great wisdom;
as for my body today, it is the Tathāgata of Great Wisdom.
At that time, Mañjuśrī had finished speaking these verses.
Innumerable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings all formed the aspiration and desire to be born in the Flower Land.
Then Mañjuśrī withdrew his supernormal powers, manifesting himself as the disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, and the extent of the lands returned to its former state.

Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Eightfold Holy Fast of the Noble Ones. *The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb*, Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Eightfold Holy Fast of the Noble Ones. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa). In the past, under former Buddhas, he had cultivated the roots of myriad virtues and subdued the enmity of Māra. Through skillful means and transformations, he adorned Buddha-lands; he practiced patience for incalculable eons, never failing in his resolve for forbearance nor neglecting his practice of dhyāna. Amidst the great assembly, he let out a lion’s roar, walking alone through the three realms and ascending or descending at will. There was nowhere he could not enter, responding to circumstances with boundless adaptability; he could cause mountains, rivers, and stone walls to all become the seven treasures.

He provided the four requisites to the poor so that they lacked for nothing; he understood the contemplation of emptiness and the purity of the *dharmatā*; he discerned the rules of decorum throughout the three periods of time as being like illusions, transformations, reflections in a mirror, mirages in the heat, and echoes in the air.

Having fully accomplished the foundation of his retinue and maintained the prohibitive precepts without transgressing even a hair’s breadth, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How wonderful, World-Honored One!

The transformations manifested by the Tathāgata were all-pervasive; devas, nāgas, humans, and ghosts all arrived at the site of enlightenment. Among the sentient beings of the realm of space, as well as those born from wombs or through transformation, those who were delivered and saved were beyond measure.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will distinguish the good and evil conduct, as well as the dignified demeanor and prohibitive precepts, of the six realms of existence; may he explain them in detail—good in the beginning, middle, and end—so that those who have not yet studied may study, and those who do not yet know may come to know.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Jñānakośa: “Excellent, excellent!
You are able to inquire about the profound meaning of the Tathāgata; I shall now distinguish for you the destinies of good and evil precepts.”
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!

In the past, at one time, for incalculable kalpas, I was the King of the Golden-Winged Birds (Garuḍa). My palace of seven treasures had a rear garden and bathing pool, both made entirely of the seven treasures; I sported in the gardens and pavilions with a mind that attained mastery, and my conduct and laws were like those of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
The women of the inner palace were like celestial beings; every hundred thousand million kalpas, they would enter the sea to seek dragons for food.

At that time, there was a spontaneously born dragon prince in the sea who, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, observed the eightfold precepts of the Tathāgata’s fast: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely or frivolously, not encouraging the drinking of intoxicants, not listening to singing, dancing, or music, not using perfumes, flowers, or cosmetics, not using high or wide beds, and not eating at improper times—thus upholding these eight dharmas of the noble ones.

At that time, the body of the Golden-Winged Bird King was eight thousand yojanas long, with each of his left and right wings measuring four thousand yojanas; the great ocean was three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand li in length and breadth.

The garuḍa strikes the water with its wings to seize a nāga; before the water has even closed over him, it seizes the nāga and flies out. It is the nature of the garuḍa that when it wishes to eat a nāga, it first swallows it from the tail. To the north of Mount Sumeru there is a great iron tree called Mahāpariṣaṇḍa, sixteen thousand *li* in height. Having seized the nāga and flown there intending to devour it, the garuḍa searches for the nāga’s tail but cannot find its location, and thus a day and night pass.
Tomorrow, the dragon will emerge with its tail and say to the garuḍa:
"I am the very one who was born by transformation; if I have not observed the eightfold precepts of the fast, you may reduce me to ashes."
Upon hearing this, the garuḍa repented and reproached himself, saying:
"The Buddha's majestic spiritual power is exceedingly profound and immeasurable.
My palace is not far from here; let us go there together to enjoy ourselves."
The dragon then followed the garuḍa to the palace to observe it. [He thought:

"These attendants here have not heard the Tathāgata’s Dharma of the Eightfold Precepts; I only pray that you will instruct them in the prohibitions and dignified conduct so that, after their lives end, they may be reborn among humans."
At that time, the dragon prince fully instructed him in the dharmas of the precepts and recitations; he then spoke these verses in the palace of the bird king:
"The palaces and mansions of the seven jewels, Adorned and supremely joyful;
Yet with conduct fulfilled but precepts incomplete, One receives this body of a *garuḍa*."
I am a prince of the nāgas, who practiced the path for seventy thousand kalpas;
yet by piercing a tree leaf with a needle, I violated the precepts and took the form of a nāga.
I am not a nāga born from a womb, nor one born from moisture, nor one born from an egg.
Turning back from regression, you shall cause the assembly of the Buddha-dharma to flourish.
Now that you have received the eight precepts, transform your kinsmen and followers;
by observing the prohibitions without transgression, you will surely be reborn in a good realm.
My palace is within the ocean waters, And it is likewise composed of the seven treasures:
Maṇi jewels, crystal beads, Moon-bright pearls, gold, and silver.
You may follow me there to behold The performance of Buddha-works.
"Furthermore, it increases the roots of goodness, moistening and nourishing them everywhere.
At that time, the garuḍa heard what the nāga prince had said and received the eightfold precepts of the fast.
He spoke these words himself:
"From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas.

Once the retinue of the garuḍas had received the three refuges, they went from the dragon prince to the palace in the ocean. Within that palace was a stūpa made of the seven treasures, containing the profound treasury of all dharmas taught by the Buddhas; there were also separate caskets of the seven treasures filled with Buddhist sūtras, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the dhāraṇī-samādhis. Upon seeing the dragon prince and the various dragon maidens, he made offerings of fragrant flowers, prostrated, and served them, just as if it were the Nandanavana golden palace in the heavens, no different at all.
The dragon prince said to the garuḍa:
"I have received this dragon body; my karmic lifespan is not yet exhausted, and I have never killed living beings or disturbed the waters.
At that time, the dragon prince further addressed the garuḍa in verse:
"Killing is unwholesome conduct; it diminishes one's lifespan and leads to an untimely death.
Like a dew-insect upon a blade of grass, its life ends as soon as it sees the light."
Upholding the precepts and honoring the Buddha’s words, one attains rebirth in the Heaven of Long Life;
accumulating merit and virtue over successive kalpas, one does not fall into the realm of animals.
Though now possessing the body of a dragon, one’s conduct remains pure through the power of preceptual virtue.
"Even though you have fallen among the six classes of domestic animals, you must surely hope for your own deliverance.

When the dragon prince spoke this verse, the hearts of the dragon prince and the dragon princess were opened and their minds were liberated; after their lives ended, they were all destined to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Zhiji:

"In my past lives, I fully perfected the virtue of the precepts through my practice, thereby attaining the state of a bodhisattva. My manifestations are sovereign and penetrate everywhere; I enter among the garuḍas, I enter among the dragon sons, and I enter among the fish, turtles, tortoises, and crocodiles—such are my transformations."

Chapter 29: The Five Joys The Bodhisattva’s Abiding in the Womb Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Nine: The Five Joys At that time, the World-Honored One observed the thoughts within the minds and consciousnesses of sentient beings:

“If you wish to know the places where the Tathāgata has passed through—having once been born among the garuḍas and received the instructions of dragon sons, thereby delivering immeasurable and incalculable numbers of beings—is this all, or is there more beyond this?”
"I wish to hear its meaning.
The Buddha, knowing what was in the minds of the sentient beings, was about to manifest the dharmas of body, speech, and mind through which he had originally performed his practices.
"O sons and daughters of good family!
Listen to what I say.

Long ago there was Śakra, Lord of the Devas; since he passed away, countless kalpas have elapsed, yet his celestial merit has remained spontaneous. Among all the Śakras of the trichiliocosm, he was the most honored and supreme."
The Asura King Rāhula begot a daughter who was upright and beautiful, fully endowed with the sixty-four feminine arts.

Her gait and movements never failed to observe proper decorum; her face was like the color of peach blossoms, the breath from her mouth was like the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and her body emitted the scent of gośīrṣa sandalwood. She was neither tall nor short, neither white nor black, neither fat nor thin—she was fully endowed with all feminine qualities.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:

"The celestial maidens in my palace here are numerous, their countenances are upright and beautiful, and they are the most excellent among all the devas; yet they are not equal to those daughters of the asuras."
"Now I should assemble my hosts of troops and fight with him; thus I may obtain that woman to serve as my attendant.
Having formed this thought, he immediately summoned the various devas and discussed the matter of battle with them.
The devas said to Śakra:

"In battle, we gods will certainly not be able to match them. We should temporarily dispatch the musicians and others, who hold lapis lazuli lutes with ninety-nine strings and single-stringed lutes, to sing praises of our heaven’s immeasurable merit and the bliss of the blessings we receive."
The devas praised these words, saying they should be followed.

They immediately commanded the music-playing deva Pañcaśikha and others to prepare their musical instruments. In an instant, they vanished from the heavens; in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, they had already arrived and stood before the Asura King Pāhā.
Striking the lute to produce sound, he uttered this verse:
"I am Śakra, Lord of the Devas, A master lute-player of peerless skill;
The melody and the lyrics harmonize, And the pure sound is most exquisite."
As for the celestial pleasures of those devas, they have no thoughts of sorrow or fear;
when they think of it, food and clothing arrive, as well as the seven treasures and precious ambrosia.
There are beds of gold and silver with jade tables, and revolving mechanisms that cause the body to turn.
Beholding her music, he never tires; she is the foremost among those honored in heaven.
Now he has sent us here, wishing to speak of the practice of non-contention;
furthermore, he offers this nectar-food, seeking to form a marriage alliance.
I am the master of that palace, where wondrous jewels are beyond measure;
my retinue consists of celestial maidens, numbering more than thousands of millions.
Knowing that Vāha has a daughter, she should be given to me as my handmaid.
"If you do not see that we give it to you, our armies shall immediately set out on campaign.
When the Asuras heard these words, their fury blazed up intensely:
"This petty creature conceives such great ambitions; he truly wishes to achieve something!"
"Although I have no nectar, I have already pre-emptively filled my own belly with it;
furthermore, I possess a great host of troops, sufficient to withstand and repel you.
At that time, Pañcaśikha and the others, having heard these words, immediately returned and reported them in full to Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
At that time, the Asura King Pāpaka immediately commanded his attendants to quickly assemble the military forces, saying:
"I have a campaign to undertake; prepare everything at once, and let there be no doubt."
He then recited these verses as instructed:
"The noble and powerful Śakra, Lord of Devas, Has dispatched the messenger Pañcaśikha;
With songs and the five musical tones, He seeks me for marriage."
"Before those [Asuras] have assembled their armies, I should assemble my own forces first;
thus, by attacking them without expending much effort, we shall gain ten thousandfold for every single loss.

When the ministers and attendants of that Asura heard this instruction, they immediately assembled the fourfold army and proceeded to the slopes of Mount Sumeru. There they destroyed the palace of the Curved-Legged Devas (*Vakra-pāda*), followed by the destruction of the palace of the Wind Devas (*Vāyu-deva*), then the palace of the Horse Devas (*Aśva-deva*), and finally the palace of the Adorned Devas (*Vyūha-deva*).
At that time, there was a son of heaven named Mahābala who went to where Śakra Devānām-indra was and said:
"O Heavenly King!
You should know that the asura Pāpīyas has gathered his hosts of troops and has already destroyed the sons of heaven at the four gates."
"O Heavenly King!
What do you intend to do now?
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, recalled what he had previously recited and spoke this verse:
“By the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, they rescue and protect me from my present distress;
through patience and wisdom, they shatter anger and wrath, leading one to liberation and the state of peace and security.”
"In the past I had no sleep, but yesterday I suddenly fell asleep;
this sleep is not auspicious, for the asuras must have invaded my domain.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, recalled the virtues of the Buddha, and the asura hosts gradually retreated, entering through the four gates and the rear garden to hide within the hollows of lotus stalk fibers in the pond.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra immediately commanded his ministers:
"Quickly assemble the military forces; I wish to pursue the army of the Asuras.

At that time, Śakra’s ministers, having received the command of the Heavenly King, immediately gathered the celestial hosts and searched from the four gates, but they saw only swords, armor, bows, and arrows lying on the ground; they did not see the host of the Asuras.

Advancing further and further, he entered directly into the palace of the asuras. There he saw several tens of millions of asura maidens, including the asura woman Vāhā, yet he did not see the body of the asura king himself; taking these hosts of maidens with him, he returned to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace.
At that time, the asuras and others, seeking mercy and taking refuge, addressed Śakra Devānām Indra:

"We were foolish and deluded, not knowing that the supernatural power of the Buddha’s disciples was so magnificent. Our ancestors have long revered the Tathāgata, and we have heard that the Buddha possesses the precept of not taking what belongs to others."
"Today, King Śakra has filled the celestial palace with all my kinsmen; this is not the practice of those who are disciples of the Buddha.
Upon hearing these words, Śakra was despondent and unhappy, thinking:
"Asura, these words testify that I have violated the precept against taking what is not given. I would rather uphold the prohibitions and refrain from theft."
He immediately returned the women to them.
At that time, the Asura King offered his most cherished daughters to Śakra, the Lord of Devas;
Śakra, in turn, gave exquisite nectar to the Asuras.

The asuras harmonize with the devas to practice virtue together: they do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not deceive, do not drink alcohol, do not use perfumes, flowers, or cosmetics, and do not eat at improper times; they uphold the Three Refuges and the Dharma of the Tathāgata.

"In the past, throughout countless lifetimes, I acted as a Wheel-Turning Sage King; in countless lifetimes, I acted as Śakra, Lord of the Devas; and in countless lifetimes, I acted as Brahmā, King of the Gods."

To uphold the noble and holy Eightfold Precepts of the Fast is to overcome difficulties and rescue oneself from calamity. Even if the four continents were filled with flames like those at the end of an eon, if one single-mindedly takes refuge and invokes the name of the Tathāgata while observing the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast, even if one throws oneself into those flames, they cannot burn; if one is in water that fills [the world], the water cannot drown them. Those who observe the Eightfold Precepts are the parents of all Buddhas.

Chapter 30: The Kinnara Chapter. In the *Bodhisattvagārbha-sūtra*, the thirtieth chapter, the Kinnara Chapter: At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Śraddhāvimukta. In the past, during incalculable, asankhyeya kalpas, he had been a king of the kinnaras. To the north of Mount Sumeru, beyond Mount Vaiḍūrya; to the north of Mount Vaiḍūrya, beyond the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*); and to the north of the Iron Ring Mountains, there was a Great Black Mountain, where the kinnara king ruled and transformed the beings.

In the past, there were countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet [in that place] one neither beheld them nor heard their Dharma, nor was there any teaching by the assembly of noble ones, and it was not illuminated by the light of the sun, moon, or stars.
By virtue of the retribution for a single act of giving accumulated through past merit, he dwells in a palace of the seven treasures and enjoys an exceedingly long life.
Why is this? Because in his former human existence, he encountered a fertile field of merit when a great elder constructed a stūpa and temple for the Buddha.

This Kinnara offered a pillar for a shrine to complete the construction of a temple, and further gave pure food to the craftsmen; when his life ended and his lifespan was exhausted, he became a Śūlabhaṭa spirit, dwelling between two mountains within a palace and residence spontaneously formed of the seven treasures.

Formerly, when he lived among humans, his wealth was immeasurable. Once, there was a śramaṇa who, at midday, carried his alms bowl to beg for food. When his wife saw the śramaṇa begging at her door, she immediately lifted up some rice and gave it as an offering.
When the elder saw his wife giving food to the śramaṇa, he immediately became enraged and said:
"Why does this beggar stare at my wife? I shall cause this man's hands and feet to be destroyed!"
After his life ended, he received this hideous form and remained without hands or feet for eighty-four kalpas. While in the human world, he studied the methods of the *ṛṣis* in deep mountains;

he recited and practiced incantations (*mantra*) capable of moving the sun and moon, turning night into day and day into night. In the space of a single breath, he could spit out gold, silver, and the seven treasures; he could cause withered trees to sprout branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit; he could cause the waters of the ocean to dry up; he was not burned by fire; his body could fly; his eyes could see through all things and he possessed the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa-anusmṛti*); he knew the minds of others, heard sounds from afar, and had five hundred disciples as his retinue.

I have heard that a Buddha has appeared in the world, whose name is Pure Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. He proclaims the subtle and wondrous Dharma, excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, possessing great compassion and impartiality, and his meritorious achievements are immeasurable.
I led my disciples out from the deep mountains, and as we were flying over the bathing pool in the rear garden of the royal palace, I saw the court ladies bathing in the pool.
I and my disciples, upon seeing women, conceived thoughts of lustful attachment; we all lost our supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and immediately fell into the garden.
At that time, because of my anger, I came to seek out the Buddha and thereby lost my supernormal powers.
At that time, the assembly of female attendants saw five hundred men all within the garden; they immediately went in to inform the king, who commanded his attendants:
"Bring those men here; I wish to question them."
He then led them to the king. The king asked, "Who are you?"

He replied, “We are practitioners of the Way who study immortality in the mountains. There we recite and practice incantations and arts by which we can move the sun and moon, making night into day and day into night, and even hear sounds from afar; we have five hundred disciples and followers.”

I heard that a Buddha had appeared in the world, named Pure Light (Vimalaprabha). I led my disciples out from the deep mountains and, while flying over the royal palace’s rear garden pond, I saw various court ladies bathing in the pool.
"I and my disciples saw a woman and conceived a lustful attachment; we all lost our supernormal powers and immediately fell into this garden.
Then the king said to them, "How long has it been since you have been practicing the way of the immortals in these deep mountains?"
He replied, "Twenty-two minor kalpas.
The king asked again:
"Having studied the Way for accumulated kalpas, my mind was like dead ashes—unmoving and unshakable. How could it be that through a lustful mind I have lost my supernormal powers?
He replied, "Originally, I believed the True Way was the foremost in spiritual power, such that one could leap and submerge at will and everything one thought of would be accomplished."
"I did not expect that today you would suddenly lose the Way and feel shame before the Sage King, subjecting yourself to his punishments. The King told him:

"You originally studied the Way for twenty-two minor kalpas; though your body was withered and your mind exhausted, what you practiced was not true. You were like a foolish and deluded person seeking treasure in the air; regarding the Dharma of the True Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), you failed to attain its true mark (*lakṣaṇa*)."
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, whom you seek as your teacher, is currently staying nearby on Mount Yugandhara.
I shall lead you all to the Buddha's presence; whatever the Buddha may say, you should practice it accordingly."

At that time, the Great King immediately prepared his carriage adorned with peacock feathers and jewels, assuming the fivefold majestic deportment, and set out for Mount Yugandhara together with his retinue and five hundred practitioners of the way.

The king immediately descended from his carriage, unsheathed his sword, removed his parasol, and retreated five paces to dismount from his royal insignia; he then approached the Buddha on foot, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the king withdrew slightly from his seat for a moment and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“These five hundred men have been practicing the arts of the immortals in the mountains for twenty-two minor kalpas. Hearing that a Buddha had appeared in the world, they wished to come and see him; however, after flying over the inner palace, they became greedily attached to sensual desires and lost their supernormal powers.”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so that they may restore their five supernormal powers.
The Buddha told the Great King:

“The roots of goodness cultivated by these five hundred men were completed only to be destroyed; they never reached ultimate fruition. Originally, when they were householders, they spoke with anger to a bhikṣu who was begging for alms, saying:”
"May you be without hands or feet.

For countless kalpas, he served as the King of the Chest (Vakṣasthala-deva) between the Great Iron Ring Mountains and the Black Mountains; although he received retribution there where neither sun nor moon shines, it was because he had previously given a pillar from a monastery to others while among humans.

Because he gave the gift of a single offering to a Pratyekabuddha, he later obtained a human body and studied the arts of the immortals in the mountains; however, as his lustful mind grew intense, he lost his supernormal powers. This causal connection has existed for a long time and is not something that began only now.

When these five hundred people pass away from their lives in this world, they shall all be reborn in the presence of the Buddha Aṅgīrasa; that Buddha will explain to them the twelve links of dependent origination regarding birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Suffering, the absence of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the fruit of the Path—all are likewise thus.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the King’s mind was opened and liberated; he also desired to be born in the presence of the Buddha Aṅgīrasa.
At that time, the king and the five hundred rishis rose from their seats, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed. Chapter Thirty-one:

The Fragrant Sound Deity. In the *Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-one, "The Fragrant Sound Deity," at that time the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembled multitude, entered the meditative concentration of the formless samādhi, delivering sentient beings according to their various voices.
"In the past, when I was a gandharva in the human realm, I ruled over one Jambudvīpa, two Jambudvīpas, and even as many as countless Ganges-sands of Jambudvīpas."

The men and women of their retinue take incense as food, and all their clothing and ornaments are permeated with fragrance; they may be born in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, Aparagoyānī, or Pūrvavideha, and wherever they are born, they become Kings of Fragrant Sound, living for one kalpa, two kalpas, three kalpas, or even for incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
They recognize the existence of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, yet their minds remain constantly distant from them and do not draw near. Why is this?
