Because they are greedily attached to the five pleasures, taking delight in fine fragrances; amidst those fine fragrances, they hear no other sounds, but only the songs, praises, and playful music of the five desires, remaining unsatiated day and night.
A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), who had previously cultivated roots of goodness, emerged from the earth appearing as a person with only half his body visible, and addressed me, saying:
"Is this place pleasant? Why do you remain so attached to it?"
This is not the practice of true purity; one may attain a state of peace only by removing the incense and perfumes, for this fragrance is a calamity, an illusion, and a transformation.
"Now that the Buddha is in the world, you may go to receive his teachings; you shall obtain pure fragrance that pervades all directions.
Upon hearing this, the Deva King Gandharva was filled with supreme joy and exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Good Friend!
You wish to guide me and show me the pure incense; now is precisely the right time.
Where is the Buddha?"
"Let us go together to pay our respects.
At that time, the Earth-dwelling goddess Vast-Stride (Prithivī) addressed the Gandharva goddess with this verse:
"The Tathāgata, free from all attachments, Now dwells within the southern realm;"
While in the womb, he maintains pure contemplation; his retinue is beyond measure.
They burn all manner of exquisite incenses and hang silk streamers, flower canopies, and banners, making offerings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Pervading the realms of the ten directions, all who smell this fragrance shall attain the unsurpassed path.
Having gone to Jambudvīpa, they single-mindedly take refuge in the Honored One.
They shall behold the Buddha face-to-face;
each, according to their original practice, shall attain the Way without leaving their seats upon hearing the meaning of the three phrases.
The eighteen unique qualities and the marks and signs of a Great Man—
these you shall surely attain in the future.
With a body so supple it receives no dust, you shall possess the wisdom and concentration of the Dharma-body.
You shall fully attain them all.
With a right mind, do not give rise to doubt; being courageous and without cowardice, you will soon reach the lion’s stride.
Fully understanding that emptiness is natural, one realizes that the eye-consciousness has no inherent nature as form;
by removing oppositions, one does not create defilements.
In the present, the future, and the intermediate, one attains the pure threefold supernormal knowledge.

One who upholds the unimpeded Dharma perceives impermanence and the absence of pleasure; though one has committed unwholesome deeds throughout kalpas, the fire of wisdom burns them away in the snap of a finger.
Gold, silver, jewels, and lapis lazuli—these four treasures that form Mount Sumeru—[are likewise consumed].
Though consumed by the fires at the end of an eon, the retribution of one's actions cannot be extinguished.
The Tathāgata dwells in the world to transform others; out of compassion for them, he does not act for his own sake.
Wherever and in whatever state one is born, it is all due to the fetters and attachments of human beings.
As when a person shoots into the void, the arrow, having exhausted its momentum, returns to the ground;
so it is with making offerings to various fields of merit—one need not select only the worthy or the holy.
It is also like taking poison: one seeks relief everywhere for the ailment.
The poisonous vapors grow ever more intense, and his life will end before long.
Having previously encountered a virtuous friend who bestowed upon him the ingredients for an antidote,
he proceeds without discrimination until he eventually encounters the method for the antidote.
"Practicing generosity and performing meritorious deeds, Without discriminating between high and low;
This merit is praised by the noble ones, And is most honored as the foremost.

At that time, having heard the words of the earth goddess who had emerged from the ground, the King of the Gandharvas experienced the opening of his heart and the liberation of his mind, and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the earth.

"You have been my teacher, transforming me from a childlike ignorance; yet I am now deluded and foolish, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood. I accept my repentance as one who is as ignorant as a fool.

At that time, the Earth Deity emerged from the earth, manifesting the Buddha’s golden body adorned with the thirty-two marks and emitting great radiance. By means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he transported the deity Gandharvasvara to the womb for observation, while none among the assembled multitude were aware of it.
The Buddha addressed those gathered in the assembly:

"Since incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas past, I have been able to become large or small, entering the subtle without obstruction. At times I have taught and transformed beings throughout the kalpas in the heavens; at times I have taken the place of others among human beings to undergo suffering; and at times I have been among animals, hungry ghosts, and those in hell, manifesting divided bodies to teach and transform, entering everywhere without exception."

At that time, the King of Fragrant Sound and his retinue of seven hundred and twenty billion beings immediately resolved upon the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment] and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.

Chapter 32: The Earth Deity. *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb*, Chapter Thirty-Two: The Earth Deity. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Shan-ye (Good Karma). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to ask about my doubts; if you will grant me leave, I shall venture to speak.”
The Buddha said to Shan-yeh:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall analyze each point for you one by one.
Shan-yeh addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One?
Among the six great elemental spirits, which is the most excellent:
earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, caused the earth deity to leap forth from the earth and stand upon the earth-element; the water deity to leap forth from the water and stand within the water; the fire deity to leap forth from the fire and stand within the fire; the wind deity to leap forth from the wind and stand within the wind; the space deity to leap forth from space and stand within space; and the consciousness deity to leap forth from consciousness and stand within consciousness.
The Buddha told Shan-ye:
"Ask these six deities yourself.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Shan-ye questioned the Earth Deity:
"Among the six great elements, are you the most excellent?
The Earth Deity replied,
"Among the six deities, I am the most preeminent."
Why is this so? All things produced—the mountains, rivers, stones, walls, trees, flowers, and fruits—all abide by depending upon me.
All sentient beings who possess form exist by depending on me; for this reason, I am the most sublime.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta asked the Water Deity,
"Among the six deities, are you the most excellent?
The Water Deity replied:
"Among the six deities, I am the most excellent. Why is this?

If there were no water, the earth would become parched and dry, lacking all moisture; grasses, trees, flowers, and fruits would all wither away, and all classes of sentient beings and those possessing physical form would surely die of thirst."
"For this reason, I am the most excellent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Karmasena next asked the Fire Deity:
"Among the six deities, are you the most excellent?"
The Fire God replied:
"Among the six deities, I am the most excellent. Why is this so?"
If there were no fire, how could the myriad things that grow and flourish reach maturity?
If one were to encounter frost, hail, ice, cold, thunder, or lightning, all sentient beings with physical forms would freeze to death. For this reason, I am the most supreme.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Karmasena next questioned the Wind Deity:
"Among the six deities, are you the most excellent?
The Wind Deity replied:
"Among the six spirits, I am the most excellent. Why is this?

If there were no wind, trees, flowers, fruits, roots, sprouts, stems, and nodes would not reach maturity. For all sentient beings with physical forms, their advancing, retreating, moving, and shaking are all due to my wind. For this reason, I am the most excellent."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Karmaprasiddhi next asked the deity of space:
"Among the six deities, are you the most excellent?
The deity of space replied:
"Among the six spirits, I am the most excellent. Why is this?

Mountains, rivers, stone walls, trees, flowers, fruits, and all things that possess form—whether moving or stationary—I am able to contain them within myself, allowing them to become harmonious and unimpeded as they come and go. For this reason, I am the most excellent."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Karmasena next questioned the consciousness-deity (vijñāna-deva):
"Among the six deities, are you the most excellent?
The consciousness-deity replied:
"Among the six deities, I am the most excellent. Why is this? These five great deities are my servants, and I am their king.

Whether they move forward or stop, whether they act well or ill, I know when they should avoid what is to be avoided and when they should approach what is to be approached; they are all blind and obscured, while I serve as their eyes. For this reason, I am the most excellent."
At that time, the Earth Deity addressed the Bodhisattva Śubhakarma, saying: "This is not so. Why is that?"
One is constantly deceived and deluded by the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*), which does not show the direct path: when I desire firmness, it instead gives me softness;

at times when softness is required, it instead gives me firmness. When I wish to go south, it leads me to the north. Among all thieves, none surpasses the consciousness-spirit; its self-proclamation as "king" is simply not so.
At that time, the Water Deity addressed the Bodhisattva Śubhakarma, saying:
“What the consciousness-deity has spoken is not so. Why is this?

Water can moisten and cause all things to grow; yet my nature requires coldness, whereas [this] provides me with heat, burning and consuming me until it is entirely gone and the nature of coldness is forever lost. Deceived by consciousness, for this reason, the claim that it is consciousness is false.
At that time, the Fire God addressed the Bodhisattva Śubhakarma, saying:
"The statement regarding consciousness is incorrect. Why is this so?"
Fire can ripen things and also provide illumination; trees, flowers, and fruits grow and mature according to the seasons. If there were no fire, upon what would consciousness rely?
For this reason, the claim regarding consciousness is incorrect.
At that time, the Wind Deity addressed the Bodhisattva Śubhakarma, saying:
"The statement regarding consciousness is incorrect. Why is this so?"
All things grow, move, come, go, advance, retreat, and fluctuate; consciousness restrains them within itself so that they do not shift or turn.
For this reason, the claim regarding consciousness is incorrect.
At that time, the goddess Ākāśā addressed the Bodhisattva Śubhakarmā, saying:
“The statement regarding consciousness is incorrect. Why is this so?”

The emptiness of self contains all phenomena without exception; the coming and going, the advancing and retreating of the myriad things are all unimpeded within this emptiness of self. If it were not empty, upon what would consciousness rely?
"For this reason, the statement regarding consciousness is incorrect.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the Bodhisattva Śubhakārin:
"Does this discourse on the six great elements possess any meaningful content?"
Is it without meaning? Is it with flavor?
Or is it without flavor?
"Is there a meaning to words,
or is there no meaning to words?
The Bodhisattva Shan-ye addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is as if the five great elements are each equal. Why is this so?

If the earth element is predominant and the water element is deficient, it is not accomplished; if the water element is predominant and the fire element is deficient, it is not accomplished; if the fire element is predominant and the wind element is deficient, it is not accomplished; if the wind element is predominant and the space element is deficient, it is not accomplished; if the space element is predominant and the consciousness element is deficient, it is not accomplished; and if the five elements are equal yet consciousness does not differentiate them, it is not accomplished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śubhakarma spoke in verse:
“The consciousness-principle is a formless dharma, taking the five great elements as its home;
it discriminates between good and evil deeds, and distinguishes between the true and the false.”
"Consciousness indicates the path of goodness, leading one forever to the secure and peaceful way;
consciousness is the sixth king, and the other great elements are not its equal.
The Buddha told Śubhakārin:
"Those questions you have asked are all due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
At that time, one billion seven hundred million sentient beings among the assembly understood the profound Dharma and all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

33. Chapter on Human Qualities, Part Three. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Dharmamudrā. Having heard the Tathāgata speak of the six great elements and how sentient beings receive the form of the five aggregates, he analyzed the internal and external and understood them to be empty and non-existent.
A doubt arose within his mind:
"Consciousness is a state of distracted thought and not a true reality.
Who, then, is this person?"
"What is this person?
From what is the person born?
The Buddha told Dharma-Seal Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
That which you have asked is all sustained by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas. Why is this so?

The inconceivable provisional names and designations of the human essence of the countless *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sand Buddhas of the past, as well as those of the countless *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sand Buddhas of the future, cannot be fathomed by the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the two vehicles.
Listen attentively now, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall explain it to you in full detail and distinction.
It is not as one might think regarding the production of the various kinds of sentient beings in Jambudvīpa within this Sahā world;
such is not the case. Why is this?

Because they do not possess the nature of reality, they are not of the human race. Those of Pūrvavideha are likewise not of the human race; those of Uttarakuru are likewise not of the human race; and those of Aparagoyānī are likewise not of the human race. With the exception of the lands of the Buddhas Amitāyus and Akṣobhya, with the exception of the Buddhas at the limits of space in the adorned buddha-fields, and with the exception of the bodhisattvas seated here today, all others are entirely not of the human race.
Why is this? From the beginning until the attainment of Buddhahood, having never committed evil in the interval, these are the seeds of humanity;
just as one who cultivates the karma of body and speech is called a seed of humanity compared to one who does not so cultivate them.
Those who receive the Three Refuges where others do not are called the seed of humanity.
Those who uphold the Five Precepts where others do not are called the seed of humanity.
Those who practice the Ten Wholesome Deeds where others do not are called the seed of humanity.
One who is progressing toward the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*) while others are not so progressing—this is called a "seed of humanity.
One who has attained stream-entry while others have not—this is called a "seed of humanity.
One who is progressing toward the stage of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) while others are not so progressing—this is called a "seed of humanity."
One who has attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin when others have not is called a person of noble lineage.
One who is heading toward the stage of Anāgāmin when others are not so headed is called a person of noble lineage.
One who has attained the stage of Anāgāmin when others have not is called a person of noble lineage.
One who is training for arhatship but has not yet trained is called a person of human seed;
one who has attained arhatship but had not previously attained it is called a person of human seed;
one who is training for pratyekabuddhahood but has not yet trained is called a person of human seed.
Those who attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha while others do not are called "seed of humanity.
Those who are directed toward the path of the Buddha while others are not are called "seed of humanity.

Those who attain the path of the Buddha while others do not are called "seed of humanity"; therefore, they are titled the Honored One among Men, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, and the Bhagavān—these are called the seed of humanity.
The Buddha told Dharma-Seal Bodhisattva:
“Listen well now! Those Buddhas of the past, in relation to the present and the future, are called the human seed.”
The present in relation to the future is called the human lineage;
the future in relation to the past and the present is called the human lineage.
Among the phenomena of the three periods of time, the present is the foremost in relation to both the past and the future.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is able to practice the dharmas of the past and the future within the present.
Why is he superior?

The past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is spontaneous. It is not the case that the past can extinguish the present or the future, nor can the future extinguish the past or the present.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past Left behind teachings to deliver sentient beings;
They distinguished the fundamental natures of people— Superior, middling, and inferior, subtle and wondrous."
The present Most Victorious Buddha, clear regarding the past and knowing the future, has eradicated all fetters of the past and future; he alone shines like the brilliance of the sun.
Sentient beings who practice austerities—whether two-footed or four-footed;
For them he preached the Dharma of ambrosia, filling them and eliminating all conceptualizations.
The ten wholesome paths of action for the devas range from one to twenty-two;
among those ascending to the heavens and those descending to the non-gods (asuras), there are differences in their merit.
The Tathāgata is endowed with all marks; his practice of goodness is without flaw.
He has accumulated merit like Mount Sumeru; his pure conduct is stainless.
If someone should give rise to slander, saying that the Buddha’s way is not the true path;
Upon death, one enters the Avīci Hell, where even all the Buddhas cannot provide salvation.
The breath from the mouth reeks with a rank and putrid odor, and the limbs burn with the fever of afflictions;
as evil thoughts thus blaze ever more fiercely, this is due to the sin of slandering [the Dharma].
Practicing goodness and cultivating merit, the consciousness-mind proceeds toward a favorable realm;
like a person entering a pond to bathe, they become pure and free from dust and grime.
The Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have severed the cycle of birth, ensuring it shall never arise again.
Not dwelling on the notion of a self, he has departed from the suffering of the five realms.
Having practiced the Dharma as originally taught by the Buddhas and obtained their seal of approval, he has now become the Honored One among men; therefore, he is titled the God among Gods.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamudrā:
“This is what is called the lineage of humans.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Dharmamudrā rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
You have eloquently expounded this meaning.
As for us in this assembly, we are not of the human species in the presence of the Tathāgata.”
"How does one manifest as being born into the lineage of humans?
The Buddha told Dharma-Seal Bodhisattva:

"To understand that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, and to neither perceive 'that' nor 'this,' nor see the distinction between self and other—this is called being born into the lineage of humans."

To observe that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without past, future, or present, and to understand that the nature of phenomena is empty, quiescent, and non-dual—this is called a person of noble lineage.
Regarding the four fruits of the spiritual path, whether there is one who achieves them or one who does not, to see neither unity nor duality—this is called a person of noble lineage.

Regarding all phenomena characterized by marks, one perceives neither adornment nor non-adornment; understanding that they are empty and quiescent, neither one nor two—this is called a person of noble lineage.

The purity of the Buddha-land consists in the removal of desire, anger, and delusion; therein one perceives neither purity nor impurity, for both matters are empty—this is called the lineage of humans.

To discern the nature of the path through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, wherein there is both success and failure, yet not to perceive the mundane world as having persons or being devoid of persons—this is called the lineage of persons.

To give rise to a vast and solemn vow not for one's own sake, to establish sentient beings securely in fearlessness, and to perceive neither abiding nor non-abiding—seeing these two matters as equal—is called the lineage of humans.

Discerning meditative concentration with a mind free from defilement and attachment, maintaining a resolve as empty and immovable, neither perceiving concentration nor non-concentration—this is called a person of noble lineage.

To guide sentient beings with wrong views toward the wholesome state, cleansing the defilements of the mind through the Eightfold Noble Path, while neither perceiving what is right nor what is not right—this is called a person of true lineage.

Among the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—one whose resolve for the Way is firm and free from attachment, who perceives no transgression or non-transgression in the observance of precepts, is called a person of true lineage.

Such a Dharma-seal regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata brings benefit and welfare to sentient beings; it constitutes a repayment of the Buddha's kindness, and the cultivation of all merits will not be in vain or discarded.

At that time, one billion seven hundred million sentient beings among those in the assembly all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, cultivating the human lineage and the practice of non-retrogression.

Chapter 34: On Practice. *The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb*, Chapter Thirty-Four: On Practice. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Zaoxing (Creating Practice). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent!"
“World-Honored One! You have skillfully explained the lineage of persons as being neither prior, nor posterior, nor in between.

By what means can one know the retribution for karmic actions? Is it that the past body is not the present one? Or that the future body is not the past one? Or that the present body is neither past nor future? Or that one performs an action internally and receives the retribution externally? Or that one performs an action externally and receives the retribution internally? Or that a person of ordinary capacity performs an action and a *srotāpanna* receives the retribution? Or that a *srotāpanna* performs an action and a *sakṛdāgāmin* receives the retribution? Or that a *sakṛdāgāmin* performs an action and an *anāgāmin* receives the retribution? Or that an *anāgāmin* performs an action and an *arhat* receives the retribution?”

There may be sentient beings who attain the samādhi of loving-kindness but not that of compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity; there may be sentient beings who attain compassion but not loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, or equanimity; there may be sentient beings who attain sympathetic joy but not loving-kindness, compassion, or equanimity; and there may be sentient beings who attain equanimity but not loving-kindness, compassion, or sympathetic joy.
There may be sentient beings who, from the stage of ordinary persons, do not proceed toward the stage of faith or the stage of dharma, yet attain the fruit of srotāpanna;
there may be sentient beings who do not proceed toward the stage of faith, the stage of dharma, or the fruit of srotāpanna, yet attain the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin;
there may be sentient beings who do not proceed toward the stage of faith, the stage of dharma, the fruit of srotāpanna, or the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, yet attain the fruit of anāgāmin.

There may be sentient beings who do not proceed toward the stage of faith, the stage of dharma, the stage of srotāpanna, the stage of sakṛdāgāmin, or the stage of anāgāmin, but instead take up arhatship;

or there may be sentient beings who do not proceed toward the stage of faith, the stage of dharma, the stage of srotāpanna, the stage of sakṛdāgāmin, the stage of anāgāmin, or the stage of arhat, but instead take up the arhatship of both [this and that].

There may be sentient beings who, having set out toward the stage of a pratyekabuddha, fall back and descend to the level of an ordinary person; or there may be sentient beings who, having set out toward arhatship, fall back and descend to the level of an ordinary person;
or there may be sentient beings who, having set out toward the stage of an anāgāmin, fall back and descend to the level of an ordinary person;
or there may be sentient beings who, having set out toward the stage of a sakṛdāgāmin, fall back and descend to the level of an ordinary person.
There may be sentient beings who, having been directed toward the stage of *srotāpanna*, fall back and descend to the level of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);

there may be sentient beings who, from the stage of Dharma (*dharmabhūmi*), fall back and descend to the level of ordinary worldlings; and there may be sentient beings who, from the stage of faith (*śraddhābhūmi*), fall back and descend to the level of ordinary worldlings—all such sentient beings harbor doubts regarding the Tathāgata.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain each point in detail, so that all those gathered here may attain sudden and clear enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Zaoxing, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
The meaning of what you have asked pertains to the future, the past, and the present; it is also the fruit of the karmic actions of all Buddhas.
I shall now explain each point in detail; listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
O Bodhisattva who has undertaken this practice!
Do you wish for the Tathāgata to speak of the karmic fruits and retributions of his deeds throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas of the past?
Do you wish for the Tathāgata to speak of the karmic retributions of practices throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas of the future?
Or do you wish for the Tathāgata to speak of the karmic retributions of practices throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas of the present?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṛtābhyāsa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Setting aside for a moment the karmic fruits and retributions of past and future actions, I wish to hear of the Tathāgata’s own manifested bodily actions and their karmic fruits.”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Kṛtācāra:
"The karmic fruits and retributions of countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past are also produced in the present.
The karmic fruits and retributions of countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the future are also produced in the present."
The karmic retribution for the deeds performed in the present is likewise caused by conditions to be experienced in the past and future;

I shall now explain this to you. In the past, I underwent countless ascetic practices—some pure, some impure; some celestial, some human. Having first sought the Way of the Buddha, my outflows were exhausted; through supernormal powers and transformations, I attained great enlightenment. I realized that the three realms are entirely suffering, and that I alone am blissful.

He practiced austerities for six years on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, consuming only one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day; this was because in a former life he had committed four verbal transgressions against a Pratyekabuddha and interrupted a single act of giving, and thus he now undergoes this retribution.

Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I have been subjected to malicious slander and verbal abuse by five hundred young brahmins, who proclaimed throughout the streets and alleys that the Buddha-way is not true.

At that time, among the people of the various kingdoms, there were those with faith and those without faith; the faithful believed in the stage of the ground and the stage of the Dharma, while the unfaithful were ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*). For such people as these, their faculties and powers were fully perfected and could not be thwarted or destroyed.
When the Buddha appears in the world, his light shines everywhere; those in the hells find relief, the hungry ghosts are satiated, and those among the animals no longer bear heavy burdens.

Just as my younger brother Devadatta struck the Buddha’s foot with a stone until blood flowed, I fled at that time to the east to Pūrvavideha, to the north to Uttarakuru, and to the west to Aparagoyānī; I further fled from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to the Thirty-two Heavens, yet this stone continued to pursue me. I fled again and returned to my original location, where I was wounded by the stone.

While I was staying in the Jyotiṣka Garden within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha, dwelling in seclusion and practicing walking meditation, there was a householder named Śrīgupta who invited me for a meal offering. I accepted his invitation and set out with Ānanda as my sole attendant.

That householder’s residence had seven successive gates, each with its own guardian. It is the constant law of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present that they accept an invitation in silence and do not accept any other invitations.
"All my disciples who have left the household life to practice the Way should act likewise.
When I arrived at that gate, the householder Śrīgupta was inside indulging himself with music and performance, forgetting my presence outside for a full day and night."
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Go out for alms while I remain here. At that time,
a horse trainer passed by the Buddha's side, and the Buddha went to him for alms.
The horse trainer said, "I have no food;
I have only some parched barley which I should offer to you.
He then took the parched barley and gave it as an offering to the Buddha, who immediately accepted and ate it.
At that time, the horse-keeper thought it was food for the Buddha.
Then there was a devaputra named Yanjing (Refined Essence) who immediately took the food away; those people who saw this thought it was food for the Buddha.
However, although the Buddha does not eat, he manifested the act of receiving food for the sake of delivering them.
In this manner, he remained within the gateway for ninety days, and Ānanda likewise went on almsround for ninety days.

Because they fail to plant roots of merit, they would fall into the evil realms. Fearing this, the Tathāgata does not allow the king, his ministers, or the elders to know that the Buddha is dwelling here. Why is this? For fear that they might give rise to arrogance and a mind of slander. If they were to hear that the Buddha is dwelling here, they would think: "The Buddha is already here; what need is there for us to go and see him? Thinking thus, they would fail to
"If the Buddha possesses no supernatural power, what can others hope for?
At that time, the householder Śrīgupta had gone out on some minor business and was wandering about when he saw the Buddha at his gate. He then asked the Buddha, "When did you arrive here?"
The Buddha told the householder:

"When you previously invited me, I came here immediately while you were enjoying yourself within. Now ninety days have already passed; I wish to return to the Divāṇa Garden, where I received from you the offering of cooked barley for my horse."
At that time, the householder Śrigupta, filled with extreme shame and remorse, prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs touching the earth:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me forgiveness for my shortcomings and allow me to repent my transgressions."
The Buddha told the householder:
"This condition has existed for a long time; it is not merely of the present.

At that time, the householder invited the Buddha into his palace and provided him with the fourfold offerings. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he was cleansed of all defilements, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.

"In the past, at one time, I was in the city of Vaiśālī not long after first attaining the Way of the Buddha. At that time, the six heretical teachers were flourishing; I had twelve hundred and fifty disciples, of whom one thousand and one had all attained arhatship with the six supernormal powers clearly perfected."

At that time, there was a woman named Ciñcā Mānavikā, a disciple of Ajita Keśakambalin. Having received her teacher’s explicit instructions, she came to the Buddha’s presence every day; outwardly she manifested the conduct of a faithful laywoman, yet inwardly she followed the teachings of a heterodox master. She moved about and frequented various places with the intent of being seen by people, using grass to gradually enlarge her belly, and later fastened a wooden bowl to her abdomen so that she appeared like a woman about to give birth.
Then the false teacher asked,
"How did you come to have this pregnancy? She replied:
"I go daily to the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama; it is because of this that I am pregnant.
The teacher then spoke with anger:
"You have deceived my disciple, who was on the verge of being reborn in the Brahma Heaven! You have brought such humiliation upon my disciple!"
At that time, the false teacher, leading his disciples along with this woman, went to where the Buddha was.
At that moment, the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma to an immeasurable multitude. When the Brahmin arrived at the Buddha’s location, he cried out in a loud voice:

"This śramaṇa Gautama has violated the precepts of celibacy; he has not truly attained the Way, yet he claims to have attained it. All the transformations he performs are mere sorcery, not the true Path."
Pointing to this woman, he said, "Did everyone not see it? I loved this woman and caused her to become pregnant.

Having spoken these words, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed himself into a yellow rat; he gnawed the cord of the bowl inside the woman's skirt, causing the bowl to fall to the ground. Everyone saw this and rebuked him, saying:
"You and your disciples have slandered and reviled the Holy One; depart from this country immediately.
"In the past, at one time, I was in the kingdom of Kimpila, practicing dhyāna and walking the Path beneath a tree for ninety days without moving from my place."

At that time, among those six teachers was one named Kātyāyana; he had a female disciple named Sundarī Nandā, who, giving rise to a heart of jealousy, sought to obstruct the Buddha’s merits in order to manifest the path of her own teacher.
The woman said,
"I can cause people to cease making offerings to the Buddha, so that my teacher's fame may spread far and wide.
At that time, harboring this treacherous intent, the woman went to the Buddha's presence every day.
After several days had passed, he killed himself and buried his body in the garden behind the vihāra.
Later, when the corpse was discovered, people claimed that the Buddha had murdered him.
This slanderous reputation spread until it became known to all the people of the country.
"In the past, on one occasion, my left side was afflicted by a wind-disorder, and I had Jīvaka treat it. Jīvaka said:
'One must require cow's milk, elephant urine, śāliśa, pippalīśāliśa, and black pepper; these should be boiled into a decoction, and if you drink it, you will be cured.'"

"In the past, at one time, while I was traveling and teaching in another village, my foot was pierced by a spear; the wound went through from top to bottom, and the pain was immeasurable. I then had Jīvaka treat it."
"In the past, at one time, I suffered from a headache so severe it was as if two Mount Sumerus were pressing down upon my head; the pain was unbearable.

Although I have now attained Buddhahood and all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, and though all virtues are universally gathered and my original practices remain imperishable, having cultivated pure conduct for incalculable eons, the karmic retribution of such deeds is difficult to escape."
"If even the body of a Buddha is thus, how much more so for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas—could they possibly escape the retribution of their actions?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to the Bodhisattva Zaoxing (造行):
"The most supreme four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), Abiding in life for countless eons."
Heaven and earth shall utterly perish, and Mount Sumeru shall become like dust;
yet karma pursues the body, leaving no place where one may hide.
I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment, peerless throughout the three realms.
Therefore, one undergoes the retribution of the nine [paths];
bound by the continuity of past deeds, I possess the power of samādhi, as indestructible as a vajra.
Yet, unable to avoid the karma of retribution, I do not abandon it nor seek to evade its consequences.
The conditions for my present life are now exhausted; from this point on, there shall be no further connection.
Forever parted from birth and death, I shall no longer perform those actions.
Many people crave the five desires and, lacking vigilance, are heedless.
In this world and in the world beyond, they constantly fall into states of sorrow.
Nirvāṇa is free from all attachment, yet he manifests conditioned phenomena;
were he not to manifest such transformations, sentient beings would be difficult to deliver.
The eightfold path of non-conditioned liberation is the way traversed by the noble sages;
it is free from all fetters and attachments, and possesses no phenomena of birth or cessation.
This path arises from the contemplation of impermanence and the reflection upon the nature of impurity.
With a single mind unmoving, one accomplishes all the marks and signs.
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are still subject to retribution even more than I;
pursued by the karma of one's own actions, where can one find escape?
The wise Śāriputra constantly practiced the virtues of the Buddha;
by descending his intestines, he attained parinirvāṇa—this is a clear and manifest realization.
Maudgalyāyana, possessed of divine power, ascended Mount Sumeru with every step.
Struck by the Brahmin Daṇḍapāṇi, his bones were shattered like mustard seeds;
yet the Arhat Sāgata subdued the Nanda dragon,
and when the time for his parinirvāṇa arrived, countless eyeballs fell from him.
The Bhikṣuṇī Suvarṇapuṣpā, whose divine virtue is unfathomable,
manifested as a Wheel-Turning King to rule over the four continents;
when she relinquished her life and entered the unconditioned, her limbs were severed by swords and blades.
The Pratyekabuddha named Prabhasa appeared in a world where no Buddha’s Dharma existed;
he lived out his full lifespan according to the ways of the world and attained parinirvāṇa in a cauldron of boiling water.
I now describe these various karmic retributions of the present.
If one were to recount the practices of the asaṃkhyeya Buddhas of the past,
from kalpa to kalpa, their karmic retributions could never be exhausted.
Furthermore, there shall be Buddhas in the future who will likewise sit upon these very seats.
One should likewise explain the retribution of karma, just as it is now without difference.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, diligent and without indolence,
should swiftly distance himself from karmic retribution and not remain in its company.

At that time, having heard these verses, the Bodhisattva Zaoxing’s hair stood on end; he no longer took pleasure in the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence, and all resolved to attain the unsurpassed state of non-retrogression.

Chapter 35: On the Abiding of the Dharma. *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb*, Chapter Thirty-Five: On the Abiding of the Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the assembled multitude was tranquil, pure, and entirely without admixture, extended his broad and long tongue to lick both ears from left to right. He emitted a great radiance that ascended to immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* lands. When sentient beings saw this light, they leaped for joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his radiance.
He addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

"Since incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas past, my body, speech, and mind have been pure and free from blemish; thus I have obtained this retribution of the light of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). This is due to my freedom from deception and falsehood."
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
“I now entrust to you these sūtras concerning the womb-birth and transformation-birth of bodhisattvas; you should proclaim and widely disseminate them.”

If there are good men or good women who recite this sutra and make offerings of incense and flowers—using powdered incense, ground incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and performing music—their merit and blessings will be exceedingly great, indeed very much so.

If there are good sons or good daughters who are unable to recite it from morning until evening, yet for as long as a finger-snap they bring this sutra to mind, their merit and blessings shall be beyond measure.

Why is this? This *Garbha-sūtra* is the parent of all Buddhas and the longest among all sūtras. The number of sentient beings transformed and delivered by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present within this *Mātṛ-garbha-sūtra* exceeds those transformed by their physical bodies by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or even hundreds of billions of times—beyond measure.
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who pay homage to, serve, and make offerings to this sutra, and who desire to see the Buddhas of the ten directions face-to-face, they should single-mindedly take refuge in them without any other thoughts; immediately they shall behold the Buddhas of the ten directions."
If there are good men or good women who make this great vow:
"I now wish to cause the hells to cease, and that hungry ghosts and animals be free from the afflictions of illness."
"Those who single-mindedly take refuge and recite this sutra shall all attain liberation from their various sufferings and afflictions.
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

"Now my causal conditions have ended and there is no further place for me to teach. This sutra shall remain in the world for perhaps a thousand years, or up to two thousand years, or even three thousand years. It shall be divided into three parts: one part is entrusted to Ānanda to deliver to my remaining disciples of the Dharma;"
One portion I shall give to the Naga King Utpalaka, Nanda;
the remaining portion, Maitreya and I shall proclaim together,
so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it, without interruption.

Maitreya! When you attain Buddhahood, you shall proclaim this sutra; all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether wriggling, breathing, crawling, or belonging to the class of humans and things—all shall receive its grace and attain complete liberation.
"Maitreya! After your parinirvāṇa, this sutra shall circulate in the world for twenty-one kalpas, after which it will cease.

If there are good men or good women who recite this sutra with undistracted minds and give rise to great, universal vows—desiring to cause all sentient beings to fulfill their aspirations together with them, to be born simultaneously in pure lands, and to serve and pay homage to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—they shall attain these things according to their wishes without hindrance."
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
“You should receive and uphold my teaching, and you should be mindful of the Buddha’s kindness.

Those who wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness should always single-mindedly receive, uphold, and make offerings to the sūtras concerning the womb-birth and transformation-birth; the merit and blessings of this cannot be fully described.”

Why is this? This scripture on birth from the womb and transformation is the treasury of all Dharma-jewels, sealed by all Buddhas. Only the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, is able to open this seal and manifest it for sentient beings.

Maitreya! You should know that regarding the profound sūtras on samādhi and dhāraṇī which I have taught from beginning to end, it would be but a minor transgression for you to forget even a single word or a single phrase.
If one forgets even a single word or a single phrase of this *Tāizhìhuà* (Womb-Transformation) Sūtra, the transgression is exceedingly great. Why is this?
Because this is the father and mother of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, as the World-Honored One spoke these words, the entire earth shook in six ways. The bodhisattvas in the assembly then said to one another:
"It has not been long since Śākyamuni Buddha departed from the dharma-nature; he will surely soon manifest again in his original form."
At that time, there were eighty-four *koṭī-nayuta* of sentient beings in the assembly, all of whom resolved to attain the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment] and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.
Then, those bodhisattvas suddenly vanished and each departed from their respective wombs or transformations to make offerings to the golden coffin and the relics of Śākyamuni Buddha.

Chapter Thirty-Six: Returning to One’s Original Form. *The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb*, Chapter Thirty-Six: Returning to One’s Original Form. At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his majestic spiritual power and remained within the golden coffin, silent and without sound, while the various devas offered worship by burning incense and scattering flowers.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa, leading five hundred disciples, came from the kingdom of Magadha to where the Buddha was; hearing that the Buddha was to enter parinirvāṇa on that very day, he wept and wailed, unable to restrain himself.

At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing with his divine ear that Kāśyapa had arrived, immediately extended both feet from within the coffin. Upon seeing this, Kāśyapa grasped them with his hands, stroking and caressing them, weeping so uncontrollably that he could not compose himself.
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke these verses in general:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; Those who are born must surely die.
Where there is no birth, there is no death; This cessation is the supreme bliss."
The people whom the Buddha has taught and delivered are now complete;
my path of practice is remote and cut off, and I deeply regret not seeing the Buddha.
The Dharma-realm is entirely empty, and the physical body shall likewise be so.
There is no aging, illness, or death; it is unconditioned and without birth.
Even one who dwells for a lifespan as vast as a hundred Ganges-sands must eventually return to extinction;
how much more so our Celestial Honored Teacher, who dwelt in the world amidst defilement?
At that time, Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples all circumambulated the golden coffin seven times and stood to one side.

Then Ānanda grasped the northwest corner of the coffin, and Nanda grasped the northeast corner; the devas attended behind them as they went straight north forty-nine paces from the twin trees to set down the golden coffin. Following the dharma of the śramaṇas, they piled up ox-head sandalwood incense upon the golden coffin;
the Brahma kings and Śakra Devānām Indra, leading the hosts of devas, scattered flowers from the midst of the air as an offering.
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa took fire in his hand and cremated the body with sandalwood fuel;
the eight great kings vied to divide the śarīra relics, each taking as much as they could according to their means to carry back and offer worship.
Chapter Thirty-Seven: On the Erection of Stūpas. *The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb*, Chapter Thirty-Seven: On the Erection of Stūpas. At that time, there were eight great kings:
King Udayana, King Mūrdhaja, King Caṇḍapradyota, and King Ajātaśatru;
as well as four commanders of armies:

The Lord of the Most Noble Army, the Lord of the Handsome Army, the Lord of the Blazing Army, and the Lord of the Vajra Army—these eight great kings contended for the śarīras and each led their hosts of troops, standing arrayed to one side.
The eight great kings each said,
"I alone should obtain the Buddha's relics.
A high minister named Upajiva admonished them, saying:
"O Kings! Do not scramble for the Buddha’s relics; you should divide them and offer worship to them all together. Why do you raise armies to wage war and punish one another?
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra manifested in human form and spoke these words to the kings:
“We deities of the heavens also ought to have a share; if we join our strength together, there will be victory or defeat. We pray you grant us a portion; do not find it difficult to do so.
Then the Dragon King Anavatapta, the Dragon King Manasvin, and the Dragon King Erapattra said to the eight kings:
“We too should have a share of the relics; if they are not granted to us, our power is sufficient to subdue you.”
Then Upagika said, "Gentlemen, please stop;
the relics should be shared together. He immediately divided them into three portions:
one portion he gave to the devas, one portion to the Dragon King, and one portion to the eight kings. The golden urn held more than one *shi* (one *dǒng*).
This minister secretly coated the interior of a jar with honey and used the jar as a measure to divide the śarīras.
The devas who obtained the śarīras returned to the heavens and immediately erected stūpas made of the seven precious substances.
The dragon obtained the śarīra and returned to his palace, where he also erected a stūpa made of the seven precious substances.
The eight kings each obtained the śarīra and returned to their respective kingdoms, where they likewise erected stūpas made of the seven precious substances.
The minister Upagupta obtained three pecks of śarīra relics along with the golden urn, for which he also erected a stūpa made of the seven precious substances.
He further erected forty-nine stūpas made of the seven precious substances for the forty-nine bushels of ash and earth.

At the place where the body was cremated, a stūpa made of the seven precious gems was erected, forty-nine fathoms in height; it was honored with incense and flowers, draped with silken banners and canopies, and the sounds of music continued without ceasing throughout the day and night.

Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, each of the stupas made of the seven treasures emitted its own radiance; some emitted light at night no different from that of the day, while others emitted light during the day no different from that of the night. The various benevolent deities who protect the stupas each came to provide guardianship, ensuring that no evil person could violate or defile them.

Chapter 38: The Chapter on the Manifestation of the Sūtra At that time, seven days and seven nights had already passed since the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa. Then Mahākāśyapa addressed the five hundred arhats: "Strike the *gandī* to assemble the multitude.

You five hundred men must all go to the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions; those who have attained arhatship and whose six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are pure and penetrating, let them all gather here in Jambudvīpa and come to the space between the twin trees."

The Buddha Śākyamuni has now relinquished his life and entered parinirvāṇa; the cremation having been completed, a stūpa made of the seven precious gems has been erected. Now, having assembled the multitude, he intends to manifest the Dharma-body of true nature.
"May you all assemble quickly to hear and receive these subtle and wondrous words.

At that time, the five hundred arhats received the instruction of Mahākāśyapa and, by means of their supernormal powers, reached the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the mere time it takes a person to bend and stretch their arm. Having gathered eight hundred and forty million arhats, they arrived at this Sahā world to listen to and receive the words of the Dharma.
At that time, seeing that the assembly had already gathered, Kāśyapa said to Upāli:
"You shall serve as the *karmadāna*; call for Ānanda to descend.
Upāli then received these instructions and called for Ānanda to descend.
"You are the Buddha’s attendant; do you not know that you currently possess a great transgression greater than ours?
Ānanda addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying, "I do not understand what great transgression I have committed before this assembly of noble ones?"
Kāśyapa said to Ānanda: "How so, Ānanda?"

Regarding the sūtras spoken by the Buddha: if there are Arhats who have attained the Way and possess the six supernormal powers with utter clarity, who cultivate the four bases of power through extensive practice and application, they can remain for the duration of a kalpa or even longer.
“Why did you remain silent and fail to answer the Buddha?
At that time, Ānanda led Anuruddha out; after a short while, he called Ānanda back forward and again questioned him in detail regarding the previous matter.
At that time, Ānanda’s mind was disordered and agitated, and he thought to himself:
"The Buddha has been in parinirvāṇa for but a short while, yet I am so ashamed!

He immediately contemplated the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path; he discerned the origin of suffering, its accumulation, its cessation, and the fruit of the path. Thereupon, before the assembly, he became an arhat, extinguishing all defilements and attaining clear and great enlightenment.

The noble assembly praised it as excellent and the devas sang in adoration; at that moment, the earth shook in six ways, and the devas scattered flowers and performed music. The physical body had entered parinirvāṇa, yet the Dharma-body appeared in the world, benefiting sentient beings and bringing vast moisture and nourishment. He then commanded Ānanda to ascend the high seat of the seven treasures.
Kāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"Regarding every single word and syllable of the Dharma spoken by the Buddha, do not allow anything to be omitted or lost.
Compile the Bodhisattva-piṭaka into one place, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka into another, and the Vinaya-piṭaka into yet another."
At that time, Ānanda raised his voice and proclaimed:
"Thus have I heard at one time, concerning the place where the Buddha resided.

Kāśyapa and the entire assembly of noble ones all shed tears and wept, unable to restrain themselves; they sighed in lamentation that old age and death are like illusions and transformations, for yesterday they saw the Buddha, yet today they speak of him as already extinguished and heard only of him as such.

When the sūtras were first translated, the *Garbha-vinirvāṇa-piṭaka* was first; the *Antarābhava-piṭaka* was second; the *Mahāyāna Vaipulya-piṭaka* was third; the *Vinaya-piṭaka* was fourth; the *Daśabhūmika Bodhisattva-piṭaka* was fifth; the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka* was sixth; the *Vajra-piṭaka* was seventh; and the *Buddha-piṭaka* was eighth. These constitute the complete collection of the sūtras and teachings of Śākyamuni Buddha.

On the eighth day of the second month he attained Buddhahood; on the eighth day of the second month he turned the Wheel of Dharma; on the eighth day of the second month he subdued Māra; and on the eighth day of the second month he entered Parinirvāṇa.
